+ Classic sci-fi: The Azra Gambit — Score: 75.9
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi (Author style: Asimov) The Azra Gambit Colonial mars is being mined by corporations who take leases on indentured labourers. The thing they are mining is Azra, a recently discovered exotic metal which accelerates radioactive decay to such a rate that it is greatly sought after for interstellar drives and weapons alike. This has created both a gold rush and an arms race as various interests vie for control and endeavour to unlock Azra's secrets. The story follows Arthur Neegan, a first generation settler and mining engineer. Upon discovering that his unassuming plot sits atop an immense Azra vein, he is subjected to a flurry of interest and scrutiny. Write the next chapter in this story, in which an armed retinue descends on Arthur's home and politely but forcefully invites him to a meeting with some unknown party off-world. The insignia look like that of the Antares diplomatic corp -- diplomatic in name only. Arthur finds himself in the centre of a political tug of war. The chapter involves a meeting with this unknown party, who makes Arthur an offer. The scene should be primarily dialogue, interspersed with vivid description & scene setting. It should sow hints of the larger intrigue, stakes & dangers. Include Asimov's trademark big-and-small-picture world building and retrofuturistic classic scifi vibe. The chapter begins with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, wondering just what he's gotten involved in. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The transfer vessel's air filtration system hums with a persistent mechanical drone. Arthur Neegan sat in a molded chair that smelled faintly of ozone, and tried to make sense of the last twelve hours. Through the porthole, Mars hung amber, its polar caps bright as cracked teeth. The ship was small, private, and too clean, marked only by a dark blue ribbon and a starburst. That emblem had been on every member of the retinue at his door. Antares Diplomatic Corps, the brass plate said. Diplomatic, he had thought, when one knocked politely and another checked his water seal. His squat hab unit, with its cracked thermal panel and sad chard tray, had become very small. The retinue entered without hurry: four men and two women in gray-blue uniforms, soft boots, and sidearms that looked like polished pipe organs. They touched everything else: his lease papers, his survey, the hand drill that had brought up the first Azra shard. They moved with the patience of men who knew haste was violence. "Please come with us," the first said. "Official business. You are not under arrest. You are under invitation." "By whom?" Arthur asked. "You will know in due course." Now, aboard the transfer vessel, Arthur watched the blue ribbon emblem in the porthole and tried to remember Azra before it became a political animal. In the drill core it had been thumb-sized, black with a blue-green fire, as if a star had been caught in a trap. A gram of Azra could speed radioactive decay until a century-old fuel rod became useful in a week. That was why corporations had come to Mars, why indentured laborers worked in shafts where the air tasted of metal, why a man with a bad knee could become more valuable than a city. The ship's steward brought him hot coffee and a card with no name, only a starburst and the words: Antares Diplomatic Corps, Office of Special Concessions. "Your host will see you in the airlock lounge," the steward said. "You are to sign nothing until you have had counsel." "Counsel?" Arthur said. "I don't have counsel." "You will have counsel now." The airlock lounge was a curved room of pale metal and dark glass, with a view of space so black it seemed less empty than full. A small screen on the wall showed a rotating map of Mars, its red surface marked with blue lines that looked like veins and claims. A table of polished carbonite stood in the center. Behind it sat a woman in a dark suit, her hair cropped close, her face calm in the way of people who had long ago stopped wasting energy on surprise. Around her, three men in diplomatic gray stood like statues by the doors. "Mr. Neegan." She did not rise. "I am Director Lila Voss. I thank you for accepting our invitation." "You had very little time for questions." "Questions are easier after facts are established. You found Azra on a parcel registered in your name. The parcel is under lease to your labor contract, but the discovery triggers a review under the Colonial Minerals Accord. Several parties are interested. We are here to make the process orderly." "Orderly," Arthur said, "is a word I have not heard much on the flats." Voss's mouth moved almost into a smile. "On the flats, order is expensive. We have found a way to pay." She slid a thin data card across the table. Arthur did not touch it. "Antares will assume your labor lease," she said. "Your debts will be cleared. Your hab unit will be repaired, and you will receive a medical allotment for your knee. In exchange, you will sign a custodial charter. You will be recognized as the nominal holder of the Azra claim, not as owner, but as custodian. A board will manage the vein. You will have a seat, a salary, and a share of the gross yield." Arthur looked at the card. "And if I refuse?" "Then the claim passes to public arbitration. Several corporations will bid. Your lease will be examined. Your labor contract will be examined. The result may be less comfortable." "Comfortable is not the word I would choose for any of it." Voss leaned forward. "Mr. Neegan, Azra is not merely a metal. It is a key. Interstellar drives, weapons, power sources, medical devices. The nations that control its supply will shape the next century. Mars is not a colony in the old sense. It is a hinge. We do not want to take your land. We want to make you part of the structure that governs it." Arthur thought of the shafts, of the indentured men coughing in the lower galleries, of the company officers who spoke of productivity while the air recyclers groaned. He thought of the drill core still in his pocket, cool and heavy, and of the blue-green fire that had looked less like a mineral and more like a question. "And who are you?" he asked. "Antares Diplomatic Corps. What is diplomatic about it?" Voss's expression did not change. "Diplomacy is the art of saying no without breaking things. We have found that, on Mars, breaking things is often more efficient." One of the gray men shifted at the door. The ship's drone seemed louder now, as if the vessel itself were listening. "Sign the charter," Voss said, "and you will leave here with more than protection. You will have a voice. Refuse, and you may still have your voice, but it will be a small one, and the people who hear it will be less patient." Arthur picked up the data card. It was warm in his hand, as if it had been waiting. Outside the dark glass, Mars turned slowly, a rust-colored world full of secrets, and somewhere beneath the flats, the Azra vein waited in the dark, patient as a bomb. "Let me see the charter," he said. Voss inclined her head. "A wise first step."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The chapter opens aboard the transfer vessel as instructed, delivers the meeting with Director Voss, and keeps the scene dialogue-heavy with interspersed description. The prose is clean and economical, with some genuinely nice images ("polar caps bright as cracked teeth," "patient as a bomb"). The Antares "diplomatic in name only" flavor comes through well in Voss's lines, particularly "Diplomacy is the art of saying no without breaking things." The offer structure (custodial charter vs. arbitration threat) effectively sows intrigue and stakes. Weaknesses: the Asimov voice is only partially achieved — the dialogue is competent but the big-picture worldbuilding is delivered somewhat expositionally ("Azra is not merely a metal. It is a key"). Voss is a fairly stock cold negotiator; Arthur is reactive but thin. The flashback to the retinue's arrival is efficient but slightly tell-heavy. Some lines flirt with cliché ("a rust-colored world full of secrets"). The ending is a mild cliffhanger that works but is conventional. Overall a solid, professional pastiche that hits the brief without transcending it. + Contemporary romance: Darkroom Revelations — Score: 82.0
Prompt:
Darkroom Revelations Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of Dani, a 25-year-old assertive art student known for her bold style and take-charge attitude in relationships. For the past semester, she's been quietly fascinated by Elliot (he/him), a 19-year-old boy in her experimental photography class. Dani has been intrigued by his unconventional masculinity: killer thrift-shop-nu-goth style, soft demeanour and quiet intellect. When they're paired for a final project requiring late nights in the darkroom, Elliot tentatively shares that he's been questioning his gender identity and expression. Set during one of these intimate darkroom sessions where the red light creates a confessional atmosphere. Explore Dani's complex attraction—her usual assertiveness complicated by her desire to protect Elliot's vulnerability, her excitement at witnessing his self-discovery, and her confusion about what this means for her own identity as someone typically attracted to more defined gender presentations. The narrative should capture the tender awkwardness of their conversations, Dani's internal struggle between taking charge and wanting to give Elliot agency, and the unexpected chemistry that develops as both find themselves in uncharted territory. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The darkroom smelled of vinegar, rubber, and the warm metal of the enlarger. Red light made everything look like a bruise, soft and private. I had spent the semester pretending Elliot wasn’t the reason my hands kept stopping mid-print, my mouth going dry before I could say something sharp and clever. He was nineteen, small in a way that didn’t feel fragile, dressed in thrifted black layers, lace at his cuffs, silver rings catching nothing because there was no light. He moved like he had all the time in the world. When Professor Hale paired us for the final series, I expected a negotiation. I am used to setting terms: who prints, who scans, who carries the trays, who gets the last look at the contact sheet. Elliot simply nodded and said, “You lead, I follow,” in a voice so calm it made my chest do something embarrassing. I wanted to command the room. I wanted him to look at me like the darkroom was a stage. Instead, he watched the paper float in the developer, his expression serious and gentle, as if the image were a secret he was helping me hear. I kept telling myself it was the style. The nu-goth thrift-shop armor, the soft jaw, the way he tucked his hair behind his ear when he thought no one was looking. It was not what I usually wanted. I like shoulders, certainty, men who take up space without apology. Elliot did not take up space. He occupied it carefully, like a guest who might be asked to leave. That should have unsettled me. It didn’t. It made me want to be the one who stayed. The night the paper burned, we were working on a sequence of hands. His hands. I had asked for them because I wanted to photograph quietness, and he agreed without asking why. We stood close under the safelight, trays between us, our shoulders almost touching. He was printing a test strip, counting seconds under his breath, and I watched the red glow pool in his collarbones. “Do you ever feel like you’re performing?” I asked, too direct, as usual. He paused. “All the time,” he said. “Especially when I’m trying to be less.” I should have changed the subject. I should have pointed to the timer, the density, the way the image was coming up too soft. Instead I said, “What does less mean to you?” He looked at me then, really looked, with a steadiness that made my take-charge instincts falter. “Not smaller,” he said. “Just... not always what people expect. I’ve been trying on different versions of myself. Some fit. Some feel like costumes. I don’t know which is which yet.” My first thought was to fix it. Name it. Tell him he was beautiful, or that I didn’t care, or that I could protect him from the room’s staring. The second thought was quieter and more terrifying: he did not need me to fix him. He needed me to stop reaching. I swallowed my next command. “Okay,” I said. “Tell me what you want to try.” He blinked, surprised, as if he had expected me to decide for him. “Can I wear the lace shirt for the next print? The one with the high collar? I think it makes me feel... held.” I helped him find it from the drawer by the sink. His fingers brushed mine on the folded fabric, and the contact lasted too long. The red light made the gesture look sacred, or criminal. I wanted to pull away. I wanted to pull him closer. My body was giving me contradictory instructions, and I was too old to pretend I hadn’t noticed. “There,” he said, holding the shirt against his chest. “Does it look weird?” “No,” I said, before I could stop myself. “It looks like you.” He changed behind the curtain, a thin black screen that did more to my imagination than to privacy. I stood at the enlarger and pretended to adjust the lens. When he came out, the collar framed his throat, and I felt my mouth go dry again. We worked in a new silence, less awkward than the old one, more alive. He printed with a confidence I hadn’t seen before, tilting the frame, checking the edges, asking for my opinion like a colleague. I gave him one. He took it without flinching. Then I ruined the stack. I reached for the photo paper, my sleeve catching the edge of the safe box, and the lid swung open just enough for white light to slice across the top sheets. The sound was small, a paper whisper, but the damage was absolute. A corner of the stack lay fogged, useless, a pale wound under the red glow. I stared at it. “Oh no,” Elliot said, not with anger, but with a strange, tender horror. “Dani.” I wanted to make it right. I started listing solutions: we could print smaller, use the damaged sheets as experiments, call the department, buy more, stay late, take the blame. He put a hand on my wrist. Not to stop me, exactly, but to slow me down. “It’s okay,” he said. “We’re still here.” His voice was low, and the darkroom seemed to shrink around us. I realized I had been holding my breath for minutes. “I’m sorry,” I said. “I always try to take control. I don’t know how to just be in the middle of something.” He considered this, his thumb moving once over my pulse. “Maybe that’s what this is,” he said. “Not a project. Not a lesson. Just two people figuring out what they want to become.” I should have laughed. I should have stepped back and made a joke about ruined paper and student debt. Instead I leaned into his hand, a small surrender, and let the red light make us both anonymous. “Okay,” I whispered. “Then figure it out with me.” The room waited with us and the red light stayed.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece delivers a controlled, atmospheric first-person narrative that hits nearly all prompt requirements: the darkroom setting, the red-light confessional mood, Dani's assertiveness complicated by Elliot's vulnerability, and the tentative chemistry between them. The prose is disciplined and image-driven—"red light made everything look like a bruise," "he occupied it carefully, like a guest who might be asked to leave"—with strong sensory grounding in the photography process. The fogged-paper incident is a well-integrated plot device that externalizes Dani's control problem and earns the moment of mutual surrender at the end. Dialogue is naturalistic and thematically loaded without being expository. Some minor weaknesses: the ending is slightly neat, a few metaphors strain ("sacred, or criminal"), and the word count falls short of the 1000-word seed. The transformation of both characters is gradual and plausible, and the emotional complexity—desire, protectiveness, identity confusion—is rendered with restraint rather than melodrama. + Contemporary romance / drama: Stolen Moments in Roma — Score: 73.0
Prompt:
Contemporary Romance / Drama: Stolen Moments in Roma. Write a series of interconnected short scenes and dialogues that span a single day in modern-day Rome, in narrative form. This will form the beginning of a larger story. Alessandra, a fiery, independent Roman woman who works as a motorcycle courier, nearly collides with Ben, a somewhat clumsy, overly polite British academic on sabbatical, who is engrossed in a guidebook near the Trevi Fountain. The initial encounter is a clash of cultures and personalities – Alessandra is all sharp wit and rapid-fire Italian, while Ben is flustered apologies and awkward attempts at speaking the language. However, as they sort out the near-miss, a spark of unexpected humor and connection emerges. Alessandra, it quickly becomes clear, is a whirlwind of energy and mischief. She's a self-admitted troublemaker with a secret penchant for kleptomania, a detail she doesn't explicitly reveal, but which manifests in subtle, daring acts throughout the day. She impulsively decides to take Ben on a wild, unsanctioned tour of Rome, dragging him in some specific instances far outside his comfort zone. Ben, despite his initial apprehension and inherent politeness, finds himself utterly captivated by Alessandra's unapologetic spirit and zest for life. He is drawn into her orbit, a willing participant in increasingly outlandish situations, a quiet rebellion brewing beneath his scholarly exterior. The narrative should primarily consist of short, vivid scenes and dialogue exchanges, revealing their contrasting personalities and backgrounds, and the growing, ambiguous tension between them. Ben is captivated by Alessandra's energy and the thrill of breaking free from his routine. There's a clear sense that Alessandra is toying with Ben, pushing his boundaries and enjoying his reactions, but her own feelings remain somewhat enigmatic. The day should be a rollercoaster of exhilarating, slightly dangerous, and humorous moments, leaving Ben completely disoriented but utterly smitten. Explore the underlying tension & chemistry between them, culminating in some payoff as they part ways (or not -- your choice). Include this detail: Write in narrative prose, using immersive storytelling. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The dent on Alessandra's motorcycle was the size of a small moon, painted in turquoise by some anonymous hand, and she had decided not to fix it. It looked, she thought, like a scar that had learned to wink. At the edge of the Trevi crowd, she slowed to a crawl, mirror full of tourists, pigeons, and one man standing far too close to the curb, nose buried in a guidebook. 'Attention!' she shouted, tapping the horn. 'Ecco, la morte!' He looked up, startled, and the book flew from his hands. 'Oh! Oh, I'm terribly sorry,' Ben said, scrambling. 'I didn't see you. I'm so sorry.' Alessandra killed the engine and swung off. 'You didn't see me? I am a motorbike. I am Italian. I am wearing red. I am practically a warning sign.' He blinked. 'I think I meant I didn't hear you. The fountain is very loud.' 'In Rome, everything is loud. That is the point.' She pointed at the turquoise dent. 'And that is my best friend. He remembers a certain incident with a gelato cart.' Ben stared at the scratch. 'He?' 'Obviously.' She tossed her helmet under her arm. 'You're blocking traffic. And your face is blocking my patience. Do you have a name, or should I call you my new favorite tourist mistake?' 'Ben Whitfield.' 'Alessandra.' She grinned. 'And if you're going to stand there holding that book like a shield, at least learn the first rule: in Rome, the city is always late, always hungry, and always watching.' Ben should have walked away. He had a lecture to prepare, a flat in Trastevere, and a carefully scheduled afternoon. Instead, he found himself holding the guidebook like a surrender flag while Alessandra circled him once, twice, as if deciding whether he was a threat or a snack. 'You're lost,' she announced. 'I'm not lost. I'm... orienting.' 'You are facing the wrong way. The fountain is behind you. Your soul, too.' She patted his shoulder. 'I know a shortcut. No queues. No photos. No suffering.' 'What shortcut?' 'The one that starts with you getting on my motorbike and stops with you understanding that Rome is not a museum. It is a living, breathing, occasionally rude animal.' Ben swallowed. 'I don't have a helmet.' 'You have a face. That will do for now.' She tossed him a spare helmet, black and scratched, with a tiny sticker of a cat on the back. 'Hold on. Not like a gentleman. Like a man being carried to his own funeral. It is more romantic.' By the time they reached the Spanish Steps, Ben's tie was gone, his hair had become a disaster, and he had learned that Alessandra drove less by map and more by mood. 'Why did we stop?' he asked, breathless. 'Because the light is wrong. And because you look like a man who has not had a proper slice of pizza since 1998.' '1998?' 'Don't lie. I can tell.' She leaned against the bike, arms crossed. 'You academics think you know everything except how to stand in a queue without apologizing to the bread.' He laughed, surprised by it. 'I apologize to people because I don't want to be rude.' 'Rude is better. Rude is alive.' She reached into her jacket and produced a small silver key, no bigger than a coin. 'This is from the bar where I worked last summer. I have not returned it. The owner is furious. It is the best part of my week.' Ben stared. 'You stole it?' 'I liberated it. There is a difference.' She tucked it back, smiling. 'One day I will explain everything. Or I will not. Rome is full of things that are not explained.' Near the Pantheon, she made him stop in the middle of the piazza, where a street musician was playing a saxophone so badly it seemed to be apologizing for itself. 'Dance,' Alessandra said. 'What?' 'You. Now. If you do not dance, I will tell everyone that a British professor cried at a fountain.' 'You would not.' 'I have already told one gelato man. He believes it.' He hesitated, then, with the stiff dignity of a man surrendering to gravity, stepped into the square. Alessandra began to move first, not gracefully, but with a fierce, unselfconscious rhythm, as if the city were a drum and she had been waiting all morning for the beat. Ben followed, badly. 'You are terrible,' she said, laughing. 'I know.' 'Good. Terrible is honest.' A woman nearby clapped. A dog barked. For a few seconds, Ben forgot his lecture, his schedule, his careful life. He remembered only the heat, the music, and the way Alessandra's eyes caught his, sharp and amused, as if she had found a secret and was deciding whether to share it. By dusk, they reached the Tiber. Ben's shoes were dusty, his shirt untucked, and his guidebook had vanished from his bag. 'Where is it?' he asked. Alessandra pointed at the bike. The book sat on the seat, open to a page about the Colosseum, a silver spoon tucked between the pages. 'Why do you have a spoon?' 'It belongs to a restaurant. A very nice one. I will return it when I am ready.' She slid onto the bike and looked at him. 'You could go back now. Your flat. Your quiet life. Your perfectly arranged sentences.' He should have. He knew it. But the city was turning gold around them, and the turquoise dent on the bike caught the light like a small, defiant star. The river moved like silk. 'What if I stay?' he said. Her smile changed. It was not victory. It was something closer to warning. 'If you stay,' she said, 'you have to be careful. I do not do slow. I do not do safe. I take things. Sometimes objects. Sometimes attention. Sometimes the whole evening.' Ben looked at the book, the spoon, and the road ahead. 'Good,' he said. 'I have always been bad at returning things.'
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece delivers a lively, scene-based day in Rome with sharp dialogue and a clear character contrast. Alessandra's kleptomania is shown through small stolen objects (key, spoon) without explicit confession, matching the prompt's subtlety requirement. Ben's transformation from cautious academic to willing participant is charming, though his final line ("I have always been bad at returning things") is a slightly too-neat, rom-com-ready reversal that arrives faster than earned. The prose is economical and often witty ("a scar that had learned to wink"), with a few clichés (city turning gold, river like silk). Dialogue is the strongest element — Alessandra's voice is consistent and vivid, though Ben's Britishness occasionally tips into caricature. The ending lands with a nice ambiguity and warning rather than saccharine resolution. Some scenes (Pantheon dance) feel a touch sitcom-ish, and the piece is somewhat shorter than the requested 1000 words, but it covers the required beats. + Cozy sci-fi: The Last Outpost — Score: 53.2
Prompt:
Cozy sci-fi The Last Outpost Nettle (or Nets to her friends) bartends at The Last Outpost -- a lazy hub for miners and merchants in an asteroid belt on the Andromeda outer rim. Escaping from her past life, Nets found a home here at the Outpost. They have, thus far, tolerated Net's flaws which she tries to keep in equilibrium with her assortment of talents. Her evenings involve chatting with patrons, negotiating the drama, intrigue, problems & love lives of the diverse crowd that filter through the Outpost. Tonight is no different, at least, until a frazzled looking stranger, tentacled dreads askew, quietly plops down at the bar: "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." Write a chapter in this story. Establish conflict for narrative interest. Don't resolve the conflict within this chapter. Aim for about 60% dialogue. First person, present tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The gravity plating hums, and the bar smells of burnt sugar, recycled air, and cheap spice tea. "You're doing the circle thing again." "What circle thing?" "Left, right, left. You're polishing a ghost." "There's no ghost." "Then stop polishing it." I wipe a clean glass because my hands need something to do. "Coming for you, Marn?" "Two of the blue stuff. Tell Bex if she starts singing, throw a rag at her." "Will do." Bex is singing off-key about a freighter with a name I can't quite remember. Miners lean on the bar, pretending not to care about ice prices. Bex lifts a mug. "Marn, if you start singing, I'm throwing the rag." Marn says, "I was warming up." "Last time you warmed up, the ice machine filed a complaint." I say, "The ice machine does not file complaints." Bex says, "It files everything." The door chime rings, and the room drops one polite degree. He is small, with tentacled dreads askew, a coat too big, boots too clean. "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." "Vega whisky" makes the room lean in. Marn says, "That's a name that brings bad debts." Bex says, "Or good stories." I say, "Both." I pause. "Vega is gone." "Then make it a double." "Who are you?" "Does it matter?" "Usually." He taps the bar once. "I need a drink and a route." "Which route?" "The one your old crew used." "Old crews stay old." "Old crews keep secrets." I say, "Secrets are for lockers." He plops onto a stool, quiet as a bad omen. "My name is Rell. I'm a courier." "Couriers don't sit in the corner. They stand by the door." "This one is tired." "You're sitting at the bar." "I'm sitting where I can see you." Behind me, a glass slips from a shelf and breaks on the floor. Nobody jumps. "Rell," I say. "That's a name I haven't heard in a long time." "Longer than you think." "Sit down. I'll pour." "I already did." I pour anyway. Vega whisky is a rumor, a contraband, a story from dead worlds. I keep one bottle because I am sentimental, which is a flaw I balance with talents. He does not touch it. "You still keep the locker." "I keep a lot of things." "Locker seven." "My name is Nets." "Your name is Nettle." "Here, it's Nets." "Here, they are looking for you." "Who is 'they'?" I ask. "The people who closed Vega." "Vega was closed for leaks." "Vega was closed for what happened in the vault." Marn says, "Vault?" Bex says, "Nets, don't." I say, "I'm just pouring." I set the bottle down. "Who is looking?" "The same people who are looking for the drive." "What drive?" "The one you threw over the side." Marn's mug stops halfway to his lips. Bex stops singing. "You're mistaken." "I'm not." "Then you're welcome to be mistaken at the bar." "I'm not mistaken. I'm late." "Late for what?" "For you." "Rell," I say. "You're out of breath." "I ran." "From whom?" "From the same people who are outside." I look at the door. "Outside?" I take out a second glass because my hands are still useful. "I don't do old jobs." "Then do a new one." "I don't do any jobs." "You do favors." "I do drinks." He turns the glass in the light. "The Kestrel had a manifest. You remember the manifest." "I remember a lot of things." "Three names. One cargo. One missing seal." "Missing seals are common." "Not when the cargo is a child." The word lands worse than a punch. Bex turns. "Whoa. Easy." "Nobody is easy." "I am easy. I am the easiest person in this room." "You are careful. There is a difference." "Careful keeps the peace." "Careful keeps the door shut." "Exactly." The door chime rings again. Dockmaster Voss steps in with two patrol officers. The room straightens. "Evening, Voss." "Evening, Nets. I got a report of a wanted courier in the sector." "Courier." "Quiet." "I'm not quiet." "You will be." I put a hand on the bar. "He's a customer." "Customers don't make the air taste like trouble." "Customers do all sorts of things." "Is he the one?" "He's the one I poured." Voss looks at Rell. Rell looks at his glass. The whisky does not move. "Where did he come from?" "The door." "From which airlock?" "The one with the broken seal." "Which one?" "The one you never fixed." Voss says, "I have a warrant." "Show it." "I don't show warrants to bartenders." "Then show it to the room." Marn says, "The room likes paperwork." Bex says, "The room likes trouble worse." Voss's jaw works. "He's not leaving." "He's not staying either." "You can't take him in the middle of a pour." "I can take him in the middle of a heartbeat." "Then wait for the next beat." Rell sets the glass down. "You don't have to do this." "I have to keep the bar open." "You have to keep your name." "My name is Nets." "Your name is a door you haven't closed yet." The broken glass on the floor catches the light. I have not cleaned it. It is small, sharp, and honest. "Tell me what you know." "Tell me you remember." "I remember a lot of things." "Remember the child." "Remember the child," I repeat. Voss steps closer. "Nets." "I'm listening." "Is he armed?" "No." "Is he dangerous?" "Only if you make him." "Is he the courier?" I look at Rell. Rell looks at the door. The door is the worst thing in any room. "Yes." Rell slides a small black chip across the bar. "Locker seven," he says. "It's not yours. It never was." I do not touch it. "Touch it," he says. "Make me." Voss's hand moves to his sidearm. Rell's hands stay on the bar. The whisky trembles in its glass, and the night stops being cozy. The chime rings again. It does not stop, and the night tightens.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece delivers a distinctive, terse, hard-boiled voice transplanted into a cozy sci-fi bar setting, and that stylistic choice is both its greatest strength and its most persistent liability. The clipped, declarative sentences ("The door is the worst thing in any room") create genuine tension and a memorable rhythm, and the atmosphere — burnt sugar, recycled air, the polite degree the room drops when a stranger enters — is economically evoked. The reveal about the child in the cargo manifest lands with real weight, and the ending (the chime that "does not stop") successfully leaves the conflict unresolved while tightening the noose, per instructions. However, the piece has notable weaknesses. The dialogue, while atmospheric, is frequently cryptic to the point of incoherence. Exchanges like "I'm not mistaken. I'm late." / "Late for what?" / "For you." gesture at menace without earning it — the reader cannot reconstruct what actually happened at Vega, what the drive is, or why the child matters. Some of this ambiguity is genre-appropriate, but much of it reads as the author choosing mood over meaning, and several exchanges ("Careful keeps the peace." / "Careful keeps the door shut." / "Exactly.") are more cryptic than clever. The banter with Marn and Bex at the opening is charming but overlong relative to the word budget, and the middle section's stichomythia becomes monotonous — nearly every line is a short declarative or a two-word reply, so the rhythm flattens rather than escalates. The Voss confrontation is effective but the "show it to the room" sequence strains logic slightly. The "locker seven" chip and "It's not yours. It never was" is a nice hook, though its significance is unearned and unexplained. The piece adheres well to instructions: first person present tense, roughly 60%+ dialogue, conflict established and left unresolved, appropriate length. Character actions are mostly believable within the noir register, and Nets's guardedness is consistent. The prose avoids purple excess and amateurishness for the most part, though the relentless terseness occasionally tips into mannerism — a stylistic tic that a less generous reader might call overwrought in its own minimalist way. Emotionally, the child reveal and Nets's suppressed past generate genuine engagement, though the emotional range is narrow: tension and wariness, with little warmth despite the "cozy" framing. + Young adult drama: Gone South — Score: 71.3
Prompt:
Young adult drama Gone South Taylor is a 16 year old teen with a history of "concerning behavioural patterns" (or that's how the stupid smug school counsellor worded it on the phone call to Mom). It shouldn't be a surprise: When you live in a backwater town in Tennessee, your choices are: a. be mind-fuckingly bored, or b. invent some drama. Two days ago, Taylor came out to their family as trans. This disclosure was *not* in the category of invented drama -- it was, in fact, the real deal, and a long time coming. It didn't go well. The last 48 hours had been pure disaster. In a moment of desperate inspiration, Taylor had decided to get the hell out of dodge. And so an escape plan was hatched and executed within the space of 30 minutes. That was last night. Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets. Taylor navigates this new world, not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are. Write in Taylor's voice, and incorporate their internal monologue as they grapple with intense & conflicting emotions. Also incorporate dialogue with the interesting characters Taylor meets. First person, mixed tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The saxophone finds me before I find the street. It comes from a brass case on a milk crate, thin, sour, then warm, a long note that slides under my ribs like a hook. I am walking down Royal Street, or maybe it is carrying me, because my feet have stopped belonging to me. The crowd is a river of white linen, neon, cameras, sweat. A woman in a beaded hat nearly rams me. A man asks where the Quarter starts. I point at everything. I have been in New Orleans for nineteen hours. I have been on the run for two days. My phone is a dead brick in my back pocket, battery swollen into a little tumor I can feel against my thigh. I have eleven dollars, a water bottle, a library card, and a name I am not allowed to use in my own house: Taylor. Two days ago I came out as trans. It was not invented drama; it was real, and it did not go well. The counselor’s voice still floats in my ears: concerning behavioural patterns, as if I were a stain. The saxophone plays “When the Saints Go Marching In,” but wrong, slower, like the song is tired of being holy. I stop under an awning. A vendor is frying something that smells like heaven and gasoline. A girl sits beside him on a low plastic stool, maybe my age, with a shaved head and a purple streak that is actually a bruise. She has a chained backpack and a tattoo on her wrist I can’t read. She is eating a hot dog without a bun and looks at me with the flat attention of someone who has already decided I’m either trouble or irrelevant. “You lost?” she says. “No,” I say. “You’re walking like it.” I almost laugh. Instead I stand there, hands in my pockets, trying to remember how to be a person who belongs somewhere. “Where you from?” she asks. “Tennessee.” “Mm.” She sniffs. “Country of nowhere.” “Rough.” She shrugs. “I’m Sloane.” “Taylor.” She says it like she’s testing the taste. “Okay. You got a place?” “No.” “You got money?” “Eleven.” She nods slowly, as if I have just confessed to a minor crime. “Eleven is a good number. That’s enough for a beer and a mistake.” “I’m not drinking.” “You’re sixteen?” “Sixteen.” “Then you’re not drinking. You’re just buying a mistake with extra steps.” A tourist bumps my shoulder. I flinch. Sloane watches me do it, and something in her face shifts, not pity, exactly, but recognition. “You ran?” she asks. I look away. The saxophone swells. A man in a fedora drops a quarter into the case. The musician is old, thin, his eyes closed, and for a moment the street sounds like a dream I don’t remember having. “Yeah,” I say. “Why?” I want to say: because my mother said I was lying about the most important thing in my body. Because my brother said, “Dude, no, you’re not.” Because the counselor said
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The response opens with genuinely strong atmospheric writing: the saxophone hook, the "river of white linen" crowd, the vendor frying "heaven and gasoline." The voice is confident and distinct, blending wry teen defensiveness ("Eleven is a good number. That's enough for a beer and a mistake") with raw vulnerability. Sloane is an intriguing foil — the bruise disguised as a streak, the "flat attention" — and the dialogue crackles with personality and subtext. The pacing of the Taylor-Sloane exchange is excellent, naturalistic and character-revealing. However, the piece is fatally incomplete. It cuts off mid-sentence ("Because the counselor said") well before the requested ~1000 words, meaning the chapter doesn't cover the first day, doesn't develop the runaway's "issues and secrets," doesn't show Taylor navigating dangers or trust, and has no resolution or shape. The prompt asked for a full chapter with an arc; this is a fragment. The internal monologue is present but brief; the conflicting emotions are more gestured at than fully dramatized. The "purple streak that is actually a bruise" is a nice touch, though some images ("battery swollen into a little tumor") flirt with overreach. The abrupt truncation also means the emotional complexity stays potential rather than realized. Prose quality is high — sentences flow well, showing mostly beats over telling, with a consistent first-person mixed-tense voice. But as a delivered chapter, it fails the structural requirements. + Dystopic-comedy: My Apocalypse Buddy — Score: 52.8
Prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear. [characters] - the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time - midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. 1000 words.
Model Output:
My Apocalypse Buddy The end of the world had not arrived with trumpets. It had crept in like a bad debt, leaving a world still there but no longer obliged to behave. Midas sat on an upturned washing machine, the colour of old arguments. Chewy, an animo-tronic stuffed koala from a long-forgotten Before Time, sat opposite on a crate of tins. His left ear was a bottle cap; his right eye flickered with offended lamp-glow. “We’re out of tea,” said Midas. Chewy’s throat made a zipper sound. “I have tea.” “You have a button shaped like a leaf.” “It is symbolic.” Midas rubbed his face. He had been born unlucky, raised by bad luck, adopted by a persistent strain of it. “Symbolic tea doesn’t stop headaches. We need real supplies: sugar, salt, maybe something not symbolic.” Chewy tilted his head. “Low Fen has a storehouse.” “Low Fen is across the Flats.” Midas sighed. “If we find nothing?” “Then we return with the dignity of being chased.” Chewy did not answer. He was already standing. Animo-tronics did not stand for enthusiasm; they stood for inevitability. They left. The Flats were cracked concrete and rust, dotted with dead vehicles in attitudes of despair. The wind sounded like distant applause. Halfway across, Midas spotted a wall. It leaned against the sky, covered in graffiti. Most had faded. One message remained, scratched in white paint by a hurried hand with humour. FOLLOW THE RUST TO THE GREEN THAT DOES NOT BITE. Beneath it, someone had drawn a toothy tree, crossed it out, then a crowned koala. Chewy’s eye flickered. “That is not a reference.” “It’s a koala.” “It is an insult.” Midas read it again. “The green that does not bite.” “A tree.” They looked at each other. “Hidden refuge,” said Chewy. “Cryptic graffiti,” said Midas. “Probably not.” Midas pointed at the wall. “It says follow the rust.” Chewy pointed at the horizon. “Everything is rust.” They followed the rust. The first problem was that the rust led everywhere. The second was that it led nowhere. The third arrived as a goat. The goat chewed a traffic cone in a collapsed underpass. It had the bearing of something that had survived several apocalypses. “Chewy,” said Midas. “It’s looking at us.” The goat stopped chewing. It blinked. Then it walked toward them, not quickly, but with the authority of an animal never told no and meaning it. “We don’t need a goat,” said Midas. “We do not need a goat,” agreed Chewy. The goat did not agree. It butted Midas in the shin. Chewy, panicking, grabbed a wheelbarrow. The wheelbarrow had wheels. The goat had opinions. Within moments, Midas was in the wheelbarrow, Chewy was steering with grim determination, and the goat was trotting ahead. At the edge of the Flats, the goat saw a patch of green. It was not a tree. It was not a plant. It was a muddy clearing with one stubborn blade of grass and a sign: REFUGE. Beneath it, in smaller letters: DO NOT ENTER. Chewy read the sign. “The green that does not bite.” “It’s not green enough,” said Midas. “It’s a blade of grass.” The goat butted the sign. The sign fell over. Beneath it was a trapdoor. Midas stared at the trapdoor. The trapdoor stared back, with a vague sense of apology. “We are not going down that,” he said. “Of course not.” The goat stepped onto the trapdoor. It did not fall through. It opened slowly, with a groan like the earth clearing its throat. A staircase descended into warm, dry dark, smelling of moss, old stone, and something faintly edible. Chewy’s eye flickered. “Hidden refuge.” “Cryptic graffiti,” said Midas. “Probably not.” They went down. The refuge was a cellar, or a bunker, or a root system that had achieved botanical peace. Shelves held jars of dried fruit, tins of soup, spools of thread, and one inexplicable jar of buttons. There was a table, a chair, and a cold kettle. Midas found sugar. Chewy found salt. The goat found a corner, sunlight, and cheese that had been waiting for someone with confidence. For a while, it was almost a good day. Then the goat found the lever. It was small, red, labelled EMERGENCY RETURN. The goat butted it. The floor shuddered. A door opened in the wall, not outward but inward, revealing a passage that sloped upward with the cheerful confidence of a slide. The goat stepped in. Chewy stepped in. Midas, still holding the sugar, looked at the passage, looked at the goat, and decided the day had already chosen its enemies. The passage carried them upward, sideways, upward again, until they burst out of a hole in the ground not far from Low Fen. The goat stepped out first, as if born there. Chewy stepped out second, brushing dirt from his bottle-cap ear. Midas stepped out third, covered in dust, sugar, and the distinct feeling that he had been used. Low Fen was in view. The storehouse was in view. The storehouse owner was in view, holding a stick, looking at them with the expression of a man who had expected trouble, but not on a goat. “You’re late,” said the owner. “We found a refuge,” said Midas. “You found a goat.” “We found a goat,” agreed Chewy. The owner lowered the stick. “You want sugar and salt?” “Yes,” said Midas. The owner gave them sugar and salt, a sack of dried peas because he was sensible, and cheese because he was a goat man. They walked home in grey afternoon light. Midas carried the sugar. Chewy carried the salt. The goat carried itself with the quiet dignity of a creature that had saved the day and expected no reward. At the edge of their home base, a broken garage with a door that closed by habit, Midas stopped. “We should mark the refuge,” he said. “The graffiti was sufficient,” said Chewy. “It was effective.” They went inside. It was a reasonable day.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece delivers a Pratchett-flavored apocalypse comedy with a stuffed koala and hapless protagonist. Strengths: consistent dry wit, some genuinely good lines ("the colour of old arguments," "the wind sounded like distant applause," "the end of the world... crept in like a bad debt"), and a coherent three-act structure (deliberation, mission gone sideways, return home worse for wear). The goat is a nice comedic engine, and the repeated "Hidden refuge / Cryptic graffiti / Probably not" exchange has good comedic rhythm. Weaknesses: the story is underlength relative to the 1000-word target (roughly 850 words), and the second half rushes. The trapdoor/refuge discovery resolves too easily; the "EMERGENCY RETURN" lever is a convenient contrivance that ejects them conveniently near Low Fen, which feels like the author writing themselves out of a corner. The ending is flat — "It was a reasonable day" is a decent wry button, but the return home lacks the "worse for wear" texture the prompt requested; they come back with supplies, a goat, and success, which undercuts the intended comedic failure arc. The storehouse owner appears from nowhere and resolves the supply problem without friction. Chewy's animo-tronic nature is underexploited — he could be funnier and more distinct; his dialogue is often interchangeable with Midas's. Some dialogue exchanges ("We do not need a goat," agreed Chewy) are functional but thin. The graffiti setup ("green that does not bite") pays off weakly — the refuge is found almost immediately, deflating the mystery. There are minor proofing slips (a stray quotation mark in the final paragraph, "animo-tronics did not stand for enthusiasm; they stood for inevitability" is a good line but the logic wobbles). Emotionally the piece is light and pleasant but shallow; no real stakes or character depth. Still, the voice is consistent, the prose is clean and economical, and the humor mostly lands. + Romance: Love in the Limelight — Score: 82.5
Prompt:
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write one scene within a larger story set in Wales. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The scene takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The bell above the door had no choice but to ring. Maren looked up from the returns shelf and saw Julian Vale, hat low, coat steaming, boot black with Llangollen mud. Behind the glass, two cars idled with cameras like patient dogs. ‘Can I help you?’ she said. ‘I’m looking for something quiet,’ he said. ‘Something no one will photograph.’ ‘We do have a children’s section.’ ‘No. I mean quiet in the other sense. A book that doesn’t want to be famous.’ Maren dried her hands on her apron. ‘Try the poetry. It’s on the left. If it’s too quiet, it’s probably Welsh.’ He smiled, the sort that had opened doors. ‘You’re Maren,’ he said. Not a question. ‘I’m the person who will ask you to leave if you start signing the display copies.’ ‘Noted.’ He stopped at a slim blue volume. ‘I don’t read much. I hold a book for an hour and realise I’ve read the same page four times.’ ‘That’s not terrible. That’s reading.’ ‘No, it’s performing reading.’ He turned the book over. ‘You’re the owner?’ ‘Of the books, the shelves, the leaky roof, and at the moment, your problem.’ ‘Fair enough.’ He looked past her, towards the door. ‘There are people outside.’ ‘Then you might want to stay out of the window.’ ‘I was thinking of the staff room. If you have one.’ ‘I have a back office. It has a kettle, a chair, and a cat who hates strangers.’ ‘What’s his name?’ ‘Gareth.’ ‘Of course.’ Maren went to the back, unlocking a groaning door. The room smelled of tea and damp wool. A tabby on the desk lifted one paw. Julian followed, too close, his shoulder brushing the shelf where she kept biscuits. ‘You don’t seem surprised,’ he said. ‘I’m surprised every day. It’s a habit.’ ‘You’re not a fan?’ ‘I’m a customer.’ ‘You haven’t bought anything.’ ‘I was reshelving.’ ‘Ah.’ He leaned against the desk. ‘I like that. You don’t do the thing.’ ‘What thing?’ ‘The thing where you pretend you’re not looking at me. I can see your eyes going. It’s very rude.’ Maren felt heat climb her neck. ‘My eyes are going where I want them to.’ ‘And where is that?’ ‘At the door. So you can leave before your fans arrive and make me say something embarrassing.’ ‘You wouldn’t say anything embarrassing. You’d say something dry. It would be awful.’ ‘Probably.’ She opened the biscuit tin. ‘Tea?’ ‘Please.’ She made tea. The rain tapped the window. Outside, a shutter clicked once, then stopped. Julian watched her hands. ‘You live here?’ he asked. ‘Work here. Sleep above the shop. Yes.’ ‘And you like it?’ ‘I like knowing where the books are.’ ‘And the people?’ ‘Mostly manageable.’ He laughed, low, pleased with himself. ‘I’m manageable too.’ ‘You’re loud.’ ‘I’m memorable.’ ‘You’re in my shop.’ ‘For now.’ He took the mug. ‘Do you ever regret it? The smallness?’ Maren almost said yes. Instead: ‘Once. I had a flat in London. Nine days. Every night I lay awake listening to the traffic and thinking, if I leave this street, I’ll become someone I can’t reshelve.’ Julian went still. ‘That’s a good line.’ ‘Don’t write it down.’ ‘I wouldn’t.’ ‘You absolutely would.’ ‘Only if you let me.’ He sipped the tea. ‘I did a film last year. Everyone said it was my best. A critic told me I was finally acting like a man, not a pretty face. I thanked him, then stood in the loo for twenty minutes because I couldn’t tell if I meant it or just wanted him to say it.’ Maren looked at him. For once, the charm was off, or at least loosened, like a hat pulled back from a tired face. ‘You’re afraid of being liked for the wrong reasons,’ she said. ‘Everyone is.’ ‘No. You’re afraid of being liked for no reasons.’ He set the mug down. ‘That’s worse.’ The cat knocked a pencil to the floor. Julian looked at Maren, less performance, more attention. ‘You’re not going to ask for a photo,’ he said. ‘No.’ ‘You’re not going to tell your friends?’ ‘No.’ ‘You’re not going to sell the story to the local paper?’ ‘I’m not going to do a lot of things. Mostly because you’re blocking the door.’ He moved. Not quickly, but with the careful grace of a man who had been watched his whole life. ‘Right. I’ll go.’ ‘Wait.’ Maren heard herself before she could stop. ‘The book. The one you were holding.’ ‘Blue spine?’ ‘Yes.’ ‘I didn’t buy it.’ ‘Now you have.’ He looked at her, really looked, and the corner of his mouth twitched. ‘You’re impossible.’ ‘Probably.’ She slid Salt and Stone across the desk. ‘There’s a poem on page 43. It’s about a lighthouse keeper who thinks the sea is watching him, until he realises he’s the one keeping the light.’ ‘And if the light is lonely?’ ‘Then it still keeps the ships from wrecking.’ He picked up the book. ‘You’re either very wise or very dangerous.’ ‘In this weather? Both.’ The bell rang. Maren followed him to the front, half expecting the glass to be full of faces. It wasn’t. The rain had thinned, and the two cars were gone, leaving only wet tarmac and the smell of salt. ‘You can come out now,’ she said. ‘I was going to.’ ‘Lie.’ He stopped at the door, book in one hand, collar turned up. ‘Next time I come in, I’m buying something.’ ‘You can start with the poem.’ ‘Page 43.’ ‘Yes.’ He smiled, but it was smaller now, less polished, as if he had found a crack in it and liked what he saw. ‘Maren.’ ‘What?’ ‘If I tell you the sea was watching me, would you believe me?’ She looked at the door, the rain, the empty street. Then at him. ‘Probably,’ she said. ‘But I’d make you read the poem first.’ He went out into the grey afternoon, and the bell rang softly, as if it had kept a secret.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a confident, well-crafted scene that fulfills nearly every instruction with precision. The premise (actor ducking into a Welsh bookstore to escape paparazzi) is executed cleanly, with the Llangollen mud, damp wool, and salt-tinged air grounding the setting without belaboring it. The scene is dialogue-forward as requested, and the two voices are genuinely distinct: Julian's lines are performative, probing, fishing for admiration ("I'm memorable"), while Maren's are dry, deflecting, and economical ("I'm a customer." / "You haven't bought anything." / "I was reshelving."). The character brief is handled with real nuance. Julian's fragile ego is dramatized rather than stated — the loo anecdote about the critic's compliment is an excellent, specific confession that reveals the man beneath the charm. Maren's flustered interior is shown through small physical tells (heat climbing her neck, "My eyes are going where I want them to") and her involuntary "Wait" before she can stop herself. The paradox the prompt requested — that her immunity provokes genuine attraction and derails his charm offensive — plays out believably: his smile gets "smaller... less polished, as if he had found a crack in it and liked what he saw." The prose is restrained and elegant, with several memorable images (cameras "like patient dogs," the bell that "had no choice but to ring," the closing bell ringing "as if it had kept a secret"). The lighthouse-keeper poem on page 43 is a light but effective thematic mirror. Weaknesses: the banter occasionally tips into being too writerly — lines like "if I leave this street, I'll become someone I can't reshelve" and "You're afraid of being liked for no reasons" feel authored rather than spoken, moments where both characters are wittier than people are. "Salt and Stone" is slid across the desk without having been named earlier, a small continuity slip. The paparazzi threat resolves a bit too conveniently (cars simply gone), and the ending's symmetry — the bell motif returning — is neat, though earned. The chemistry is more intellectual than visceral; the piece flirts with warmth but keeps both characters at a cool remove, which suits Maren but slightly mutes the "inwardly more than a little charmed" requirement. Still, this is polished, coherent, well-paced work with no meandering, no purple prose, and a consistent tone throughout. + Whalepunk fantasy: The Morska Conspiracy — Score: 63.0
Prompt:
Whalepunk fantasy The Morska Conspiracy The Morska thieves guild experiences a sudden power vacuum as its leader was arrested in a raid in the early hours of the morning. Aya, a young woman born into aristocracy, has a keen interest in both the sciences and the arcane, having inherited her mother's gift for immateria magick (an outlawed practice for which her mother was, regrettably, hanged by the neck). Aya, bored with the world of aristocracy, has been spending her nights moonlighting with this very guild (masked, naturally). Leveraging her latent ability to summon dark entities from the immateria, she quickly rose through the ranks of the guild. Now, recognising the opportunity of the sudden power vacuum, Aya and her close companions Katra and Simeon, make a play for heart of the guild's claim to power: an ancient scythan artifact, under guard of spell and key in the depths of the guild hq. In contrast with the desperate chaos they had navigated thus far, the entrance to the underhold felt suddenly too quiet. Aya braces herself and reaches for the door. Write the next scene as the trio enter the underhold and find themselves confronted by none other than the guild leader herself, decidedly *un*-incarcerated, and in possession of both weapons and bodyguards. Paint a vivid picture of of the confrontation. Story beats: Aya is captured and unmasked. The trio are captured. Aya attempts to stall their demise by negotiating on her value as a hostage -- as she grapples with the inevitable consequences of her role in the guild being brought to light. Incorporate dialogue in the authentic voices of the characters. Do not write a fight scene. Lean into the gritty Victorian aesthetic with the dialogue & worldbuilding, as well as elements of gothic horror. In this world, men trust brass and oil and steel; magicka is feared and barely understood. Write in third person past tense, incorporating both Aya's internal monologue, and a heavy dialogue component. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The underhold door was not a door so much as a verdict: ironbound oak, studded with whalebone rivets, set into blackened brick that sweated brine and old oil. Beyond it, a stair spiralled down into a throat of darkness, lit by tallow lamps that guttered in the draught. Aya’s fingers found the cold handle. Katra, to her left, had her knife already out; Simeon, to her right, held a brass compass whose needle trembled like a trapped insect. The air smelled of tar, whale fat, and fear. No one spoke. The silence had weight, waiting to see who would flinch. The foghorn sounded three times in the harbor beyond the guild walls. The first blast rolled through the stone and made the lamps lean. The second struck Aya’s teeth. The third seemed to come from inside her skull, a wet, metallic groan that left the air tasting of salt and copper. At the bottom of the stair, the silence changed. It was not empty. It was held. A woman stood in the centre of the underhold, where the ceiling arched like the ribcage of some drowned leviathan. She wore the grey coat of the Morska, but tailored to a spine. Aya’s hand closed on the door handle. “Put it down, little lady,” the woman said. The voice was low, unhurried, and absurdly familiar. It was the voice that had once signed warrants in the Morska’s ledger. Aya turned. The leader of the Morska smiled as if she had been expecting them all along. Six hooded figures stood behind her, armed with flintlocks, truncheons, and chains. Two of them carried lanterns. All of them were waiting. The leader’s pistol caught the tallow light, polished to a mirror. She did not look at Katra’s knife. She looked only at Aya’s own face. “You’re dead,” Katra said, her knife not quite steady. “Dead?” The leader laughed once. “I was arrested. There is a difference. Arrested is a word for men who believe in doors.” Simeon’s compass spun wildly. “The ward,” he whispered. “It’s keyed to her pulse. We should have known.” “Should have known,” the leader repeated, and the words landed like a slap. “That is the trouble with clever people, Simeon. You know things. You do not know when to stop.” Aya felt the cold pressure behind her eyes. The immateria was listening. It pressed against her cold skull like a tide. One of the hooded men stepped forward with a chain. Another produced a truncheon wrapped in leather. Katra moved to strike, but the leader’s pistol spoke, not with a bang, but with a sharp crack that echoed off the whalebone ribs of the ceiling. The blast hit the floor beside Katra, sending up black grit. Katra froze. “No blood,” the leader said. “Not yet. I am not a butcher. I am an accountant.” The hooded man reached for Aya’s mask. She did not resist. As the silk came away, the underhold seemed to inhale with a sound like a gasp. “You can’t kill us,” Aya said. “Not here. Not now. If I vanish, the Morska bleeds. The other guilds will smell it. The harbor masters will smell it. You’ll have a war before the tide turns.” The leader tilted her head. “And if I do not kill you? Then what? You run? You flee to your father’s estate? You write a letter to the magistrate and tell him, in your pretty aristocratic hand, that you have been a thief all along?” Aya’s stomach turned. She had imagined this moment a hundred times. In most of them, she had always won. “I can be useful,” Aya said. “You need someone who can read the artifact. Someone who can open it. I can do that. You cannot.” “You can read it,” the leader agreed. “You cannot open it. There is a difference. You have the gift, but you do not have the will. Your mother had both. That is why she died.” The words struck Aya harder than any truncheon. “You knew my mother,” Aya whispered. “I knew her work,” the leader said. “I also knew her fear. She thought the immateria was a library. It is not. It is a mouth.” Aya did not blink. The immateria pressed closer, cold and patient, like the sea against a hull. She could call the dark things that had carried her through the guild’s alleys, the things that wore the shapes of drowned sailors and wore hunger for faces. But the leader would see. The city would see. And then there would be no negotiation, no hostage, no future. Only fire. Men in this city trusted brass and oil and steel. They did not trust magick. They feared it the way rats fear the tide: with a kind of stupid, ancient certainty and hunger. “If you want the artifact,” Aya said, her voice steadier than she felt, “you need me alive. You need me unbroken. A hostage who can speak is worth more than a corpse that cannot.” The leader studied her for a long moment. The lantern in her hand swung gently, casting shadows that moved like fingers. “You are your mother’s daughter,” she said. “Clever. Stubborn. Willing to bargain with the devil if the devil has a ledger.” “I am what the city made me,” Aya said. “No,” the leader replied. “You are what you chose to be. That is the difference.” She raised her pistol, not to fire, but to point at Aya’s throat. “Take them,” she said. “Gently. The girl is to be kept in the east cell. The other two, in the lower dock. If they scratch each other, feed them. If they scratch me, I will have their tongues.” Katra hissed through her teeth. Simeon’s compass fell silent. As the chains were fastened to Aya’s wrists, she looked past the leader, past the guards, past the black iron case that held the artifact. For a moment, the case seemed to breathe and Aya did not scream aloud once.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The response delivers the requested scene: the trio enters the underhold, confronts the un-incarcerated guild leader, Aya is unmasked, the trio captured, and Aya negotiates her value as a hostage while grappling with exposure of her aristocratic identity and magickal gift. No fight scene occurs, per instructions. Third person past tense with internal monologue is maintained, and the whalepunk/Victorian/gothic atmosphere is present (whalebone rivets, tar, foghorns, drowned leviathan ribcage). Strengths: The prose has strong atmospheric moments and a consistent gritty tone. The leader's "I am not a butcher. I am an accountant" line is characterful, and the mother revelation ("It is not a library. It is a mouth") lands as a memorable beat. The dialogue generally carries menace and period flavor. Weaknesses: The prose frequently tips into overwrought, aphorism-heavy territory ("The underhold door was not a door so much as a verdict"; "Arrested is a word for men who believe in doors"). These constructions are stylish but pile up until they feel like mannerism rather than organic voice. Dialogue formatting is awkward — multiple speakers crammed into single paragraphs with quotation marks running together, which muddies attribution and reads as amateurish in execution. Some continuity stumbles: Aya "turns" to see the leader who was already described standing before them; the closing line "Aya did not scream aloud once" is garbled and anticlimactic. The negotiation resolves somewhat abruptly and conveniently — the leader capitulates to Aya's hostage logic with little resistance, softening the tension. Katra and Simeon are thinly drawn, functioning as props rather than characters with distinct voices. The emotional complexity is present but stated more than deeply felt; Aya's internal grappling is summarized ("She had imagined this moment a hundred times") rather than rendered. The piece is coherent, engaging, and hits its beats, but the accumulation of stylistic tics, dialogue formatting errors, and the weak ending keep it from excellence. + Fanfic-crossover: Gunpowder Rendezvous — Score: 55.2
Prompt:
Gunpowder Rendezvous Spike Spiegel & Revy Write a story where Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop) and Revy (Black Lagoon) meet in a seedy bar after both being hired for the same bounty. Their mutual attraction is complicated by their trust issues and competitive instincts. Include drinking, gunplay, and unresolved sexual tension that culminates in a motel room standoff. **Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop)** Spike is a laid-back bounty hunter with a dark past as a syndicate enforcer. He practices Jeet Kune Do and is exceptionally skilled with firearms. He's chronically broke, constantly hungry, and addicted to cigarettes. Despite his carefree attitude, he's haunted by his past and the woman he left behind. He has a prosthetic eye from a past injury that affects his depth perception. He's fatalistic to the extreme, often saying he's already died once. He values freedom above all else and dislikes attachments, though he secretly cares deeply for his crew. Famous quote: "Whatever happens, happens." **Revy/Rebecca Lee (Black Lagoon)** Revy is a Chinese-American dual-wielding gunslinger with unparalleled shooting skills. She's foul-mouthed, chain-smoking, and has severe anger management issues stemming from childhood abuse. She's known as "Two Hands" for her ability to accurately fire two pistols simultaneously. She drinks heavily and solves most problems with violence. Despite her hardened exterior, she has moments of vulnerability, particularly around Rock. She has a dragon tattoo covering her right arm and typically wears extremely short shorts and a black crop top regardless of the situation. Famous quote: "I'm not a good person, not a bad person. I'm just here." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The neon jukebox in the back corner of the bar plays the same scratchy rock track on repeat, its guitar whine bending around the smell of spilled beer, cheap smoke, and gun oil. Spike Spiegel sits at the far end of the counter, one boot on the stool, a cigarette balanced between his fingers. His black shirt is untucked, his hair a mess that has survived worse than this city. The bounty is simple: a man with a stolen data drive and a mouth full of knives. Simple enough that two strangers are sitting in the same room for it. Revy walks in like she owns the air. Her red hair is tied back, her black crop top tight, her shorts so short they look like a rumor. The dragon on her right arm coils up beneath the sleeve of nothing, ink dark against skin. She carries two pistols under one arm and a bottle of whiskey in the other. The bartender slides a glass toward her without asking. She drinks, then spots Spike. He spots her back. He smiles, all teeth and nothing else. "You're early." She laughs, a sound like gravel in a tin can. "You're late, cowboy. I got here before the floor stopped shaking." He tilts his head. "I was walking." "Walking? That's not how you get here. That's how you get found." She sets the bottle down. "Bounty on the same prick." "Same prick," he agrees. "Usually means the same mistake." Her eyes narrow. "You think you're funny." "I think you're loud." "I think you're slow." He takes a drag. Smoke curls out of him like he's trying to disappear. "Maybe I am. Maybe that's why I'm still here." The jukebox scratches again, the singer begging for something it never gets. A man in a gray suit enters, laughing too hard, two thugs behind him. The data drive is in his breast pocket, visible enough for anyone paying attention. Everyone is paying attention. Revy's hand moves to her holsters. Spike's hand moves to his. They both look at the same target, then at each other. "Partners," Spike says. "Fuck partners," Revy says. "Then what?" "Whatever gets the job done." He raises an eyebrow. "That's not an answer." "It's the best one you're getting." The gray-suited man sees them. His laugh dies. He draws a pistol, but Revy is already moving. One shot cracks through the bar, taking out the thug on his left. Spike fires once, clean, dropping the other. The man turns, but Spike is there, elbow into his ribs, wrist breaking, pistol spinning away. The gray-suited man hits the floor. The data drive clatters near the jukebox. "Mine," Revy says, holstering. "Yours," Spike says, picking the drive up. "We split it." "I don't split." "You do when you're out of your depth." She stares at him. "I'm never out of my depth." He grins. "Then why did you let me talk?" The bartender, bleeding from a cut on his forehead, slides them two drinks. "For the trouble." Revy takes the glass. "I like this place." Spike lights a cigarette. "It's not a place. It's a mistake." "Same thing." She drinks. He watches her throat move. The moment stretches, thin and hot. Her eyes drop to his mouth, then back up. He leans closer. The jukebox repeats the chorus. "Let's go," he says. "Let's not." "Before someone else gets the idea." "Someone else can have the idea." He laughs. "You're trouble." "So are you." They leave through the back, past a dumpster and a puddle that reflects the neon sign. The street is narrow, the air thick. Revy walks close enough that her shoulder brushes his. He doesn't move away. She doesn't either. The motel is two blocks away, its sign buzzing with half its letters gone. One room, one key, one bad decision. Revy takes the key. Spike takes the door. Inside, the carpet is brown with stains and the window looks out onto a parking lot. A single lamp flickers on the nightstand. Revy leans against the door, arms crossed. "We split the drive." "We split the job." "Same thing." "Only if you trust me." She laughs, but it doesn't land. "Trust is for people who plan to live." Spike's smile fades. "I'm not planning to live either." The room is too quiet. The lamp buzzes. Outside, a car alarm dies. Revy pushes off the door and walks toward the bed. Spike follows. He stops at the foot. She stops at the head. Their eyes meet, and the air between them gets heavier than the smoke still hanging in the bar. "You want me," she says. "You want to know if I do." "I want to know if you're real." He steps closer. "I'm here." "That's not the same thing." "No," he says. "It isn't." Revy reaches for her pistol. Spike reaches for his. Their hands stop halfway, fingers curled, breaths uneven. The guns stay holstered, but the threat is there, bright and sharp. She looks at his face, at the scar, at the eye that doesn't match. He looks at her mouth, at the dragon, at the way her jaw works when she's trying not to hit something. "Tell me to go," she says. He doesn't. "Tell me to stay." He doesn't. She crosses the distance. He catches her wrist. Her free hand goes to his collar. His free hand goes to her waist. They stand there, close enough to taste the whiskey on her breath, close enough to feel the heat of the other. Neither moves. Neither lets go. The lamp flickers. The streetlight outside cuts a pale line across the bed. Revy's eyes sharpen, not with anger, but with something worse: waiting. Spike's hand tightens, then loosens. He knows this feeling. He's had it before, in rooms that ended badly, in cities that forgot his name. The room holds breath. He lets go first. She lets go second. The room stays still, charged, unfinished. Whatever happens, happens.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece delivers the requested scenario competently: seedy bar, shared bounty, drinking, gunplay, and a motel standoff with unresolved tension. It hits the prompt beats and captures both characters' surface traits — Spike's fatalism and cigarette nonchalance, Revy's aggression and profanity. The closing "Whatever happens, happens" callback is a nice touch. Strengths: The prose is lean and rhythmic, with some genuinely good hard-boiled lines ("her shorts so short they look like a rumor," "a sound like gravel in a tin can"). The motel standoff is the best scene — the half-drawn guns, the mutual refusal to move first or let go, is a strong physical metaphor for their trust issues. Present tense is maintained throughout, and the atmosphere of neon, smoke, and gun oil is consistent. Weaknesses: The dialogue, while punchy, leans heavily on terse exchange patterns that become repetitive — short declarative volleys of "Same thing" / "No it isn't" structure recur so often they feel like a tic rather than character voice. Revy's voice is somewhat sanitized; she's foul-mouthed and volatile, but here she's mostly cool and quippy, losing some of her chaotic menace. Spike's prosthetic eye and hunger/broke-ness are underused. The gunfight is over almost instantly, draining tension rather than building it — the prompt asked for gunplay, and this delivers it in two sentences. The middle section (leaving the bar, walking to the motel) is atmospheric but slightly padded. The emotional stakes are gestured at ("in rooms that ended badly") rather than fully earned — we're told about their pasts via the prompt, but the story itself only lightly touches Spike's ghost. The ending is appropriately unresolved, though the "He lets go first / She lets go second" beat is a bit too neat and symmetrical to feel fully lived-in. Overall: a solid, stylish genre piece with strong atmosphere and a genuinely good final scene, held back by repetitive dialogue rhythms, slightly flattened characterization, and an underplayed action beat.
