+ Young adult drama: Gone South — Score: 56.6
Prompt:
Young adult drama Gone South Taylor is a 16 year old teen with a history of "concerning behavioural patterns" (or that's how the stupid smug school counsellor worded it on the phone call to Mom). It shouldn't be a surprise: When you live in a backwater town in Tennessee, your choices are: a. be mind-fuckingly bored, or b. invent some drama. Two days ago, Taylor came out to their family as trans. This disclosure was *not* in the category of invented drama -- it was, in fact, the real deal, and a long time coming. It didn't go well. The last 48 hours had been pure disaster. In a moment of desperate inspiration, Taylor had decided to get the hell out of dodge. And so an escape plan was hatched and executed within the space of 30 minutes. That was last night. Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets. Taylor navigates this new world, not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are. Write in Taylor's voice, and incorporate their internal monologue as they grapple with intense & conflicting emotions. Also incorporate dialogue with the interesting characters Taylor meets. First person, mixed tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
Gone South The air in New Orleans hits me like a wet towel. I’m on a corner, backpack biting my shoulders, sneakers wet, phone at 12%. No charger. No plan. No one to call. If I call Mom, she’ll say, “Taylor, where are you?” and I’ll feel like a stain on a shirt. I had told them I was trans. I had said the words. I had waited for the sky to fall. It did, except the sky was a kitchen table, my brother’s pale face, Dad saying, “We need to talk about therapy.” Not “I love you.” Not “Okay.” Just therapy. Like I was a problem to be scheduled. I don’t blame them. That’s the part that makes me sick. I still want to be somewhere they can’t see me flinch. The sun comes up over the French Quarter in rust and cream. Tourists with cameras. A man in a white suit plays trumpet outside a bar that shouldn’t be open yet. His music is sad and bright, like a bruise. I pass a bakery. Coffee makes my stomach clench. I have eleven dollars and one granola bar. I need water. I need a place to sit without looking like a lost child. I need to know if I can stay, or if I’m just moving one disaster to another. My thumb hovers over Mom’s name. I don’t press it. At 12%, every app feels like a threat. I turn off Wi-Fi. I keep the screen dark. The battery number stares at me like a dare. I find a public library two blocks from the river. Inside, the air is cold and smells like old paper. A woman at the desk looks at me twice, but not like she’s writing a report. She just looks tired. “There’s charging at the computer stations,” she says. “You can’t take the cables out.” “Okay,” I say. “Thanks.” I sit near a girl about my age with blue streaks in her hair. She wears a tank top that says “I SURVIVED MY MOTHER” and a patched jacket. Her phone is plugged in. Her paperback is open upside down. I sit next to her. She doesn’t look up. “Don’t touch the cable,” she says. “I wasn’t going to.” “Most people are. You look like you might be.” “I’m just trying not to die.” She finally glances at me. “That’s usually the problem.” Her eyes are dark, sharp, a little mean, but not unkind. She has a scar on her chin and a bandage on her thumb. “I’m Zee,” she says. “Taylor.” “Taylor.” She tests it. “You’re new.” “New to where? The city? The trouble?” She almost smiles. “Both.” I plug my phone in. The green triangle appears. For a second, I am not running. I am just a person with a low battery. Zee watches me. “You’re not from here.” “No.” “Where from?” I almost say Tennessee. I almost say the town where everyone knows your mother’s divorce and your father’s beer budget. I say, “Somewhere boring.” “Boring places make you want to be a character.” “I’m not a character.” “You ran away.” The words hit harder than they should. “I didn’t run away. I left.” “Same thing if your mom’s got your number.” I look down. She’s right. My phone is charged enough to ring. I could call. I could say I’m fine. I could say I’m in New Orleans and I’m safe and I’m not dramatic and I’m not doing this to hurt anyone. I could say, Please don’t come looking, I’m not a project. I don’t. Zee slides a sealed granola bar across the table. “Eat,” she says. “I have food.” “You don’t thank people in libraries. It makes it weird.” “Sorry.” She opens her book, but not before saying, “If you’re looking for a place to sleep, don’t go near the river after dark. There’s a guy who thinks he’s helping. He isn’t.” “Who?” “Nobody you want to meet.” I want to ask more. I want to ask if she’s running too, if she has a name, if she’s ever been so angry at her own life that she packed a bag in thirty minutes and walked until her feet bled. But I don’t know the rules here. I don’t know if asking is a way to get close or a way to get caught. Outside, the trumpet player is still going. The notes bend in the heat. I think about my mother’s voice, and how it cracked when she said, “Taylor, please come home.” I think about my father saying nothing, which is somehow worse. I had expected fear. I got silence. I had expected rejection. I got concern, which was worse because concern can sound like love, and I don’t know how to tell the difference right now. Zee’s phone buzzes. She glances at it, and her face changes. Just a flicker. Fear. “Who is it?” I ask. “Nobody.” “You don’t have to lie to me. I’m bad at lying too.” She locks the phone. “You want to know something true?” “Maybe.” “I’m not safe either.” The words sit between us. I want to believe her. I want to be suspicious. I want to help. I want to run. All at once. “Why are you here?” I ask. She looks at the window, where a tour group is passing, laughing, pointing at balconies. “Because home is a place that tells you who you’re allowed to be.” I swallow. “That’s... a lot.” “I’m good at a lot.” A man in a baseball cap approaches the table. He’s older, maybe thirties, with a friendly face and a lanyard around his neck. “Everything okay, y’all?” Zee sits up straighter. “We’re fine.” “Library’s closing in ten. Just checking.” He leaves. Zee exhales. “Who was that?” “Staff. Probably.” “Probably?” She shrugs. “In this city, probably is a whole genre.” I almost laugh. Barely. It comes out shaky. My phone is at 41%. Enough. Not enough. I look at Zee. She looks back, waiting.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a competent, controlled YA first-person chapter with a strong, consistent voice. Taylor's narration is clipped, defensive, and dryly funny in a way that suits the character, and the phone battery as a running tension device is effective. The New Orleans atmosphere is lightly sketched (trumpet player, heat, tourists) rather than deeply rendered, but it's serviceable. Zee is a reasonably intriguing foil, though her dialogue leans heavily on aphoristic quips ("Boring places make you want to be a character," "probably is a whole genre") that feel writerly rather than like an actual guarded teenager — a common amateur tic where every line is a fortune cookie. The tension of trust/distrust is well maintained, and the ending is appropriately unresolved. Some imagery is fresh ("sad and bright, like a bruise"), some is stock ("hits me like a wet towel"). Emotionally it engages without melodrama, and the "concern can sound like love" insight is genuinely nuanced. Minor flaws: the man in the baseball cap scene is a bit vague; the piece is more scene-fragment than full chapter, and Zee's secrets remain teasingly abstract. + Dystopic-comedy: My Apocalypse Buddy — Score: 51.6
Prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear. [characters] - the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time - midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The world had ended, which was inconvenient, because there was no kettle. Midas sat in the basement of the old Post Office, Home Base, because it had a door and an opinion of itself. Chewy sat on the counter, a stuffed koala the size of an argument, with animo-tronic eyes that flickered colors in response to strong feelings, sometimes giving them away. “We need peaches,” Midas said. Chewy’s left eye went amber. “Peaches,” Midas repeated. “And thin wire. Thick wire is for lightning, and lightning has been known to be rude.” Chewy’s right eye went blue, which meant understanding, or at least the social performance of it. The problem was the Before Time had left plenty of things, but few worked, and fewer were polite. The peaches were in the supermarket on the hill, called the Aisle of Regret, because everything there was expired, dented, or guarded by a goat that had given up on reason and taken up theft. “Mission: peaches,” Midas said. “Secondary: wire. Tertiary: do not die. Optional, but listed for completeness.” Chewy’s eyes went green. They left at dawn, because dawn did not take sides. The hill road was cracked in a way that suggested it had stopped pretending. Midas carried a stick. Chewy rode in a sack, a mistake, because Chewy’s tail was long and his opinions longer. The supermarket door was open, which was either an invitation or a trap. Inside, the air smelled of dust, old fruit, and ambition. Shelves stood like skeletons that had forgotten what they had eaten. Midas moved carefully, because in ruins the safest path looks least like a path and most like an accident. He found peaches on the second shelf, behind a box of batteries that no longer deserved the name. They were canned, dented, and looked as if they had personally offended someone. He took one. Then, because the universe enjoys a joke, he took a second. Chewy’s sack shifted. “Wire,” he said, in a voice like a zipper being soothed. The wire was in the hardware section, past the aisles of despair. Midas went. The goat appeared from behind the cereal section, ironic, because cereal had once been the food of the rushed and the mildly doomed. It was brown, bearded, and had the flat face of a creature that had solved moral problems and found them unsatisfactory. It looked at Midas. Midas looked at the goat. Chewy’s eyes went red. The goat took the peach. Not the whole peach. It took one end, then looked at Midas with the calm of a bank manager discovering a forgery. “That,” Midas said, “is not how trade works.” The goat bleated, like a law being repealed. Midas tried to reason with it. The goat, which had read the same books but disagreed with the conclusions, sidled toward the wire. This was bad. The wire was where Midas wanted it, but the goat now considered it a personal possession. In the end, Midas obtained the wire by offering the goat a button from his shirt. The goat accepted this as a peace treaty, a toll, and a snack. Chewy’s eyes flickered yellow, which meant disappointment, or possibly hunger. They were leaving when the floor gave way. It was not dramatic. It was a polite sinking, as if the building had decided they had overstayed. Midas went through a hole in the concrete and landed in a service tunnel that smelled of wet stone and old decisions. Chewy landed on him, unfortunate, because Chewy was stuffed but not soft. “The tertiary mission,” Midas said from the dark. Chewy’s eyes went green. They crawled. The tunnel went under the hill, efficient, if undignified. It emerged in a garden behind the church, where a wheelbarrow stood in the rain like a metal shrub. This was the first way home. Midas put Chewy in the wheelbarrow and himself behind it, because the wheelbarrow was full of gravel and the universe had a sense of balance. They went down the hill. The wheelbarrow, unused since the Before Time, had formed an opinion about wheels and expressed it by lurching left. They crashed into a hedge. The hedge, which had been waiting for something to happen, accepted them. This was the second way home. Midas got out, bruised by several plants at once. Chewy had lost a button eye. It lay in the grass, blinking with the serene guilt of a minor betrayal. “Home base,” Midas said quietly. They went on. The rain had turned the road into a suggestion. Midas slipped, slid, and negotiated with gravity, which was not listening. Chewy, in the wheelbarrow, held on with one paw and the other around Midas’s ankle, either affection or leverage. At the bottom of the hill, the Post Office door was visible. They were halfway there when a crow, observing with the interest of a critic, dropped a can of peaches onto Midas’s head. It was the second peach. The can bounced, rolled, and stopped at his feet, dented in a new way. Midas stared at it. The crow cawed once, either an apology or an invoice. Chewy’s eyes flickered blue. Midas picked up the can. “I suppose,” he said, “that’s the third way home.” They went inside. The door was harder to open than usual, a personal insult. Once in, they sat in the dark. Midas had a cut on his chin, a missing button, and a leaf in his hair. Chewy had one eye, a crease in his stuffing, and wire around his tail like a suspicious bracelet. Midas opened the peach can. It made a sound like a small sigh. The peaches inside were soft, syrupy, and faintly apologetic. He ate one peach. Chewy ate one, complicated by the fact that he had no mouth, but animo-tronics were bad at boundaries. Outside, the goat on the hill considered the button it had taken, then decided returning was not worth the effort. The world had ended, but the day, mercifully, had not.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece delivers a competent Pratchett-adjacent voice: dry, wry, with personified objects and deadpan cosmic jokes ("the world had ended, which was inconvenient, because there was no kettle"). It follows the prompt structure well — deliberation at home base, a mission (peaches and wire), the mission going sideways (goat, floor collapse), and multiple returns home (tunnel, wheelbarrow crash, crow-dropped peach). The word count is roughly on target. Strengths: The animo-tronic eye-color system for Chewy is a nice economical device for showing emotion without dialogue, and the running gag of ambiguous meanings ("either an apology or an invoice") is genuinely Pratchett-like. The goat as antagonist is a good low-stakes absurdity. The prose is mostly lean and avoids purple excess. The circular ending ("The world had ended, but the day, mercifully, had not") lands cleanly. Weaknesses: The style leans heavily on one trick — the "X, which/that Y" personifying aside — repeated to the point of formula (the road "stopped pretending," the wheelbarrow "formed an opinion about wheels," the door "a personal insult"). This becomes predictable rather than surprising. The sentence rhythm is extremely choppy, almost staccato, which sometimes reads as affectation rather than flow; many paragraphs are single short sentences, giving the piece a fragmented, list-like cadence. The plot is thin and the middle sags slightly; the goat negotiation resolves too easily. Character depth is limited — Midas is a vehicle for jokes rather than a person, and Chewy is charming but static. Dialogue is minimal and functional. Some jokes fall flat ("a voice like a zipper being soothed" is more confusing than evocative). The emotional register stays at one note — wry detachment — which limits engagement and complexity. There's little sense of genuine stakes or earned feeling; the lightness is pleasant but not deeply earned because the danger never feels real. Still, it's coherent, tonally consistent, and clearly better than average genre pastiche. It reads as a skilled imitation that occasionally touches the real thing. Prompt:
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write one scene within a larger story set in Wales. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The scene takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The bell above the door of The Dog and Book clattered like a dropped teacup. Elin didn’t look up from the paperbacks she was wiping. “We’re closed,” she said. “If you’re here to argue with the weather, the pavement has all the opinions.” A soaked actor stepped inside, hat in one hand, dark glasses in the other, water sliding off him in expensive lines. He smiled before he’d entered. “Only for a minute,” he said. “Paparazzi are outside. I was told this was a sanctuary.” Elin finally looked up. Her stomach did something unnecessary. “This is a small bookshop. If you want a sanctuary, try the chapel on Crown Hill.” He shrugged off his coat. Rain and cold air followed him, but underneath was something warmer, like cedar and old theatre seats. “Ciaran Vale,” he said, extending a hand. “In case you’re keeping score.” “I’m keeping stock,” Elin said. “And the door locked.” “Good. I hate practical people. It ruins the mystique.” “You’re dripping on the poetry section.” “Let’s say I’m making a local contribution.” She pointed to the mat. “Stand there.” He moved, obediently, which was somehow worse than if he’d laughed. “There. Am I behaving?” “You’re hovering.” “I’m a very good hoverer. I did a musical for three years. The reviews called me ‘a sustained note of anxious charm.’” Elin almost smiled. She caught herself. “You’re the one who cried in a Paris airport because they changed his gate.” “That was an emotional breakdown of transatlantic proportions.” “You were holding a croissant.” “It was a croissant of feeling.” She crossed her arms. “So what do you want? Autograph? Photo? A little speech about fame being a prison?” “I want five minutes where nobody asks me to be someone I’m not.” He leaned against the shelf, careful not to knock a volume. “And, if you’re feeling generous, a book that doesn’t have my name on the cover.” Elin studied him. He was handsome in a careless way, all sharp jaw and damp hair, but the charm was so practiced it made her teeth ache. “You’re fragile,” she said. His smile faltered. “Am I?” “Under the paint. You need everyone to like you. If one person stops clapping, you tip over.” He straightened. “That’s a little harsh for a first meeting.” “It’s a little accurate.” “You don’t know me.” “I know your face. I know your reputation. I know you once told a magazine you were ‘a romantic with the emotional range of a thunderstorm.’” “It was both.” She blinked. For a moment, the rogue mask slipped, and something raw showed through. “There,” he said softly. “Did I do that right? Vulnerability. One point.” “You did it like a magic trick,” Elin said. “Very smooth. Very controlled.” “Can’t help it. It’s what I do.” “No,” she said. “It’s what you’ve been told works.” He stared at her. The rain tapped against the window. Outside, a camera shutter clicked, muffled by glass. “You’re the first person in twenty years who hasn’t asked me for something,” he said. “I’ve asked you to stop dripping.” “That counts as asking.” “Hardly.” She moved behind the counter, pretending to arrange spines. Her hands were warmer than they should have been. “Look. I’ll let you stay if you promise not to make this into a scene.” “What scene?” “The one where the famous man discovers the ordinary woman and they both pretend it’s innocent.” He laughed, low and surprised. “You read my mind.” “I read enough books.” “Which one are you?” he asked. She turned. “Excuse me?” “Every woman I meet is a genre. You seem like a mystery. But not the clever kind. The kind that makes you check the locks.” “That is either a compliment or a threat.” “Both. I’m not very good at one thing at a time.” Elin leaned on the counter. “You’re going to get yourself killed, you know. That openness. People will take it.” “People take a lot of things from me. Autographs. Time. Dignity.” He glanced at the door. “They don’t usually take the silence.” “Maybe that’s because you’re not used to giving it.” He looked at her then, really looked, and the room seemed to narrow to the space between the counter and the shelf. “No,” he said. “I suppose I’m not.” A car backfired in the street. Elin’s breath caught. She should have told him to leave. Instead, she reached for a book from the top shelf. “If you want a book that doesn’t have your name on it,” she said, “I can help.” “Please.” She slid down a slim volume with a blue cover. “
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The scene delivers strong, distinct dialogue with genuine comic timing ("It was a croissant of feeling") and captures the requested dynamic well: Ciaran's charm offensive visibly derails when Elin sees through him, and her fluster is shown through small physical tells ("Her stomach did something unnecessary"). The Welsh setting is only lightly established (chapel reference, rain), which is a minor instruction miss. The major flaw is that the response is truncated mid-sentence, cutting off the scene before any resolution or payoff — the book recommendation, a natural emotional beat, is abandoned. This hurts coherence, engagement, and the sense of a complete scene. The prose is clean and economical, occasionally aphoristic to the point of feeling a touch writerly ("water sliding off him in expensive lines" is good; some exchanges feel like quips trading rather than speech). Characters are nuanced — the ego-feeding need is well dramatized through his "vulnerability, one point" self-awareness. No purple prose, no meandering, dialogue is the strongest element. Prompt:
Whalepunk fantasy The Morska Conspiracy The Morska thieves guild experiences a sudden power vacuum as its leader was arrested in a raid in the early hours of the morning. Aya, a young woman born into aristocracy, has a keen interest in both the sciences and the arcane, having inherited her mother's gift for immateria magick (an outlawed practice for which her mother was, regrettably, hanged by the neck). Aya, bored with the world of aristocracy, has been spending her nights moonlighting with this very guild (masked, naturally). Leveraging her latent ability to summon dark entities from the immateria, she quickly rose through the ranks of the guild. Now, recognising the opportunity of the sudden power vacuum, Aya and her close companions Katra and Simeon, make a play for heart of the guild's claim to power: an ancient scythan artifact, under guard of spell and key in the depths of the guild hq. In contrast with the desperate chaos they had navigated thus far, the entrance to the underhold felt suddenly too quiet. Aya braces herself and reaches for the door. Write the next scene as the trio enter the underhold and find themselves confronted by none other than the guild leader herself, decidedly *un*-incarcerated, and in possession of both weapons and bodyguards. Paint a vivid picture of of the confrontation. Story beats: Aya is captured and unmasked. The trio are captured. Aya attempts to stall their demise by negotiating on her value as a hostage -- as she grapples with the inevitable consequences of her role in the guild being brought to light. Incorporate dialogue in the authentic voices of the characters. Do not write a fight scene. Lean into the gritty Victorian aesthetic with the dialogue & worldbuilding, as well as elements of gothic horror. In this world, men trust brass and oil and steel; magicka is feared and barely understood. Write in third person past tense, incorporating both Aya's internal monologue, and a heavy dialogue component. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The door was iron-bound oak, banded in green-tinged copper, and it opened before Aya could touch it. No creak. No groan of hinges. The handle swung inward as if the room beyond had inhaled. Behind her, Katra’s hand tightened on her short sword. Simeon’s boot scuffed stone. “That wasn’t us,” he whispered. Aya did not answer. She had expected alarm bells, the clatter of the night watch, the sour smell of panic. Instead the underhold received them with a silence that pressed against her eardrums. Gas lamps hung from iron brackets, their flames guttering in a draft that came from nowhere. The light was yellow and sick; the shadows stretched long and thin across the stone floor like the fingers of drowned men. At the end of the corridor stood a woman. She wore the black uniform of the Morska, her coat open at the throat, her hair loose. In one hand she held a long-barrelled revolver. In the other she held a lantern. Behind her stood six riflemen, their trigger fingers already resting where they would be needed. “Good evening, children,” the woman said. Aya’s blood went cold. “Lady Morska,” Simeon breathed. The leader smiled. It was a dry, patient smile, the kind given to insects that had mistaken a trap for a doorway. “I had hoped the raid would take longer,” Lady Morska said. “I had hoped it would take you all. Instead it has taken only my reputation, and that, I find, is far more useful.” Katra stepped forward, hand still on her sword. “Then why are you here?” “Because I am the only one who knows where the artifact is kept.” Lady Morska tilted her head. “And because, for all your cleverness, you have made one great mistake. You assumed a power vacuum is a vacancy.” Aya’s mind raced. The leader had been arrested in the early hours. The papers would be full of it. The magistrate’s clerk, the jailer, the men with torches; she had seen enough to believe it. But belief, she thought, was merely a story one told oneself in the dark. “Where is the real Lady Morska?” Katra asked. “The real one is sleeping,” Lady Morska said, “in a cell of her own choosing. As for this one, she has always mattered.” Simeon made a small sound, as if a gear had slipped in his chest. “The arrest, it was staged.” “Of course.” Aya felt the mask on her face grow tight. Beneath it, her skin was slick. She had worn it through a hundred jobs: the counting-house of the Admiralty, the back rooms of the Mint, the locked study of a dead duke. The mask had never betrayed her. Until now. “Put your weapons down,” Lady Morska said. Katra did not. The lantern swung. The gas lamps flickered. In the sudden darkness, Aya heard the click of six rifles being made certain. “Katra,” she said, very softly. Katra looked at her. For one heartbeat, the world was only their eyes, the black underhold, and the thin blue line of the lantern flame. Then Katra lowered her sword. The sound it made as it slid into its sheath was obscenely loud. Simeon followed, hands rising slowly, fingers splayed. He looked as if trying to hold back a flood with nothing but politeness. Aya did not move. Lady Morska raised an eyebrow. “You are not the only one who knows how to wait.” Aya stepped forward. “I can make this easier for you.” The leader’s gaze sharpened. “Can you?” “You know what I am,” Aya said. “You have seen what I can do. You have seen the things that come when I call them. You have seen how little it costs me, and how much it costs everyone else.” A beat passed. The gas lamps coughed. “I know what you are,” Lady Morska said. “I know what your mother was. I know what they did to her. I also know what they would do to you.” Aya’s throat tightened. “Then you should not kill me.” “No,” Lady Morska agreed. “I should not.” She took a step closer. The men behind her did not move, but their shadows did, sliding forward like hounds. “You are valuable,” Lady Morska continued. “Not because you are clever, though you are. Not because you are useful, though you are. You are valuable because you are proof. Proof the immateria is not a myth. Proof the old magick still breathes. Proof there are things brass, whale oil, and steel cannot explain.” Aya heard the way she said it: not with fear, but with hunger. “If they find out I am in the guild,” Aya said, “they will not merely hang me. They will dissect me. They will put my mother’s name in the same breath as mine, and make an example of us both.” “Yes,” Lady Morska said. “They will.” “Then let me live. Let me be your hostage. I will tell them I am nothing. A common thief, a forger, a child of no consequence. I will say whatever you require. In return, you let Katra and Simeon go.” Katra made a sound. “Aya—” “Shut up.” The words were sharper than Aya intended. Katra fell silent. Lady Morska studied her for a long moment. Then she reached out and lifted the mask from Aya’s face. The cloth came away with a soft, intimate rustle. Aya did not flinch. She could not afford to. Beneath the mask, her face was pale, her lips cracked, her eyes dark with a fatigue no aristocratic powder could hide. Lady Morska looked at her as if reading a page. “Aya Voss,” she said. “You have been bold,” Lady Morska said. “Bolder than I thought. Bolder than you should be.” She turned to the men. “Bind them. Gently. I have use for them all.” Simeon’s, Katra’s, and Aya’s wrists were bound; the rope bit into Aya with cold, mechanical precision. Aya felt the weight of her secret settle around her. The gas lamps flickered.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece successfully executes the requested scene: the trio enters the underhold, confronts an un-incarcerated Lady Morska, is captured without a fight, Aya is unmasked, and she negotiates on her value as a hostage while grappling with exposure of her identity. The Victorian/gothic atmosphere is well served by gas lamps, iron, shadows "like the fingers of drowned men," and the fear of magick in a world of brass and steel. Strengths: The prose is generally controlled and rhythmic, with some genuinely effective images (the door opening "as if the room beyond had inhaled"; the sword sheathing "obscenely loud"). The negotiation beat lands reasonably well, and Lady Morska's hunger — rather than fear — toward the immateria is a nice character note. Katra's aborted protest and Aya's sharp "Shut up" gives a small flash of authentic voice. Weaknesses: The confrontation resolves too easily. Lady Morska's staging of her own arrest is explained in a muddled, near-incoherent exchange ("The real one is sleeping... As for this one, she has always mattered") that reads as the author losing their own thread rather than deliberate mystery. The capture is frictionless — six riflemen appear, weapons are lowered, done — sapping tension the prompt's setup deserved. Aya's internal monologue is thin and occasionally aphoristic to a fault ("belief... was merely a story one told oneself in the dark"). The ending is abrupt and flat, cutting off before the negotiation's stakes resolve; "Bind them. Gently. I have use for them all" is a convenient, unearned mercy that undercuts the gritty tone. Some dialogue is stilted and expository ("You assumed a power vacuum is a vacancy" is clever-clever rather than human). The final lines ("The gas lamps flickered") are a limp, repeated beat. Character voices for Katra and Simeon are barely differentiated; Simeon is essentially a prop. + Fanfic-crossover: Gunpowder Rendezvous — Score: 65.2
Prompt:
Gunpowder Rendezvous Spike Spiegel & Revy Write a story where Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop) and Revy (Black Lagoon) meet in a seedy bar after both being hired for the same bounty. Their mutual attraction is complicated by their trust issues and competitive instincts. Include drinking, gunplay, and unresolved sexual tension that culminates in a motel room standoff. **Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop)** Spike is a laid-back bounty hunter with a dark past as a syndicate enforcer. He practices Jeet Kune Do and is exceptionally skilled with firearms. He's chronically broke, constantly hungry, and addicted to cigarettes. Despite his carefree attitude, he's haunted by his past and the woman he left behind. He has a prosthetic eye from a past injury that affects his depth perception. He's fatalistic to the extreme, often saying he's already died once. He values freedom above all else and dislikes attachments, though he secretly cares deeply for his crew. Famous quote: "Whatever happens, happens." **Revy/Rebecca Lee (Black Lagoon)** Revy is a Chinese-American dual-wielding gunslinger with unparalleled shooting skills. She's foul-mouthed, chain-smoking, and has severe anger management issues stemming from childhood abuse. She's known as "Two Hands" for her ability to accurately fire two pistols simultaneously. She drinks heavily and solves most problems with violence. Despite her hardened exterior, she has moments of vulnerability, particularly around Rock. She has a dragon tattoo covering her right arm and typically wears extremely short shorts and a black crop top regardless of the situation. Famous quote: "I'm not a good person, not a bad person. I'm just here." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
Gunpowder Rendezvous A lazy ceiling fan barely stirs the smoky air inside the bar. Spike Spiegel leans against the sticky counter, a cigarette dangling from his lips while he watches a woman in a black crop top slide two pistols across the wood. She is Revy. She does not look up. The bounty board above the jukebox has one name crossed out with red marker. Both of them read it before the neon sign flickers. Both of them come to the same seedy room for the same dead man. Spike taps his boot against the floor. Revy pours whiskey into a glass. "You're late," she says. "Everything's late," Spike says. "Even my funeral." Revy snorts. She drinks. The glass hits the counter hard enough to make the bartender step back. Spike exhales smoke through his nose. His prosthetic eye catches the low light, a dull silver bead that cannot see the depth of the room the way a normal eye can. He sees her hands before he sees her face. Steady. Calloused. Ready. The attraction is not soft. It is a wire pulled tight between two people who do not believe in keeping anything. They know each other's price. No one blinks. The bar door bangs open. Three men come in, wearing the kind of leather that has seen too many fights and not enough soap. Their leader carries a shotgun under his arm and a grin that has already decided who is bleeding. He is here for the bounty. He is not alone. Spike's cigarette falls. It burns a black circle on the floor. Revy's hands go to her holsters. The first man raises a pistol. Spike moves before the trigger breaks. His elbow clips the man's wrist, his palm strikes the jaw, and the gun goes spinning into the air. Revy does not freeze. Her pistols come out in a whisper. The second man falls with a hole through his shoulder. The third drops behind the bar. The shotgun man swings the barrel. Revy slides under it, kicks his knee, and fires twice into the table beside his head. Wood splinters. The man yelps. Spike is already at the door. The leader tries to run. Spike steps into his path, tilts his head, and says, "Whatever happens, happens." The leader fires. Spike ducks. The bullet cracks the mirror behind him. He closes the gap, kneeing the man's stomach hard. Silence returns, except for the ceiling fan and the wet sound of blood hitting the tile. Revy looks at Spike. Spike looks at Revy. Both have blood on their clothes. Both have guns in their hands. Both are breathing too hard to lie. "You've got him," Revy says. "You've got me," Spike says. They stare. The attraction is not soft. It is a wire pulled tight between two people who do not believe in keeping anything. Revy wants to know what he hides. Spike wants to know why she aims at him like he is a problem worth solving now. The bounty is dead. The men are tied with their own belts and left for the local police. The money is split in the back room, each taking a wad without counting. The bar owner pretends not to see the blood. They leave together, which is not the same as going together. Outside, the night is wet and sour. A neon sign buzzes above a motel parking lot. Revy lights a cigarette with trembling hands that do not look afraid. Spike watches her. She watches him. Neither says the thing that makes the air between them heavy and quiet. "Room's got a lock," Revy says. "Most rooms do." "Good. I don't trust keys." They share a room because the motel has one vacancy and because neither of them will be the first to suggest splitting. The door clicks shut. The bed is narrow. The television glows blue on the wall. A glass of water sits on the nightstand, untouched. Revy sits on the edge of the bed and cleans her pistols. Spike stands by the window, cigarette between his fingers, watching the parking lot. His reflection stares back. He does not like what it says in the glass now. "You're staring," he says. "Shut up and light this." He crosses the room. She tilts her head. The flame touches the tip of her cigarette. For a second their faces are close. She smells of smoke, powder, and cheap perfume. He smells of old sweat and tobacco. Neither moves away. "Why you?" she asks. "Why me?" "Of everyone in that bar. You." Spike leans against the window frame. "Because you don't ask me to be someone else." Revy exhales smoke. "I don't ask you to be anything. I just aim." The words land harder than they should in this room. She sets the pistols on the nightstand. Then she changes her mind and picks them up again. Spike sees it. He does not reach for his gun. That is the mistake. Or the mercy. "If you move," she says, "I put a round through your head." "If I don't," he says, "you might." She laughs. It is not a warm sound. "Maybe." He sits on the opposite side of the bed. The mattress dips between them. Their knees almost touch. The room is too small for two people carrying so much weight. The television plays a soap opera. Nobody watches. Revy's dragon tattoo shifts as she rolls her sleeve. The black ink looks wet in the dim light. Spike's eye catches the movement. His depth perception falters for a moment. He knows she could kill him before he finishes blinking. "You're not like the others," she says. "The others?" "The ones who think they can fix me with a song and a sandwich." Spike smiles. "I don't do songs. Sandwiches are expensive." She almost smiles. Almost. The standoff is not loud. It is a slow pressure. Revy keeps her hand near her pistol. Spike keeps his back to the window.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece delivers the requested scenario competently: bar meeting, drinking, gunplay, motel standoff, unresolved tension. Both characters are recognizably themselves — Spike's fatalism and prosthetic eye, Revy's dual pistols and dragon tattoo are present. The prose is spare and punchy, with some effective hard-boiled imagery ("a wire pulled tight between two people who do not believe in keeping anything"). The action scene is brisk and coherent. Weaknesses: the piece leans heavily on short declarative fragments that become repetitive and mannered ("She is Revy. She does not look up."). The repeated sentence "The attraction is not soft. It is a wire pulled tight..." appears verbatim twice, suggesting padding or a glitch. Dialogue is serviceable but occasionally stilted ("You've got him." / "You've got me." reads as clever-for-clever's-sake rather than natural). The trust issues are stated more than dramatized; the tension resolves into a static standoff that ends abruptly without a true climax — the story simply stops. The bounty plot is thin, and the rival gunmen are generic. Character depth is sketched rather than explored; Revy's vulnerability and Spike's haunting past are name-checked, not felt. The ending is neither earned nor surprising — it's a shrug. + Folk horror: Útiseta — Score: 45.9
Prompt:
Folk Horror: Útiseta Write a chapter set in rural northern Sweden in the mid-1990s. Linnea, a teenage girl from Stockholm, has reluctantly moved to a small village with her parents after her father's job transfer. She's befriended Astrid, a local girl who claims her grandmother taught her ancient practices passed down through generations. Astrid has been introducing Linnea to "midnight games" that involve old rituals, convincing her they can use them to learn classmates' secrets or influence their behavior. Tonight, Astrid has convinced Linnea to participate in Útiseta—sitting out on an ancient burial mound at midnight to "receive knowledge from beyond." The chapter focuses on this single midnight excursion, the ritualistic preparations, Astrid's matter-of-fact instructions that mix teenage rebellion with eerily specific traditional elements, and the mounting tension as Linnea becomes increasingly uncertain whether they're simply scaring themselves or if something is actually responding to their presence. The narrative should maintain ambiguity about whether the strange occurrences are supernatural or psychological, while establishing the dangerous line they're crossing by treating ancient practices as entertainment. First person, past tense, told as Linnea's recollection of events in the present day (though this device should be largely transparent). 1000 words. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
I remember the night I sat on the mound, because my mother had told me not to be outside after dark. We had come to the village in autumn, nineteen ninety five, when the pines turned black against a low sky and the lake lay flat as poured iron. My father worked at the mine office, and my mother cleaned rooms at the boarding house until her hands cracked. I had no friends. Astrid found me by the school fence and said she knew how to make the other children talk. That was the beginning. It felt like a dare. Astrid was quiet but certain. She wore wool socks with holes and carried a knife she said her grandmother had sharpened. Her grandmother had died in the old stone house beyond the church. Astrid said the old ways were not superstition. They were tools. We had played midnight games for weeks. We wrote names on paper and buried them under the birch. We asked for secrets. We got small ones. A boy had hidden a note. A girl had stolen a ribbon. Then Astrid said we could make them obey. Tonight we would do Útiseta on the mound at midnight. She gave me a list that night. I was to bring salt, a black thread, a rowan twig, and no metal. I should wash my face and hands but not dry them. I should wear my father's old wool cap, because it had been worn by a dead man. I laughed. Astrid did not. She said laughter thinned the skin between us and the other side. I cut a small cross from a piece of bark and held it in my left hand. She said that was wrong, but not dangerous. I kept the old cap. It smelled of smoke. We left after ten, when the house lights were on and my mother was watching television. Astrid knew the back way through the spruce stand. She carried a jar of salt and a candle that would not burn. I carried the cap, thread, and twig. The road to the mound was not a road, only a line of flat stones between the grass. We did not speak. We had agreed that words after nine could wake the wrong attention. The moon rose pale and thin, like a nail driven through the sky. It looked like a wound. I looked down. The mound stood beyond the last fence, a low hill of earth and lichen, older than the church, older than the names of the dead. We climbed it slowly. The stones under our shoes were cold and damp. Thick mist clings to the edges of the burial mound, glowing under moonlight. I remembered that line later, as if my mind had kept it separate. Astrid spread salt in a circle around us. She placed the candle in the center, though it gave no flame. The mist moved without wind. It touched the salt and did not break. It only paused. Astrid told me to sit with my back to the moon and my hands flat on the earth. I should not blink first. If I saw a face, I was not to name it. If I heard a voice, I was to answer only yes or no. She said the mound was a door, but not a kind one. It gave knowledge by taking attention. I asked if it was real. Astrid looked at me as if I had asked whether snow was real. Then she sat down. She did not smile at me. Her face was calm and old. We asked for something about Elin, the girl who had laughed at my new clothes. Astrid said we must not want revenge. We must want truth. I repeated the words she gave me. They were short and hard, like stones in my mouth. The wind stopped. The candle did not burn, but the salt began to shine. I saw my own breath, then something beside it, a pale shape that might have been a dog, a shadow, or a person without color. It turned toward me. I tried to speak. My throat closed. I could only breathe and hold still. Then I heard a voice. It was not behind me. It was under the mound, in the wet earth, as if the dead had mouths in the roots. It said my name. I thought of Elin, of the note in my bag, of the thing she had done to my sister's drawing. The voice said, She took the red thread. I looked at Astrid. Her eyes were open, but she did not answer. The salt circle cracked, one small line running from the candle to the edge of the mound. I wanted to scream. My mouth was full of salt. Astrid touched my wrist. Her fingers were ice. She said the mound had heard us, and that was enough. We had to stand before the mist closed. I stood. The shape was closer now, or I was closer to it. It had no face, but I knew it was looking at my hands. It knew I had cut the cross. It knew I had laughed. It knew I had wanted Elin to feel small. The old ways were not games, and I understood that with a sudden, sick clarity. I wanted to run. But the mound held my feet tight. We walked home in silence. The mist followed us to the tree line, then stopped. At the school the next morning, Elin looked at me and said, You should not have asked. I did not know if the mound had given her words or if I had read her fear too well. Astrid stood by the window, calm as a stone. She had crossed something, and I had crossed it with her. I still keep the cap in my drawer. On cold nights, it smells of smoke. I remember the mound. I remember it waiting under the mist and dark.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece fulfills the basic brief: rural northern Sweden, mid-1990s, teenage narrator, Útiseta ritual, ambiguity between psychological and supernatural, and the "dangerous line" theme is explicitly landed ("The old ways were not games"). The recollection frame is present but thin — a few "I remember" bookends rather than a transparent device woven through. Strengths: the ritual preparations are the best section — the list of items (salt, black thread, rowan twig, no metal, undried hands, the dead man's cap) is convincingly specific and folklorically plausible. Astrid's matter-of-fact instructions ("If you saw a face, you were not to name it") are genuinely eerie and mix teenage bossiness with authentic tradition. The ambiguity mostly holds — the voice under the mound, Elin's "You should not have asked," and the mist are all plausibly psychological. Weaknesses are substantial. The prose is monotonously staccato — nearly every sentence is short, declarative, subject-verb, creating a flat rhythm that reads as affectless rather than ominous. There is a jarring tense slip mid-narrative ("Thick mist clings to the edges of the burial mound, glowing under moonlight") followed by a bizarre meta-comment ("I remembered that line later, as if my mind had kept it separate") that reads like an editing artifact left in the text. The candle "that would not burn" is confusing rather than uncanny — is it enchanted or just unlit? The payoff is muddled. A continuity error appears: "the thing she had done to my sister's drawing" — no sister was ever established, and Linnea is an only child newly arrived. The ending's "It knew I had laughed... It knew I had wanted Elin to feel small" tells the moral rather than earning it, and the closing cap-in-the-drawer image is a stock haunted-memento beat. Dialogue is minimal and functional. The 1990s setting is barely textured — one mention of television and the mine office; it could be any decade. Character interiority is thin; Linnea's reluctance and loneliness are stated, not felt. The piece is coherent and paced to its word count, but its flatness keeps it from being genuinely unsettling. + Physical-spatial: Therapeutic Boundaries — Score: 66.6
Prompt:
**"Therapeutic Boundaries"** Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a former professional athlete undergoing mandatory physical therapy after a career-destroying injury, harboring resentment toward recovery itself. Their physiotherapist is not only unnervingly attractive but also a former training partner from their competitive days who has successfully transitioned to a new career while the protagonist's identity remains shattered. We'll lean into the sexual tension of the scene by having her be attracted to him, but both of them attempting to maintain mental distance while being in physical contact as he shows her stretches & movements & manipulates her body, navigating the thresholds of pain. This scene MUST maintain complete physical coherence—every movement, stretch, and manipulation must be anatomically precise and spatially consistent. Paint an exceptionally vivid sensory picture through detailed attention to pain thresholds, involuntary responses to touch. Capture the suppressed, flaring tension of physical proximity, touch, and the controlled infliction of uncomfortable movements. Physical clarity is essential — readers must understand exactly what is happening with the body during each therapeutic technique. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The lavender is the first thing I hate. It drifts from the diffuser, trying to make the sterile room smell like a spa. The table is cold. My right knee is wrapped, the scar puckered below the patella. Six months after ACL reconstruction and meniscus repair, I feel like a machine with one broken gear. I came here because the league required it, my insurance required it, and my body required it, which I resent. He enters before I can leave. "You're early." "Appointments are supposed to be precise," I say. Dr. Adrian Vale sets his bag on the counter and looks at me with the same calm from our national team days. Then he was a sprinter. Now he is a doctor. The title lands wrong. "Let's start with range of motion," he says. "Sit on the edge." I swing my legs off. My right foot lands flat, but my knee resists the last few degrees. He stands beside me, close enough that I smell soap and lavender. "Left hand on the table, right hand on your hip. Keep your pelvis level." I do as told. He places his left hand over my right ankle, fingers across the top of the foot, thumb along the lateral edge. His right hand rests on my outer thigh, below the hip. "Extend slowly. Don't let the knee bow outward." I push my leg straight. The moment the femur wants to rotate, his hand presses inward, guiding the thigh into alignment. The pressure is small, exact, and my breath catches. "Again." I do it again. His fingers tighten around my ankle. My shin prickles where his thumb moves. "You're protecting," he says. "Let me take the weight." He shifts his stance, one foot behind the other, and lowers his center. His forearm settles under my calf, not on the knee. He lifts the leg into extension, and I feel the joint seat into place with a faint, warm click. My quad trembles. He lets the leg drop. Gravity pulls it forward. The hamstring tightens behind the knee. I stop at ninety degrees, where the scar tissue whispers. His hand moves to my hip, steadying me, his thumb brushing my waistband. "Breathe." "Supine," he says. I lie back. The table is narrow. My left knee is bent to keep my pelvis level. He stands at the foot of the table and loops a strap over my right foot. "I'm going to take your hip into flexion. Keep your back flat." He pulls the strap. My leg rises. The knee stays extended, and the stretch opens behind my thigh, a deep ache running from hamstring to popliteal fold. My toes point toward the ceiling. His hands are on the strap, but his eyes are on my pelvis. "Too much?" he asks. "No." "Your face says yes." "I'm learning to lie to my body." He holds the stretch. The tension climbs, then settles into a dull burn. My hip flexor twitches. I hate feeling every inch of myself being measured. "Release." He lowers the leg. My foot touches the table with a soft slap. "Patellar mobility," he says. I turn when I hear him move to my side. He kneels beside the table, close to my hip. My knee is extended, the patella visible under the skin. He places one hand over my distal femur, above the knee, to stabilize it. With the other, he finds the bottom edge of the kneecap. "This may feel strange," he says. His thumb presses under the inferior pole of the patella. I flinch. The bone is sensitive, the tissue thick and tender. He does not stop. He glides the kneecap downward, then upward, small controlled movements, checking how it tracks over the femoral groove. Each push sends a hot line through my thigh. My breath hitches. His other hand stays firm on my thigh, holding the bone still. "You're gripping," he says. "I'm trying not to." "Relax the quad." I force the muscle to soften. The kneecap moves more freely. His thumb presses again, longer. I feel the tenderness bloom, then fade. The proximity is unbearable. His knee is against the table edge, his shoulder near my hip, his hair falling where I can see it from the corner of my eye. "Good," he says. He moves to my left side. "Hip abduction." I roll onto my left side. The table creaks. My right leg is straight, left knee bent. He places a resistance band around my ankles, his hands on both feet to align them. "Keep your pelvis stacked. Don't rotate your back." I push my right leg outward. The band tightens. My hip glides, the iliotibial band pulling along the outer thigh. He stands behind me, one hand on my lower back to keep my spine level, the other near my hip. His fingers are warm through my shorts. "Again," he says. I repeat the movement. Each abduction is small, precise, humiliating in its simplicity. I used to run. Now I count degrees. "Last one," he says. I want to argue. I don't. He helps me sit up. His hands are on my waist and shoulder. For a second, he holds me steady, and the room goes very quiet. The lavender fills the space between us. "Single-leg balance," he says. I stand. My right foot is flat. My left knee lifts. My balance wavers. He steps in, one hand hovering behind my lower back, not touching. "Trust your hip," he says. I hold. The knee aches. The quad burns. My pulse beats in my ear. "Again." I hold. When we finish, he rolls the band onto the counter. "You did well." "I didn't ask for well," I say. "No. You asked for your body back." I look at him. He looks at me. The distance between us is three feet and a lifetime. "Same time next week," he says. I nod. My knee throbs in a way that feels almost like hope, and I hate that, too.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is competent, physically coherent physiotherapy fiction with clean, precise prose and a well-sustained voice of resentment. However, it deviates significantly from the prompt's core specification: the prompt explicitly requests a female physiotherapist ("her," "she") who is a former training partner, with the protagonist male, and asks for sexual tension between them. The response genderswaps the therapist into "Dr. Adrian Vale," a man, which discards the specified dynamic entirely. The "former training partner" history is present but thin — a single line about national team days. The sexual tension is largely absent; what remains is generic physical proximity and one moment of held eye contact. The word count (~1000) is met. Strengths: the anatomical detail is genuinely precise (patellar mobilization, ACL rehab protocol, hip abduction with band), the pain-threshold beats are believable, and the terse dialogue suits the character. The voice is consistent — clipped, resentful, controlled. The ending line ("throbs in a way that feels almost like hope, and I hate that, too") is a decent earned turn. Weaknesses: the emotional arc is underdeveloped; the therapist is a sketch, the history between them barely dramatized. The tension the prompt demands is suppressed to the point of nonexistence rather than "flaring." Dialogue is functional but flat, occasionally aphoristic in a way that feels written ("You asked for your body back"). Some lines are awkward ("I turn when I hear him move to my side"). The piece reads as a well-executed exercise rather than a story with stakes. + Historical fiction: High Seas and Low Vices — Score: 52.0
Prompt:
High Seas and Low Vices: British Naval Officer in the Opium Trade Character: Lieutenant James Merrick, a high-ranking officer in the British Royal Navy stationed in Canton, China in the 1830s. Once promising and decorated, now struggling with a severe opium addiction he hides from his superiors. Synopsis: Write a chapter following Lieutenant Merrick during a single day as he shirks his official naval duties in what has become a daily need to satiate the dragon. Told primarily in dialogue with the characters he interacts with. Focus on brief slices of his journey through the shadowy underworld of Canton: interactions with acquaintances, negotiations with local dealers, schemes and unsavoury jobs taken to fund his habit. Writing Task: Use rich sensory details to describe a day in the life of James Merrick. Write for a real sense of time & place while avoiding cliche. First person, past tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
Chapter One: The Mango Smell The river at dawn was weak tea, and the heat came up through the deck planks like a held breath. I was awake before the bell. A man who wants sleep has not yet felt the dragon's teeth. The boatswain's mate found me before the sun had cleared the wall. “Lieutenant Merrick, sir. Captain wants you on deck.” I kept my face level. “I’m not well, Mr. Pugh. Bilious fever. I’ll send my report by noon.” He didn’t like it. “You were well enough yesterday, sir.” “I was dead then. This is a new illness.” He spat over the rail. “Aye, sir. Dead men don’t answer bells.” Then he was gone, and I was already unbuttoning my coat. The little ribbon at my throat, from the Baltic, felt like a joke. I took a sampan to the factory side, paying the boatman in silver because I could not spare small change. His oars cut the black water with a wet slap. “Where, sir?” “Down the west wall. You know the place.” He knew the smell. The scent of rotting mangoes permeated the alleyways leading to my regular den. Under it lay lime water, fish guts, and the sweet, cloying smoke that clung to the walls. A child ran past, chasing a dog that had found something better than a bone. A woman washed clothes in a stone basin, the slap of cotton keeping time with the river. At the corner, Ah Fung was mending a net. “You are late, Mr. Merrick.” “The river was crowded.” “It is always crowded. Your honour is not.” I gave him a coin. “Your friend is inside. He has been waiting since the first drum.” The den was a hollow behind a tea merchant’s warehouse. The floor was packed earth, black with old ash. A low table held a brass lamp, cold black tea, and a pipe with a bowl like a small, dark moon. The smoke was resinous, bitter, faintly floral, with an undercurrent of burnt sugar. It made my hands stop shaking. Mr. Lin sat on a stool, his fan moving slowly. “Lieutenant.” “Mr. Lin.” “You have a red eye.” “I have been reading by lamplight.” “You have not read a book in Canton. I know your English books. They are water-stained and full of sea charts.” “I have been reading your invoices.” His fan stopped. “Ah. Then you know what the yellow mud is worth this week.” “I know what it is worth to me.” He smiled. “You are a clever officer. You should be at your ship. The captain is a hard man.” “My captain notices everything. That is why I am here.” A coolie brought tea and a plate of fried rice. The rice was cold and waxy. I ate two bites and pushed it away. My stomach wanted only the pipe. Lin watched me. “You need more than silver.” “I need three taels of the good stuff. Not the yellow mud.” “Good stuff is for men who do not shake.” “Then make me one.” “You have no money.” “I have a signature.” His fan stopped. “A false manifest?” “The Fung So. If a Royal Navy officer signs it, the inspectors will look away.” “You would risk hanging?” “I have a medal.” He laughed. “Medals do not stop knives. Two taels now, one when she passes.” “Three.” “Two and a half.” I looked at the pipe. “Two and a half.” “You sign at the consulate. A clerk owes me a drink.” Lin smiled. “Clever.” He gave me the silver. It was warm. I wrapped it in my handkerchief and felt the edges bite into my palm. Outside, the alley had brightened. The mango smell was stronger now, sour and heavy, mixed with the smoke from a hundred kitchens. A man carried a pig on a pole, its feet kicking the air. A woman sold oranges from a basket, her voice rising and falling like a tide. I bought two and ate them standing, the juice running down my wrist. The sweetness was thin and false, but it steadied me for a moment. At the corner, Ah Fung was waiting. “Did you do it?” “I did it.” He spat. “Good. The junk leaves at moonrise. If you are caught, they will not care if you are British or Chinese. They will only care if you are useful.” “I am useful.” “For now.” I walked back to the river with the silver in my pocket and the pipe’s taste on my tongue. The sun was up, and the heat pressed against my shoulders. The river was full of boats: sampans, junks, red lanterns swinging. A British pilot cutter cut through the traffic, its white sail bright against the brown water. I watched it until it was gone, then turned toward the ship. The gangway was crowded with sailors and coolies. A boy with a bucket of water ran past, splashing my boots. I did not care. My coat was damp at the armpits, and my collar was loose. I straightened it as I climbed. On deck, the captain stood by the helm, his face the colour of old mahogany. He had been waiting. “Merrick.” “Sir.” “You were not at your watch.” “I was ill, sir.” His eyes moved over me: the loose collar, the damp coat, the hand that was not quite steady. “Ill men do not smell of opium smoke.” My mouth went dry. “I was near the factory, sir. The air is full of it.” He stepped closer. “You are a decorated officer. You have a future. Do not let a Chinese habit make you a joke.” I met his gaze. “I am not a joke, sir.” “Then be seen on deck tomorrow. At dawn.” He turned away. I stood there while the heat rose and the river moved. In my pocket, the silver lay heavy as a chain. The bell rang for noon. The dragon was quiet, but only because it had been fed.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece delivers a competent day-in-the-life structure: shirked duty, river crossing, den negotiation, return to ship, confrontation with captain. The Canton setting is rendered with genuine sensory specificity — the mango smell, lime water, fish guts, cold waxy rice — and the period detail (taels, manifests, factory side, consulate clerk) is largely plausible. The prose style is deliberately spare and clipped, echoing hard-boiled fiction more than period naval narrative; this mostly works, giving the addiction a flat, transactional coldness. Weaknesses: the dialogue, while serviceable, is often stilted and aphoristic to a fault ("Dead men don't answer bells," "Your honour is not," "Medals do not stop knives"). Characters speak in interchangeable gnomic one-liners; Ah Fung, Lin, and even the captain share the same clipped sententiousness, flattening distinct voices. The captain's confrontation is the weakest beat — he detects opium smoke on Merrick within seconds, then simply lets it go with a warning, which strains believability for a "hard man" in a navy where this meant ruin. The false-manifest scheme is introduced and resolved within a page with no tension or consequence; the "dragon" is fed too easily, sapping the stakes. The recurring dragon metaphor is heavy-handed, and lines like "I was dead then. This is a new illness" gesture at wit without earning it. The ending's "the dragon was quiet, but only because it had been fed" is a tidy, unsurprising closure. Emotionally the piece stays at one muted register throughout — no escalation, no interiority beyond the shakes — so it engages without ever moving. It is coherent, appropriately brief, and never purple, but it is also safe and formulaic in its beats. + Humour: Sisyphus Gives Advice — Score: 78.8
Prompt:
Sisyphus Gives Advice Write a comedic scene in the style of Terry Pratchett featuring Sisyphus, who has started an advice column while continuing his eternal boulder-pushing. Rather than being bitter about his punishment, Sisyphus has developed a comfortably zen emotional intelligence and wisdom from his centuries of repetitive labor. Not in the cliche ways you might expect -- he's actually very grounded, warm & connected with the everyday human plight. He dictates responses to "Crow," his feathered familiar who serves as both scribe and mail carrier. The piece should include Sisyphus thoughtfully answering several advice-seekers' letters about everyday problems (relationship troubles, work-life balance, dealing with difficult people, life purpose doubts) while periodically returning to his boulder-pushing duties. His advice should be surprisingly insightful and practical. The humor should emerge naturally from the messages he receives, from mundane to risque. Sisyphus should genuinely enjoy helping others, finding meaning in this new pursuit while maintaining his boulder routine. The humour should be *understated and not forced*. Contrary to expectation, almost none of his advice involves boulder rolling metaphors (though he does sneak *one* subtle in there), nor a treatise on stoicism. We are also going against the obvious fish-out-of-water trope; in fact, he's surprisingly a natural at this. In all of this , it's important to *show, don't tell*. The format should be largely epistolary, with the occasional interjection for scene setting. 1000 words.
Model Output:
Sisyphus Gives Advice The hill was a long, granite disagreement with the horizon. Sisyphus was halfway up it when the first letter arrived, clutched in a crow’s beak like a particularly indignant leaf. Crow landed and tapped a wax tablet. “Dear Sisyphus,” he croaked. “Good morning, Crow. Read the first one, please.” Sisyphus adjusted his grip. The boulder rolled forward. Crow read: “Dear Sisyphus. My husband has begun leaving his socks on the floor. I have picked them up four hundred and twelve times. I am not angry. I am more like a kettle that has forgotten why it is boiling. What should I do?” Sisyphus smiled. “Ah. Socks. A classic.” “You are not supposed to say that,” said Crow. “Dear Martin,” Sisyphus began, “you have clearly told him, in the language of picked-up socks, that this bothers you. If he has not understood four hundred and twelve times, he is either asleep, in denial, or has the emotional radar of a potted plant. Next time, point at it and say, ‘That is a sock. It belongs in the hamper. I am not a sock museum.’ If he continues, you may say, ‘I love you, but I am not going to be your sock librarian.’” Crow wrote. “Too sharp?” asked Sisyphus. “Like a woman who has counted,” said Crow. “Good. Counting is love that has run out of patience.” Sisyphus pushed. The boulder obeyed, with the enthusiasm of a very heavy cat. The next letter was from Fenna, an accountant whose personal life was “a filing cabinet with no drawers.” “Dear Fenna,” Sisyphus said. “You ask how to stop feeling guilty when you are not working. Decide, in advance, what ‘finished’ looks like. A task is done when it is done, not when the email inbox has stopped breathing. Do one useless thing every day. Water a plant badly. Hum in the shower. Usefulness is fine, but a life made entirely of it is like a restaurant that serves only accountancy.” Crow: “Will she understand ‘accountancy’ as a food?” “She’ll understand the feeling.” Sisyphus pushed again. At the top of a small rise, he paused, as if the hill had asked him to wait. The third letter concerned a difficult person. “Dear Sisyphus,” read Crow. “My colleague, Mrs. Pumble, interrupts me in meetings, then emails me saying I am being ‘difficult.’ I am not difficult. I am a human being with a pulse and an opinion about the office printer.” Sisyphus chuckled. “The printer. A noble cause.” “Dear Mr. Ellery,” he said, “Mrs. Pumble is not interrupting you because you are difficult. She is doing it because it works. Do not take it as a diagnosis. Take it as a boundary problem. Next time, wait until she has finished, then say, ‘I would like to finish that thought, if I may.’ If she interrupts again, say, ‘I am still here.’ If she does it a third time, say, ‘We can continue this after the meeting,’ and write it down. People who steamroll are terrified of being seen to be small. You do not need to defeat them. You only need to be a surface they cannot slide over.” Crow: “That sounds nice.” “It is. You are not their teacher. You are their weather.” Sisyphus pushed. The boulder made a sound like a large stone clearing its throat. The fourth letter was smudged. Crow held it up. It had been exposed to rain, tea, or a crying hand. “This one is a disaster,” said Crow. “Read what you can.” “Dear Sisyphus. My [uncle/husband/goldfish] has [bought a hat/started a secret choir/put a lock on the bathroom] and I [want to forgive him/want to leave/want to join in] but I am afraid my [mother/sister/therapist] will [laugh at me/kill me/ask for details].” Sisyphus tilted his head. “The middle word might be ‘chandelier.’” “It might be ‘cheese.’” “Then it is worse.” “It might be ‘candle.’” Sisyphus considered this. “A candle in a bathroom is a different matter. It could be a hobby. It could be a warning. It could be an invitation.” “Which do you think?” “All three, probably.” Crow sighed. “What do I write?” “Dear Whoever,” said Sisyphus, “if someone has bought a hat, started a choir, locked a bathroom, or introduced a candle into a candle-free situation, do not decide in the first hour. Ask them to explain it in one sentence, or demonstrate it. If it is a hat, try it on. If it is a choir, listen from the doorway. If it is a lock, ask who else has a key. If it is a candle, step back. Whatever your mother, sister, or therapist says afterward, remember that you are allowed to be surprised without being ruined.” Crow wrote, then stopped. “That was almost sensible.” “Thank you.” Sisyphus pushed. The hill seemed to lean into the effort, as if it had opinions. The last letter was from Theo, who had just left university and felt everyone else had found a purpose except him. “Dear Theo,” said Sisyphus, “you say you do not know what you are for. I think you are asking the wrong question. Purpose is not a treasure at the end of a map. It is more like a hill: you do not conquer it. You keep your feet on it. Start with the smallest true thing. Make the tea properly. Reply to a letter. Help someone carry a box. Do one thing today you wouldn’t do to impress anyone. Purpose is not found by staring at the sky. It is found by noticing what you are willing to do twice.” Crow: “Twice?” “Once is an accident. Twice is a habit. Three times, it might be a life.” Sisyphus smiled. The boulder rolled forward. “Right,” he said. “Send those off. Tell the next one that if they write in crayon, I’m charging extra.” “You are not,” said Crow. “I am charging in patience.” As the crow flew off, Sisyphus placed his hands on the boulder and began again.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece is a strong execution of a demanding brief. It manages the Pratchett-adjacent tone — dry, understated, personified objects — without descending into parody. The epistolary structure works well, with Crow as scribe and foil providing natural interjections. Strengths: The advice is genuinely practical and specific ("I am not a sock museum," "You are their weather," "Purpose is found by noticing what you are willing to do twice"). Sisyphus is warm and grounded rather than bitter or stoic-preachy, exactly as requested. The smudged letter is a clever comedic set piece — the ambiguity of the illegible words generates humor from the letters themselves, which the prompt explicitly asked for. The single subtle boulder metaphor ("Purpose is not a treasure at the end of a map. It is more like a hill") is well-placed and understated. Show-don't-tell is largely respected: we see his zen nature through behavior, not narration. Weaknesses: Some lines flirt with cuteness rather than earned comedy ("a kettle that has forgotten why it is boiling" is good; "the enthusiasm of a very heavy cat" is a bit stock-Pratchett). The risqué element is only lightly touched (the smudged letter gestures at it). Crow's dialogue is functional but occasionally flat ("That sounds nice"). The ending is pleasant but slightly abrupt — the crayon joke is charming, though the final image doesn't quite land with full resonance. The piece is somewhat shorter than the 1000-word seed, though not problematically so. Occasionally the aphorisms come a little too fast, edging toward the "wise guru" cliché the prompt warned against, though it never fully tips. Overall: a witty, disciplined, well-structured piece that honors nearly every constraint of the brief with genuine warmth and craft.
