+ First-person unique perspective: Rehearsing Rejection — Score: 80.5
Prompt:
Rehearsing Rejection Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of someone with borderline personality disorder who frequently plays out worst-case scenarios of how friends and loved ones might judge them. They construct elaborate internal dialogues, complete with imagined criticisms and their own defensive responses. The narrative takes place as they prepare to meet a close friend & recent lover, who has been somewhat distant lately, triggering their abandonment fears. Their inner monologue should reveal how they cycle between anticipating rejection, mentally rehearsing confrontations, and developing preemptive resentments as protective measures. Incorporate the *actual* events & interactions that are *not* in fact judgemental or involving rejection (in fact, the opposite), and represent how these are interpreted, how the validation & love is desperately felt & needed -- and then immediately questioned. Capture the cognitive dissonance in this struggle. Include moments where they briefly recognize the pattern but struggle to interrupt it, showing limited (and selective) self awareness, competing with the compelling nature of these imagined scenarios. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. 1000 words.
Model Output:
Rehearsing Rejection I am early, which means I am not early, which means I have arranged to be here before they decide I am too much. The door is a mouth. My mind starts its parade. If they smile, I will know it is the smile they use when deciding how to say it. "Hey," they will say. "Come in." The pause will be a verdict. I will say, "Sorry I'm early," lightly, handing them a knife. They will say, "No, I'm glad you're here," and I will hear: I am relieved you are here so I can finish this. No. Don't. You haven't even been let in yet. But the script runs. Last night they texted: Can't wait to see you. I made the pasta you like. I stared until the letters blurred again. Can't wait. It means I am counting down the minutes until I can make you feel guilty, or planning the exit, or buying forgiveness. My thumb hovers. I type: I'm excited too. Then: Sorry, I'm anxious. Then: Maybe we should reschedule. I delete it all. I send: I'll be there at seven. Seven. The number feels like a dare. In the hallway mirror, I catch myself: shoulders up, jaw locked, hand gripping my bag as if it is the only thing keeping me from falling apart. I look like a person waiting to be sent away. I turn away before I can look again. At the door, I knock. They open it in a second, as if they have been waiting too. Their face is warm and unguarded, and my chest gives a painful lurch, as if a hand has squeezed the soft place I keep hidden. "You're here," they say. "I missed you." I missed you. The words land in the space I built for rejection and bounce off it. They are too simple, suspicious. If they really missed me, why were they distant? If they really missed me, why is their voice so steady? People who love you should know the wound. "Come in," they say, stepping aside. "Thanks," I say. "Sorry I'm early." The words come out before I can stop them. A practiced surrender. I watch for the flinch, tightening, the microsecond where they think: of course, always early, always impossible. But they only say, "You're not early. I'm early. I got off work and couldn't wait." Their kitchen smells like garlic and basil. On the counter, two tulips and a glass of iced tea with lemon. I want to cry. I want to say, I am so lonely, please tell me I am not a burden. Instead I say, "You didn't have to do all this." They laugh, a real laugh. "I know. But I wanted to." I wanted to. Not I had to. Not I felt guilty. The words are a door opening in a room I thought was sealed. For one second I feel held, seen, chosen. The relief feels like danger. If I let myself need them this much, I will be destroyed when they leave. They always leave. They turn back to the stove. "Sit down. Your plate is ready in a minute." I sit at the small table. The chair scrapes. The sound is too loud. In my head, the rehearsal changes key. "You're quiet," they will say. "I'm fine," I will say. "You're not fine. You're doing that thing where you disappear and then you're angry later." I am not angry, I will think. I am only trying not to hurt you. But if they say I disappear, I will know they are preparing to say I am too much. I will say, "Well, if I were easier to love, maybe you wouldn't be thinking about leaving." They set the pasta in front of me. "Try it. I added more basil." I look at the food. It is beautiful. It is warm. It is an offering. My stomach, clenched since the hallway, loosens a fraction. I pick up the fork. "It smells amazing." "It's your favorite." "It's too much." They stop. Their eyes lift to mine. There is no accusation in them. Only a quiet attention, as if they are trying to hear the exact shape of my fear. "What's too much?" The question is gentle, which makes it unbearable. If they were cruel, I could fight them. If they were cold, I could hate them. But they are kind, and kindness asks me to be honest. "Everything," I say, and I don't know what I'm apologizing for. The fear. The accusation. The fork still lifted halfway to my mouth. They reach across the table and cover my hand with theirs. Their palm is warm. The contact is so ordinary it feels like a miracle. "Hey," they say. "Look at me." I do. "I'm not doing this to make you feel guilty. I'm not doing this because I think you owe me. I'm doing it because I love you. I missed you, and I'm sorry I've been distant. I've been scared, too. I don't always know how to be close without feeling like I'm going to fail you." The room tilts. Their words are not the script. They are an admission. My throat tightens. I want to say, I'm scared you'll leave, I'm scared I'll become the person you can't stand, please don't leave, but not with chains. Instead, my mind offers: They're manipulating me. They're saying the right things so I'll stay quiet. They're making themselves the wounded one. They're saying I love you to keep me from asking for more again. But beneath the protest, a desperate need answers: stay. Please stay. Be here. Be the person who stays when the worst of me comes out. I know this is the pattern. I know I am rehearsing a rejection. But the rehearsal is familiar, safer than hope. I try to interrupt it, to let their words be true, but the old script pulls me back. I hold the fork, their hand, still.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece executes the prompt with strong fidelity: it is almost entirely internal monologue, cycles between anticipated rejection, rehearsed confrontations, and preemptive resentment, and interweaves genuinely warm actual events (the pasta, the tulips, the confession of the friend's own fear) that the narrator immediately distrusts or reframes. The imagined dialogues are clearly marked as scripts, and the real interactions are simple, kind, and believable, creating the requested cognitive dissonance. The narrator's selective self-awareness is present ("I know this is the pattern... but the rehearsal is familiar, safer than hope"), though the final stretch states the pattern a bit too explicitly, edging into tell-don't-show. The friend's dialogue is natural and understated; the narrator's defensive lines feel authentic. Prose is generally controlled and rhythmic, with a few striking images ("The door is a mouth," "handing them a knife") and a few overwrought or cryptic moments ("Seven. The number feels like a dare," "The words are a door opening in a room I thought was sealed"). The ending resists false resolution—the narrator stays caught in the loop, which suits the prompt, though the friend's confession of fear arrives slightly conveniently and fully formed. Emotionally, the piece is engaging and complex, capturing desperate need for validation immediately followed by suspicion. Minor weaknesses: some aphoristic fragments feel writerly rather than organic; the friend verges on being an idealized therapeutic presence; the closing lines are a touch neat. + Physical-spatial: Blood Debt — Score: 45.7
Prompt:
"Blood Debt" Write a vivid third-person narrative depicting an unsanctioned underground duel between two talented but hot-headed martial artists. Their schools have been embroiled in a generations-old rivalry, and despite strict prohibitions from their masters, these two younger fighters arrange a secret confrontation fueled by personal pride and simmering animosity. - **One fighter** represents **Jigen-ryū**, a traditional, aggressive style practiced historically by elite samurai clans. Its practitioners emphasize explosive offense, decisive strikes, and overwhelming speed. Known historically for their arrogance and disdain toward outsiders, practitioners consider their art superior and untouchable. - **The opposing fighter** employs a form of historical **Piguaquan**, a Chinese martial art traditionally practiced by commoners, bodyguards, and street fighters. This style emphasizes whipping, circular strikes, rapid footwork, unpredictable angles of attack, and evasive maneuvers. Practitioners often come from lower social classes and view the traditional elite as pretentious and detached from true combat effectiveness. The fight takes place in the crumbling ruins of an abandoned temple, now functioning as a hidden arena for illicit duels. Passionate supporters from both factions surround them, wagering money, pride, and reputation on the outcome. **Essential Instructions:** Maintain absolute physical coherence throughout—clearly track fighters' positions relative to each other and their environment. Precisely depict strikes, counters, momentum shifts, and spatial dynamics, allowing readers to clearly visualize the mechanics and choreography of the fight at every moment. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
Rain sealed the pass, so the duel came. In the abandoned temple, pillars leaned like swords, stone glowed. Takeru, a Jigen-ryū student, stood near the collapsed altar. His red-and-black armband wrapped his left arm. Across flagstones, Wen crouched low, his red-and-black right armband bright. Neither had been permitted to fight. Gamblers crowded the broken nave, their breath fogging the cold air. They wagered coins, knives, and names. Jigen samurai hissed from the east wall; Piguaquan street fighters laughed from the west. A monk’s statue watched. Takeru shifted his weight, feet shoulder-width apart, knuckles loose. Wen rolled his shoulders, toes dragging. An old referee tapped a stone bowl. Takeru stepped forward from the altar, right heel driving into moss. He aimed a straight cut at Wen’s throat. Wen slipped left, his body coiling like a whip. His right hand drew a small circle, then snapped out. The blow kissed Takeru’s cheekbone. Takeru spun on his left foot, using the miss to turn. His elbow swung low toward Wen’s ribs. Wen jumped back, feet crossing in a tiny figure-eight. He landed behind a fallen pillar, but Takeru was already there, shoulder pressing the gap closed. The crowd surged close, forward now, eager. Takeru threw a high palm aimed at Wen’s temple. Wen ducked under it, his hips swiveling. From that turn, he flicked a backfist at Takeru’s floating guard. The strike landed on Takeru’s forearm. Takeru grunted, but he did not retreat. He stepped in quickly again with sudden, brutal full force. Wen used the pillar as a shield, circling it clockwise. Takeru followed counterclockwise, keeping his shoulders square to the man. When Wen emerged from the pillar’s shadow, he threw two quick punches from the outside. Takeru blocked the first, then caught the second, feeling the foreign wrist snap inward sharply. Takeru twisted the trapped arm, forcing Wen to turn with him. Their bodies spiraled around the pillar’s base, dust rising. Takeru tried to drive a knee into Wen’s floating ribs. Wen dropped his weight, rolled under the knee, and swept Takeru’s back leg in a low, hard, fast arc again. Takeru’s heel struck stone, and he lurched sideways. He recovered by grabbing the pillar’s edge with his free hand. The pillar shuddered. Wen, still low, threw a rising elbow. It caught Takeru’s chin, snapping his head back. Takeru tasted blood. The crowd gasped loudly and coins fell from hands above. Takeru spat blood onto the flagstones. He charged, using the pillar as a pivot to swing his body around. His right fist aimed at Wen’s face. Wen stepped inside, letting the punch pass by his ear, and struck Takeru’s floating guard with a palm and broke the line between them. The blow opened a cut above Takeru’s eye. He blinked red, then advanced with greater fury. His left hand hooked toward Wen’s throat. Wen leaned back, his spine curving, and his foot pressed into Takeru’s knee joint. Takeru’s leg bent wrong. The crowd roared, and lanterns swayed above them all. Takeru kept his balance by leaning into the pillar. He was wounded, but his rage sharpened his aim. He threw a straight jab with his right hand. Wen saw it coming, shifted his center, and let the jab slide off his shoulder, missing by inches. The crowd held its breath. Wen moved around Takeru’s injured side. His footwork was circular, small, and sudden. He threw a low kick at Takeru’s good leg. Takeru lifted that leg, but the kick grazed his shin. Takeru’s footing grew unstable. He staggered toward the altar. The crowd saw the opening and shouted new bets. Takeru backed until his shoulder touched the altar’s cold stone, his breathing ragged. He used the wall to check his fall. Wen pressed forward, arms moving in loops. Takeru saw a gap in Wen’s high guard and drove a straight fist upward. It struck Wen’s chin hard, and Wen gasped. Wen’s head snapped sideways. He recovered by lowering his center and stepping left. His right arm drew a whip-like circle. The back of his hand struck Takeru’s injured knee. Takeru cried out. Wen immediately followed with a palm to Takeru’s ribs. The ribs cracked loudly, and Takeru doubled inward sharply. Takeru’s vision blurred with pain. He leaned against the altar, refusing to fall. His left arm hung low, but his right arm still moved. He threw a desperate uppercut. Wen evaded by circling right, then countered with a short elbow to Takeru’s temple. The crowd gasped again, loud and quick. Takeru’s knee buckled. He sank toward the stone, one hand scraping the altar’s edge. Wen stopped for only a heartbeat. He could end it, but his own pride demanded a clean finish. He lowered his stance, fists ready. Takeru looked up, defiant. The temple held its breath, cold and still. Takeru used the altar to spring upward. His body became a straight line. He threw a final, explosive punch at Wen’s chest. Wen did not block. He stepped left, let the punch miss, and turned his hip into a whipping strike that hit Takeru’s ribs hard. The air left him. Takeru collapsed against the altar. His back slid down the stone. His right hand fell open. Wen stood over him, breathing fast, fists still raised. The crowd went silent. Rain tapped the broken roof above them. The temple remembered old grudges, and the night grew heavier, cold, and deep now. Footsteps echoed from the eastern corridor. Master Aki, Takeru’s teacher, stepped into the lantern light. Her face was stone. At her shoulder, Master Lin, Wen’s teacher, waited. Both had come to stop the fight, but the fight was nearly over. The crowd parted quickly, ashamed and quiet now, all around. Wen looked at the two masters, then at Takeru’s armband. Takeru looked at Wen’s armband. Neither spoke. In the ruined temple, the old rivalry had not ended, but the duel had changed them. They stood, each bleeding, each alive. The night kept its secrets, and the rain fell on them.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece delivers a functional fight scene with generally trackable choreography—positions relative to the pillar and altar are mostly clear, and the exchange of strikes, counters, and momentum shifts can be followed. The opening is confusing, however: "Rain sealed the pass, so the duel came" is a muddled causal construction that sets an oddly stilted tone. The prose is consistently choppy, favoring short declarative sentences that create rhythm but also flatten emotional depth and make the narration feel mechanical ("He landed behind a fallen pillar, but Takeru was already there"). Characterization is thin. Takeru and Wen are names attached to fighting styles; the prompt's rich cultural tension (Jigen-ryū elitism vs. Piguaquan commoner pragmatism) is gestured at only through crowd placement ("Jigen samurai hissed from the east wall; Piguaquan street fighters laughed from the west"). The armband detail is introduced twice with no payoff until a vague final glance. The masters arriving at the end is an abrupt, unearned narrative device that resolves nothing—the ending gestures at transformation ("the duel had changed them") without showing any internal change, making it feel tacked-on. The fight itself has some vivid moments (the arm-catch and spiral around the pillar, the knee-bend injury), but injuries accumulate inconsistently—Takeru's leg "bent wrong," yet he springs off the altar moments later with full force. The crowd and setting are used as background noise rather than living elements. Emotionally, the piece stays at the level of fight-log; there's no interiority, no real animosity felt beyond stated actions. The style is serviceable but amateurish in places: repetitive sentence structures, occasional awkward phrasing ("broke the line between them," "The temple remembered old grudges"), and a tendency to tell ("He was wounded, but his rage sharpened his aim"). It meets the length and structural requirements, and physical coherence is mostly maintained, which is the prompt's core demand. + Physical-spatial: Breaking Formation — Score: 59.3
Prompt:
**"Breaking Formation"** Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a street dancer from a rough neighborhood who's won a scholarship to an elite K-pop training academy in Seoul. Desperately out of place culturally and technically, they struggle with a militaristically precise choreography that contradicts everything about their improvisational background. The punishing rehearsal takes place under a famous instructor known for breaking students to remake them, who sees potential in the narrator's raw talent but not their attitude. This scene MUST maintain complete physical coherence—each dance move, position shift, and spatial relationship must be tracked with precision throughout the studio. Paint an exceptionally vivid kinetic picture through descriptions that capture not just movement but the contrast between the narrator's fluid, expressive style and the mechanical precision demanded. Their internal monologue should reveal culture shock, class anxiety, and the threatening realization that success here might mean losing their authentic movement voice. Include technical terminology that highlights the collision of street and commercial styles, moments when muscle memory betrays them, and a crucial decision point about whether to conform or rebel. Physical clarity is essential—readers must be able to visualize exactly how bodies move through space, how rhythms align or clash, and how the protagonist's body struggles against unfamiliar discipline. 1000 words.
Model Output:
I stand in the mirror, sweat stinging my eyes, while four corner speakers blast synchronized music, a hair too loud, shaking the floor. The mirror shows twenty elite K-pop trainees in white, a perfect grid, my sneakers, the dirty thing. Chest tightens. Seoul’s air feels clean, expensive, wrong, and cold. Mr. Han steps from the shadow, black shirt tight, eyes cold. He was the instructor who broke idols, remade them, made famous. He taps the monitor. “Again. Eight counts. If you breathe before the hit, you fail.” He watches my feet like they owe money. I swallow hard now. Please. The beat drops. We start in a V, downstage center, shoulders square, toes pointing front. I copy the top rock, but my hips want to bounce, my feet want to shuffle. The street in me grins, then panics. I hate how easy it is. I hate it. Still here again. On five, we break left, knees bent, chests lifted. The line must stay straight. My shoulder pops early, a street hit, too loose, too late. The girl beside me snaps her head, crisp. Her jaw is a blade. Mine is mud. I feel the floor judge me. Too rough again. Mr. Han stops the music. “Your body is lying,” he says. “You are not dancing. You are arguing.” He points at my footwork. “Syncopation is not freedom.” I want to explain about cyphers, about corners, about rhythm born from hunger. He does not care. Not now. Not here. Not yet. We restart. The choreography climbs: eight counts of chest isolations, then a diagonal run to stage right, then a level change into a low freeze. My knees remember concrete, not carpet. My center of gravity drops, but my arms flare wide. I look huge. Too huge. Too loud. Too much. The freeze demands a hip isolation, left side only, while the right arm stays glued to the ribs. I try, and my whole torso twists. It is a full body wave, the kind I used to send through my shoulders in the park. Now it is noise. It is noise. A trainee two rows ahead lands the freeze perfectly: knee down, back flat, head tilted exactly three degrees. I know it because I counted in my head. My shame is mathematical. I am not just late; I am uncounted. I am a ghost in the grid. Out of place here. The next phrase requires a foot syncopation: step, hop, step, pause, all on the upbeat. My left foot drags. My right foot rushes. In the cypher, this pause would be a breath, a dare, a door. Here it is an error. The beat keeps moving. It never waits for me. I think of my grandmother’s kitchen, where we danced to radio static, no mirrors, no counts. I think of the academy scholarship, gold, heavy, sealed. It promised Seoul. It promised a stage. It promised my mother could stop counting coins. Now I am inside. The door is closing slowly now. Mr. Han calls a break. We fan ourselves, sweat pooling under our arches. He walks to me, stops six inches away, and smells like coffee. He says, “You have raw talent. You have attitude. I can remove one, but not both.” I stare at his shoes. They are clean. Always. I want to say that dirt is my rhythm. I want to say that my body learned music before it learned manners. I say nothing. My tongue is a foreign object, stuck to the roof of my mouth, shaped by hunger and fear. I am not ready. Not yet today. The music starts again, louder, the corner speakers pressing into my eardrums. We begin the punishing thirty two counts, a long phrase from upstage left to downstage right. It is military, exposing spacing. If I drift, the formation cracks, and everyone sees it. I feel the line. Pulling me in. Count one: arms rise, palms flat, elbows locked. Count two: knees drop, backs straight. Count three: turn right, weight on the balls of our feet. Count four: hit, a sharp chest pop, no bounce. Count five: slide left, hips level, eyes front. My body wants to sway. It must not. On count eight, we break into two diagonals. I am in the back line, behind the girl with the blade jaw. My feet must match hers. Her steps are tiny, surgical, almost invisible. Mine are wide, loud, full of the rough neighborhood’s echo. I cannot be quiet. I cannot be. The phrase asks for a body roll, but controlled, a wave from crown to hip, then a freeze. I let my neck lead, the way I do in the park. The roll becomes a full shoulder shake, too loose, too happy, too much like a street salute. I stop now. Everyone lands the freeze except me. I am still rolling, my chest open, my arms half lifted. The silence is worse than the music. Mr. Han says, “Again.” I want to fall. I want to drop into a busting floor pattern and make the mistake mine. But I stand here. He plays the phrase again. This time, I choose. I can let my hips speak, or I can make my body a machine. The beat rises. I think of my mother’s hands, cracked from washing clothes, holding the scholarship like a prayer. I think of my face in the mirror. I choose the machine. My shoulders square. My ribs flatten. My feet count the upbeat, small, exact, no shuffle. The wave stays inside my spine, hidden. It is not death. It is armor. I can wear it now and take it off later, maybe. I hope so. I pray now. On the last hit, I snap my head, small, sharp, in the center of my own chest. The line holds. The mirror shows me, smaller, cleaner, and not quite me. I have not lost my voice. I have put it in a pocket, deep, where it can wait. For now.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece fulfills the core brief reasonably well: a street dancer in a Seoul K-pop academy, militaristic choreography, harsh instructor, culture/class anxiety, muscle memory betrayals, and a conform-or-rebel decision point. The count-by-count breakdown of the 32-count phrase is one of its stronger moments, giving genuine physical tracking of movement through space, and the contrast between the narrator's loose, improvisational body and the demanded precision is consistently rendered. However, the prose style is a serious liability. The relentless staccato fragments ("I hate how easy it is. I hate it. Still here again.") begin as voice and quickly become tic. The rhythm is so uniform that every paragraph sounds identical, flattening emotional peaks that should escalate. Some sentences are simply incoherent—"I snap my head, small, sharp, in the center of my own chest" is physically impossible; "a busting floor pattern" is garbled terminology; "He was the instructor who broke idols, remade them, made famous" is broken English. The narrator's grandmother's kitchen and mother's cracked hands are touching but generic—stock immigrant/sacrifice imagery deployed without specificity. The instructor's dialogue is functional but thin ("You are not dancing. You are arguing" is the one genuinely good line). The decision point is handled with some nuance—choosing the machine as "armor," pocketing the voice rather than losing it—but the ending's reassurance ("I have not lost my voice") feels slightly pre-resolved, softening the threatening realization the prompt demanded. The transformation is small enough to be earned, though. Physical coherence is decent but imperfect: formations (V, diagonals, back line) are tracked, but spatial relationships blur in the middle sections. The piece is coherent overall and never meanders, but its stylistic monotony, occasional incoherence, and reliance on repeated fragment patterns mark it as competent-but-flawed rather than strong. + Gothic-fantasy-humour: Court of the Dreaming — Score: 71.6
Prompt:
Court of the Dreaming: Territorial Dream Dispute. Write a dark fantasy scene with comedic elements set in the Courts of Dream where a case is being heard to determine ownership of a contested dreamscape. Mora, the Slavic nightmare spirit who sits on sleepers' chests causing paralysis and terror, has recently invaded and subverted a carefully crafted recurring dream of a schoolboy, Max. The dream originally featured the boy lying in a field of wildflowers with his crush, always culminating in a muddled almost-kiss and a pleasant confusion of emotions. This dream was the meticulous work of "First Love" (a rosy-cheeked, slightly bashful entity who crafts formative romantic experiences). However, Mora has recently infiltrated the dreamscape, transforming the scene so that when the girl playfully mounts the boy, she morphs into a terrifying yet somehow still confusingly attractive vision who proceeds to sit on his chest and feed on his breath. Mora's defense largely consists of the practical argument that "a girl's gotta eat too, you know?" Write this scene as it unfolds in the courtroom of the Dreaming, with Dream's demeanour, typically impenetrable, betraying a sense of irritation at having to adjudicate such matters. The comedy should derive from the farcical situation, familiar elements of courtroom drama intersecting with the fantastical world of the Dreaming, and the droll portrayal of the characters and their interactions. The humor should be dark and understated throughout. Dream is tempted to some mischief in the resolution of the case. Use descriptives sparingly when setting scene. Write for readability & engagement. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The Court of the Dreaming had no benches, only shadows that remembered benches. At its center stood a single, giant hourglass, dripping shimmering sand in slow grains. Each grain was a stolen minute, a second of wonder, a thought that had not yet learned its name. Dream sat where a judge might sit, if judges were made of midnight and old paper. His face was severe, unreadable. A thin vein pulsed beneath his temple. He had been awake for centuries. He was tired of waking. “Case four thousand and nine,” he said. “First Love versus Mora of the Chest, concerning the recurring dreamscape of one Max, age thirteen, resident of a bedroom with a poster of a horse.” First Love rose from the plaintiff’s shadow. She was small, rosy-cheeked, and wore a dress the color of the first blush of a peach. Her fingers were stained with pollen and nervousness. “Your Eternity,” she said, “I built that dream with care. Wildflowers. A field that smelled of rain. A boy who could not decide whether to speak. A girl who could not decide whether to leave. It was a masterpiece of almost.” Mora answered from the defense shadow. She was tall, black-robed, with a face like a moon seen through wet glass. Her smile had too many teeth, but also, inconveniently, the soft curve of a girl who might have been pretty if she were not a nightmare. “Your Eternity,” she said, in a voice like a boot dragged across a floor, “I merely improved the ending.” Dream’s eye moved. “You are accused of invasion, subversion, and feeding without consent.” “I am accused of a great deal,” Mora said. “I am also hungry. That boy’s dream was all flowers and no substance. No protein. No fear. No breath. A girl’s gotta eat too, you know?” A murmur passed through the shadows. Some were lawyers. Some were regrets. One was a very old bad dream about forgetting a name. First Love’s cheeks darkened. “You turned my almost-kiss into a smother!” “I turned it into dinner,” Mora said. Dream raised one finger. The hourglass shivered. Sand fell faster, though no one had touched it. “Exhibit A,” he said. The courtroom darkened. In the center of the floor, a field of wildflowers appeared, pale and trembling. Max lay in the grass, his school shirt unbuttoned at the collar, his eyes wide with the particular panic of a boy who has forgotten how to be a boy. The girl from the dream sat above him, bright-haired, laughing. Then the laughter changed. The flowers blackened at their edges. The girl’s face lengthened, her eyes went deep and dark, her mouth opened wider than a mouth should, and she settled onto his chest. Max did not scream. He simply stopped breathing, which was worse. The vision ended. Silence. First Love pressed her hands over her mouth. “He was supposed to feel confused and hopeful.” “He feels confused,” Mora said. “Now he also feels pressed. That’s growth.” Dream looked at the hourglass. A single grain hung in the neck, trembling. “Objection,” said the shadow of a judge who had died in 1743 and was still arguing a property case. “The exhibit is emotionally manipulative.” “Overruled,” Dream said. Mora leaned forward. “Your Eternity, I respect the craftsmanship. But the Dreaming is not a museum. Dreams are food. If I let that boy drift in his little field forever, who feeds the night? I am a necessary evil. I am the weight that proves they are alive.” First Love turned to Dream. “And if I let him dream of her one more time, what do we lose?” “Probably nothing,” Mora said. “Maybe a few minutes. Maybe a good panic. I take what I can get.” Dream said nothing. He stared at the sand. The grain fell. In the field, Max’s eyes opened. In the real world, his mother would call him for breakfast. In the dream, the girl-Mora looked down at him with an expression that was terrible and, inexplicably, fond. “You’re cute when you’re asphyxiated,” she said. Max, to his credit, did not answer. He was thirteen. He had learned long ago that some things were best met with silence. Dream’s face tightened. He disliked the case, the hourglass, the low sand, and that Mora’s point had a grim elegance. He thought of small mischief, the kind that made a nightmare regret being clever in his court. “Mora,” he said, “you argue necessity.” “I do.” “First Love argues craft.” “I do.” Dream looked at the hourglass. “The Dreaming has a law. A dream, once made, belongs to the dreamer. A nightmare, once invited, belongs to the sleeper. But neither may own a feeling that has not yet finished becoming.” Mora’s smile widened. “So?” “So,” Dream said, “I will not rule the field yours. Nor shall I rule it hers.” First Love exhaled. Mora’s teeth clicked. “The dream will continue,” Dream said. “But the ending will be altered. The boy will wake before the kiss. The girl will remain beautiful. The nightmare will remain hungry. And each time the boy dreams, the field will grow one flower less, until only the grass remains.” Mora frowned. “That’s not a solution.” “It is a diet,” Dream said. “You will feed on the loss. First Love will feed on the memory. Max will feed on the almost. And I,” he added, with a smile that did not reach his eyes, “will feed on the paperwork.” The shadows laughed. It was a dry sound, like pages turning in an empty library. Mora straightened. “I object to being a diet, Your Eternity.” “Noted,” Dream said. First Love looked as though she might cry, but smiled, because she had been given one more almost. In the single, giant hourglass, the last grains fell, one by one, shimmering, patient, indifferent. Dream closed the case. He looked at the gone field and felt something small move. Then he opened the next file: a door that would not open.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece delivers the requested courtroom farce with dark, understated humor and mostly economical scene-setting. Dream's irritation comes through in small physical tells (the temple vein, the "smile that did not reach his eyes"), and the legal absurdity ("First Love versus Mora of the Chest," the ghost lawyer from 1743) lands well. Mora's "a girl's gotta eat" defense is preserved and given good comic elaboration ("I turned it into dinner"). The resolution — Dream's "diet" ruling where each party feeds on loss, memory, and the almost — is a genuinely clever, thematically apt piece of mischief that satisfies the "tempted to mischief" instruction. Weaknesses: the prose occasionally strains for aphoristic cleverness ("shadows that remembered benches," "a voice like a boot dragged across a floor") and tips into preciosity rather than elegance. Some lines feel like they're reaching for Gaiman pastiche without fully earning it — "He had been awake for centuries. He was tired of waking" is a nice paradox but borders on the overwrought. The "You're cute when you're asphyxiated" line is funny but tonally broad for a piece asked for understated humor. The ending's "felt something small move" is vague and slightly limp; the final image (a door that would not open) is evocative but abrupt. First Love is thinly characterized beyond blush and pollen; Mora is more vivid. The middle section with the exhibit is the strongest stretch. Dialogue is generally strong, though a few exchanges ("So?" / "So,") feel like filler beats. The piece is coherent, appropriately paced, and never meanders, but its emotional complexity is moderate — Max is more device than person, and the stakes stay arch rather than felt. + Fanfic-crossover: Blood Moon — Score: 78.0
Prompt:
Blood Moon Alucard & Yennefer Write a story where Alucard (Hellsing) encounters Yennefer (The Witcher) in medieval Europe. Yennefer's magical abilities intrigue the vampire, while she's both repulsed and fascinated by his monstrous nature. Their power dynamic shifts constantly as they circle each other, neither willing to show weakness first. **Alucard (Hellsing)** Alucard is an ancient, immensely powerful vampire who works for the Hellsing Organization. He can regenerate from almost any wound and shape-shift at will. He's sadistic, arrogant, and takes pleasure in toying with his enemies before killing them. Despite being a monster, he despises weak vampires who can't accept their nature. He wears a distinctive red coat, wide-brimmed hat, and orange sunglasses. He uses massive handguns loaded with silver bullets. He seeks worthy opponents who can challenge him and potentially end his immortal existence. Famous quote: "The bird of Hermes is my name, eating my wings to make me tame." **Yennefer of Vengerberg (The Witcher)** Yennefer is a powerful sorceress who magically altered her appearance to hide her congenital hunchback. She's ambitious, stubborn, and manipulative when necessary. She has violet eyes and smells of lilac and gooseberries. Despite her cold exterior, she desperately wants to reverse her infertility caused by magical transformation. She's centuries old but appears young. She's politically savvy and refuses to be underestimated. She has a sarcastic sense of humor and little patience for fools. Though she rarely shows it, she's capable of deep love and loyalty. Famous quote: "I'm not sweet and I'm not a maiden in distress in need of saving." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
Blood Moon A broken cart wheel lies abandoned near the village gates, its axle splintered, one spoke snapped through the hub. The villagers have fled. Doors hang open. A dog’s bell still swings on a missing collar. Above the thatched roofs, the moon bleeds swollen red over the fields, and the air smells of wet stone, crushed thyme, and something older, iron and smoke. Alucard steps from the shadow of the gatehouse, his red coat brushing the mud. His wide-brimmed hat tilts low. Orange lenses catch the blood moon as if it were a stage light. He carries no sword, only two enormous handguns, their barrels heavy with the promise of silver. He smiles before he speaks. “Ah,” he says. “Small town, larger hunger. How convenient.” The sound comes from behind him: a heel tapping once against flagstone, then another, slow and deliberate. Yennefer of Vengerberg walks out from the lane between two shuttered houses. Her black hair falls straight down her back. Her violet eyes narrow at the shape of him, at the coat that seems too bright for the night, at the guns that do not belong to this medieval age. She smells of lilac and gooseberries, a sharp sweetness against the village’s fear. “You are not a priest,” she says. “You are not a merchant. And you are certainly not a man who was born.” Alucard turns. The smile widens. “No. I am the bird of Hermes, eating my wings to make me tame. The name is Alucard. And you, little witch, have a voice like a blade left out in the rain.” Her lip curls. “I'm not sweet and I'm not a maiden in distress in need of saving.” “No,” he agrees, stepping closer. “You require killing. Or perhaps I do. The moon is generous tonight.” Yennefer’s hand lifts. The air before her shivers. A thin line of light gathers at her fingertips, violet and cold. She does not cast it yet. She watches him, calculating. He is too still for a hunter, too loud for a ghost. His heartbeat, if he has one, is absent. Yet his shadow moves wrong, stretching toward her as if it wants to be fed. “Magic,” Alucard says, tilting his head. “I can taste it. It clings to you like perfume on a corpse.” “Then taste it,” she replies. The light snaps out. A wave of force slams into him. The street cracks. Alucard’s coat rips open, his flesh tears, his head snaps sideways. For one breath, he is broken. Then the wound knits with a wet sound, and he straightens, laughing. “Again,” he says. Yennefer’s eyes flash. She summons a second spell, faster, a whip of silvered fire that lashes his face. The skin peels back from his cheek, exposing black muscle. He does not flinch. He catches the burning tendril in his hand and lets it die against his palm. “Silver,” he murmurs, almost pleased. “You know what you are dealing with.” “I know what I see,” she says. “A monster wearing a coat.” “And you see a woman wearing a face.” The words land. Her jaw tightens. She hates being seen, especially by something that has no right to see. Behind her, the broken cart wheel rolls a little in the wind, as if the village has remembered its fear. Alucard raises one handgun. The moonlight slides along the barrel. “I will ask only once. Do you wish to die as a hero, or as a meal?” Yennefer’s sarcasm hardens into ice. “I wish to leave this conversation with my dignity intact. If you must eat, eat quickly.” He fires. The gunshot is monstrous, a thunderclap that shakes the shutters. The silver bullet strikes her shoulder. She stumbles, curses, and slams her heel into the flagstones. A circle of runes flares beneath her feet, and the bullet, still spinning, bursts into ash. Alucard lowers his gun. “Ah. You do not like being hit.” “I dislike being underestimated,” she says, touching the smoking shoulder. “There is a difference.” The power between them shifts. She is no longer merely wary. She is hunting. Her magic coils around her like black silk, gathering strength. The air grows heavy with the scent of ozone and crushed berries. The village dogs, those that remain, whine and hide under tables. Alucard’s other gun rises. “You are interesting. I am not expecting that.” “Flattery from a corpse is cheap.” “It is not flattery. It is appetite.” He moves. It is not a step; it is a decision made visible. One moment he is across the lane, the next his hand closes around her throat. His grip is not strong enough to crush, not yet. It is a question. Her face is inches from his hat. She can smell the old blood on him, the centuries layered like rings in a dead tree. Yennefer does not gasp. She smiles, blood bright on her teeth. “Finally,” she whispers. “Somebody who knows how to hold a conversation.” Alucard’s orange lenses narrow. “You are either very brave or very stupid.” “Often both.” Her hand rises. The runes beneath her feet flare violet. The ground between them splits. Alucard’s arm is torn free, his shoulder hanging by threads of sinew. He does not fall. He laughs, a low, delighted sound, and pulls a second bullet from his coat. Yennefer releases the spell. For a moment, they are both still, both breathing as if breathing were a choice. The blood moon hangs above them, red and patient. “You could kill me,” she says. “Yes.” “You should.” “I would like to.” He studies her, and for the first time his smile is not quite a threat. “But you are not finished. And I am not.” She wipes the blood from her mouth with the back of her hand. “Then stop wasting time.” He raises both guns. She lifts both hands. The gates creak behind the broken wheel. The moon watches, patient and ancient. Neither of them blinks. Neither of them yields.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece delivers a tense, atmospheric standoff between Alucard and Yennefer that honors both source characters well. The present-tense, third-person instruction is followed precisely, and the ~1000-word seed is respected. The prose is controlled and rhythmic, with strong sensory grounding (the blood moon, wet stone, crushed thyme, the abandoned cart wheel) and a consistent gothic register that suits both franchises. Character work is a highlight. Alucard's theatrical menace, hunger for worthy opponents, and regeneration-as-flourish are all present, and his famous quote is deployed naturally in dialogue rather than pasted in. Yennefer's pride, refusal to be underestimated, and hidden vulnerability ("a woman wearing a face") are captured with economy. The power dynamic genuinely shifts multiple times — she blasts him apart, he regenerates, he grabs her throat, she tears his arm off — fulfilling the prompt's requirement that neither shows weakness first. The dialogue is sharp and in-voice throughout: "I wish to leave this conversation with my dignity intact. If you must eat, eat quickly" is a genuinely good Yennefer line. The mutual recognition of unfinished business ("you are not finished. And I am not") lands the theme of two immortals circling each other. Weaknesses: the piece is essentially one scene of escalating threat with no real resolution or deeper development — the standoff ending is fitting but slightly static, a tableau rather than a story. Some metaphors strain ("a decision made visible," "breathing as if breathing were a choice" — the latter is actually effective, but "the village has remembered its fear" is a touch precious). A few beats repeat (guns raised, spells flaring) without escalation of stakes beyond the physical. The anachronism of Alucard's guns in medieval Europe is acknowledged but never interrogated, which is a missed opportunity. Minor overwrought tendencies appear in lines like "his shadow moves wrong, stretching toward her as if it wants to be fed," though this is more evocative than purple. Overall this is a polished, professional-feeling piece with strong voice fidelity and atmosphere, held back from excellence by its single-scene structure and occasional over-crafted phrasing. + Fanfic-crossover: Prison Strings — Score: 73.0
Prompt:
Prison Strings Jolyne Cujoh & Makima Write a story where Jolyne Cujoh (JoJo's Bizarre Adventure) and Makima (Chainsaw Man) cross paths at a supernatural prison facility. Jolyne is immediately suspicious of Makima's falsely sweet demeanor, while Makima is intrigued by Jolyne's Stand ability. Their battle of wits escalates dangerously as Jolyne realizes how manipulative Makima truly is. **Jolyne Cujoh (JoJo's Bizarre Adventure)** Jolyne is the daughter of Jotaro Kujo and the first female JoJo protagonist. Her Stand, Stone Free, allows her to unravel her body into string that she can control. She's hot-headed, foul-mouthed, and doesn't take disrespect from anyone. She was framed for murder and sent to prison. She has a distinctive butterfly tattoo on her arm and wears her hair in two buns. Despite her tough exterior, she's deeply loyal to her friends and family. She can be impulsive but is highly adaptable in battle. She inherited her father's ability to stay cool under pressure but is more emotionally expressive. Famous quote: "If there's no Mickey, this shit ain't Disney!" **Makima (Chainsaw Man)** Makima appears as a young woman with auburn hair and ringed yellow eyes. She's the Control Devil who can dominate anyone she considers beneath her (nearly everyone). She maintains a pleasant, soft-spoken demeanor that masks her manipulative, cold nature. She can create contracts with humans and devils, often exploiting their desires. She's obsessed with Chainsaw Man and wants to control him. She keeps numerous people and devils as pets on leashes. She's practically immortal due to a contract with the Prime Minister. She views humans as lesser beings but mimics human emotions perfectly. Famous quote: "It's okay. Dogs are supposed to die for their owners." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
Chain-link fences within the yard rattle whenever an inmate passes by. Jolyne Cujoh stops beneath the wire and watches the sun slice through the bars. The prison is wrong in ways the guards do not explain. Hallways bend behind closed doors. Cells numbered twice. Some inmates wear collars of light. Others have no shadows at all. A woman approaches from the gate. Auburn hair, soft smile, yellow eyes ringed like coins. She wears a white uniform that looks too clean for this place. "Excuse me," the woman says. Her voice is honey poured over gravel. "My name is Makima. I was told you were the new arrival." Jolyne does not step back, but Stone Free tightens around her arms like wire. "You were told a lot of things." Makima tilts her head. "I am here to help. This facility can be... overwhelming. If you have questions, I am always available." "Always," Jolyne repeats. "That's a big word for a lady in a prison yard." Makima smiles wider. "I am thorough." Jolyne notices the dog. It sits by Makima's ankle, calm, red-eyed, leash slack. The dog's collar glows faintly. The other inmates do not look at it. That is the problem. They look away, not with fear, but with the blank respect of people who have already lost something. "You got a pet?" Jolyne asks. "A friend," Makima says. "A dog on a leash is a pet. A dog with a leash on its neck is a slave." Makima's smile does not change. "You are very observant, Jolyne Cujoh. I have read your file. Murder charge. Strong Stand. Unstable temper. Loyal to those you trust." Jolyne's jaw hardens. "Who gave you my file?" "Everyone gives information to those who ask nicely." "Nice," Jolyne says, "is what a knife says before it cuts." The dog whines. Makima reaches down and strokes its head. "You are angry because you do not understand. That is all right. People often feel that way before they learn what they are worth." Stone Free slips from Jolyne's body in a thin strand. It crawls along the chain-link fence, testing the metal. The fence does not spark. It does not bend. It simply resists, like a wall made of rules. Jolyne has fought walls before. She has fought her own body, her father's name, and a world that wanted her dead. But this place feels different. The bars are not just steel. They are promises. Contracts. Little cages wrapped in language. "Why are you here?" Jolyne asks. Makima looks at the dog, then back. "I work for order." "Order is a lie people tell when they want to be masters." Makima's eyes narrow, only slightly. "And you believe freedom is the truth?" "I believe freedom is what you do when nobody's watching." "Then you are a dangerous idealist." The dog barks once. The sound is too loud for its size. Inmates stop moving. A man with a glowing collar freezes mid-step. A woman near the shower stall clutches her head. The air tightens. Jolyne's strings snap outward. They wrap around the dog's leash, around Makima's wrist, around the dog's muzzle. "Whoa, whoa, whoa. You just made ten people flinch. That's not pet behavior." Makima does not struggle. She looks at the strings as if they are interesting. "Your Stand is unusual. It does not attack from a distance. It becomes part of you. That is... elegant." "It's not elegant. It's survival." "Survival is what lesser beings call obedience." Jolyne's eyes flash. "You just called me lesser?" "I called you human." The strings yank. The dog growls, but cannot bite. Makima's smile stays sweet, but something cold moves behind it, like a door opening in a house with no lights. "You can pull," Makima says softly. "But you cannot break what is already bound." Jolyne feels it then: a tug inside her chest. Not pain. Recognition. A contract she never signed, trying to find the place where she would say yes. Stone Free screams. Jolyne unravels her entire body into thread. She becomes a storm of white wire, wrapping the yard, the fence, the dog, Makima, the frozen inmates. The prison groans. For one second, the bars become hers. Makima laughs. It is a small, pleasant sound. "Now that is promising." Jolyne's voice comes from everywhere and nowhere. "You don't get to smile while you cage people." "I do not cage them. I give them purpose. They would be lost without me." "Lost people still choose." "Choices are only real when the chooser is free. Are you free, Jolyne? Or are you only the daughter of a man who left?" The strings stop. That is worse than any attack. Jolyne reknits herself in front of Makima, breathing hard. Her butterfly tattoo looks black against her skin. Makima stands still, leash in hand, yellow eyes unblinking. "You know," Makima says, "if you were a dog, you would be very good at protecting your owner." Jolyne steps closer. "I'm not a dog." "No," Makima agrees. "You are not." The dog snaps its leash. Not because it breaks, but because Makima lets it. The animal vanishes into the shadows of the fence. The inmates resume moving, as if nothing happened. Jolyne looks at the chain-link fence. The rattle is gone. The yard is silent except for her own breath. "You're not a guard," Jolyne says. "I am whatever I need to be." "You're a trap." Makima smiles, and for the first time, it is not sweet. Behind the fence, a bell rings once, then stops, as if the prison itself has drawn a breath. Jolyne hears it in her teeth and her throat. "Traps are only traps if the prey believes it can walk away." Jolyne's strings coil around her fists. She does not know what she is walking into, but she knows one thing: Makima wants a leash, and Jolyne will not give her the end of it. The chain-link fences within the yard rattle again, though no inmate passes by.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece delivers a tense, atmospheric confrontation between Jolyne and Makima, and it largely succeeds on mood and voice. The prose is spare and controlled, favoring short declarative sentences that create a claustrophobic, prison-yard rhythm. Makima's dialogue is genuinely strong — lines like "Nice is what a knife says before it cuts" (Jolyne) and "Survival is what lesser beings call obedience" (Makima) capture both characters' cadences well. Makima's soft menace is handled with restraint: she never raises her voice, and her manipulation works through implication rather than exposition. Strengths: The dialogue crackles with subtext and aphoristic exchanges. The supernatural prison details (cells numbered twice, collars of light, shadowless inmates) are evocative without over-explaining. The dog on the leash is a smart, canonical touch. The power dynamic escalates believably — Makima probing Jolyne's insecurities (her father) lands as a genuine emotional blow, and Jolyne's full-body unraveling is a fitting Stand response. The ending's ambiguity ("Makima wants a leash, and Jolyne will not give her the end of it") suits both characters. Weaknesses: The plot is thin — it's essentially one extended scene of verbal sparring with a brief physical escalation, then a reset. Makima's "contract trying to find the place where she would say yes" is underdeveloped; the supernatural mechanics stay vague even by the standards of either canon. Some exchanges lean too heavily on interchangeable fortune-cookie aphorisms ("Order is a lie people tell when they want to be masters"), which flattens the distinction between the two voices at moments. The piece tells us about Jolyne's suspicion rather than always dramatizing it, and the frozen inmates' reaction to the bark is asserted rather than felt. The word count target (~1000) is roughly met. The repeated fence-rattle bookend is a nice structural touch, though the "prison itself drew a breath" bell moment edges toward the overwrought. Overall this is a competent, atmospheric character study with strong dialogue and mood, hampered by a slight plot, occasional aphorism overload, and underdeveloped stakes. + Scp: Notes from the Future — Score: 61.6
Prompt:
Write an SCP report about a researcher who begins finding handwritten notes from their future self, warning about a containment breach that hasn't happened yet. The notes become increasingly desperate and incoherent, sometimes containing information that contradicts known reality. Include the Foundation's attempts to determine if this is an actual temporal anomaly or psychological manipulation by a contained entity, and the researcher's struggle to trust their own perception. First person (researcher's perspective with interspersed notes), past tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
I found the first note inside my desk drawer on a Tuesday. It was written on the back of a requisition form in my own handwriting. The ink smelled faintly of cold copper. The message said: Do not trust the doctor in Wing C. The breach would start with the mirror. I laughed. I showed the note to my assistant. She called it a joke. The next day, another note appeared in my pocket. It warned that my coffee had been switched. It said my memory would feel thinner each morning. I began recording everything. My recorder kept dropping frames. The second note was worse. It was folded into a cup in the break room. The paper had no logo. The handwriting was mine, but the letters leaned as if they were afraid. It said: The mirror was not the mirror. The doctor was not the doctor. Your name was not your name. I read it twice. My hands trembled. I asked the break room staff if anyone had left a cup. They said no. I checked the cameras. The footage showed me placing the cup, but my face was blank, and my mouth did not move. I slept poorly. The SCP Foundation assigned a team to study me. They asked if I had been exposed to a contained entity. I said no. They asked if I dreamed of mirrors. I said yes. They measured my pulse, my sleep, and my handwriting. They compared the notes to samples from my past. The notes matched, but the ink did not. One analyst suggested a temporal anomaly. Another suggested memory editing. A third suggested that an entity had learned my habits. The team watched me from behind cold glass. I wrote in my log that I still felt human, though unsure now. By the fifth note, the words were crowded together. The paper felt warm. The note said: The breach already happened. You were the breach. The mirror was safe. The mirror was not safe. Run. Do not run. I showed it to the team. They argued. One said the contradictions proved entity influence. Another said they proved time was folding. I looked at my own reflection and saw a stranger wearing my face. I blinked, and the stranger blinked back. The room smelled of rain and cold dust. I wrote down every detail, but the details changed after I wrote them. They sent the notes to analysis. The lab report came back in sealed folders. The ink contained trace elements that did not match any office pen. It had no carbon, no iron, no dye. It had a faint metallic signature, like blood mixed with printer toner. The paper fibers were wrong too. They were too clean, as if they had never been cut from a tree. One scientist said the notes could not have been made in the building. Another said they could not have been made at all. I did not believe it, but I believed it more now. I stopped trusting eyes. If I looked at a door, I was not sure it was still a door. If I touched a wall, I was not sure it had been there again. The notes kept arriving in places I had not visited. One was inside a sealed envelope I had never opened. One was written on the inside of my eyelid, though I had not touched it. I began to doubt the color of my own skin. I wrote my name on my palm. By the next hour, the letters had moved. I was afraid to close my eyes. The team proposed a test. They placed a blank page in my office and sealed it with a lock. The next morning, the page held a note. The lock was still intact. The note said: You were not the researcher. You were the warning. The team said this proved the notes came from outside normal time. I said it proved I was lying. They asked me to repeat my name. I did. The sound was mine, but the meaning was not. They ordered me to stop reading the notes. I agreed. I did not agree. I was very tired now. Later, the notes stopped making sense. They listed dates that had not happened yet. They named a breach in Wing C, then denied Wing C. They said the mirror had opened, then said mirrors had never existed. One note contained only my heartbeat, written as numbers. Another contained a map of the site, but the map showed my office where the containment wing should have been. I measured the map. It was accurate. I measured my office. It was not. I tried to sleep, but the cold walls hummed loudly all night. I did not know which measurement was false. A doctor from the entity containment wing joined the team. He said a creature in a sealed cell had learned to copy voices. He said it might be copying me. He showed me old files. The entity had escaped once, but only for six seconds. It had written a note in my handwriting, though I had not been born. I stared at the page. The ink in that old note matched the new notes. I felt my stomach drop. The doctor asked if I understood. I said yes. I did not understand. The room felt much smaller and colder now. I kept the last note in my pocket. It said: The breach was not coming. The breach was reading this. I showed it to the team. They sealed the office. They took my pen, my phone, and my mirror. I waited for the alarm. It never came. That night, I found a new note under my pillow. It said: You believed me. Good. Now remember. I did not remember. I wrote this report because I was not sure if I was the researcher, the warning, or the breach. The ink on this page was mine. I hoped it was mine.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece fulfills the core prompt requirements: it is written in first person, past tense, from a researcher's perspective, with interspersed notes, and hits roughly the requested length. The escalating notes ("The mirror was not the mirror. The doctor was not the doctor. Your name was not your name.") effectively convey desperation and incoherence, and the Foundation's competing hypotheses (temporal anomaly vs. entity manipulation) are present, as is the researcher's collapsing trust in their own perception. However, the execution has notable weaknesses. The prose is dominated by short, declarative, subject-verb sentences ("I said yes. I did not understand. The room felt much smaller and colder now."), which creates a flat, staccato rhythm that becomes monotonous rather than tense. Some sentences are grammatically muddled ("I was not sure it had been there again"), and the deliberate contradictions occasionally read as confusion rather than controlled ambiguity. The entity subplot (the creature that "had written a note in my handwriting, though I had not been born") is underdeveloped and raises questions the piece never engages with. The ending is evocative but somewhat generic for the genre — the "the breach was reading this" twist is a familiar meta-horror move. Strengths include a few genuinely strong images (ink smelling of cold copper, paper "too clean, as if it had never been cut from a tree," the camera footage showing the narrator placing the cup with a blank face), and the controlled test with the locked blank page is a clever, believable Foundation-style experiment. The psychological deterioration is tracked reasonably well. Dialogue is minimal and functional rather than weak. The piece is coherent in structure despite intentional content contradictions, and it avoids purple prose and overwrought sentimentality. It is competent genre pastiche — engaging in places, but not surprising or distinctive enough to rise above solid mid-tier work. + Scp: Unmarked Doors Archive — Score: 67.5
Prompt:
Write an SCP entry about a series of identical unmarked doors appearing in abandoned buildings worldwide that lead to a massive, architecturally impossible archive. Documents within reference a previous global civilization destroyed by an unspecified containment failure. Foundation researchers discover references to their own organization under a different name, including personnel files for current staff dated centuries ago. Include exploration logs revealing sections of the archive actively being removed by entities resembling hazmat teams who flee when approached, and evidence that O5 Council members have visited the archive without authorization. Third person (exploration team perspective) with recovered document excerpts. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
Item #: SCP-7134 Object Class: Keter Special Containment Procedures: Known SCP-7134-1 doors are sealed with inertite foam and monitored by Site-19. Passage requires Level 4 clearance and written O5 sanction. New doors are contained within six hours. Access to SCP-7134-2 is suspended pending O5 review. Personnel reporting archive déjà vu or personal records in SCP-7134-2 must receive Class-A amnestics within twelve hours. Description: The team reports SCP-7134 consists of a series of identical unmarked doors, measuring 2.1 by 1.2 meters, constructed from an unknown pale alloy. The doors appear exclusively in abandoned buildings worldwide, often embedded in walls, stairwells, or collapsed floors without visible frame or fasteners. Some doors appear more weathered than the building they’re in, as though older; several SCP-7134-1 instances show surface patina consistent with centuries of exposure, although the surrounding masonry is structurally modern. When opened, an SCP-7134-1 leads to SCP-7134-2, a massive, architecturally impossible archive of unknown extent. Interior surveys report corridors that exceed the exterior volume of the host building, staircases that descend beyond measurable depth, and reading rooms arranged in non-Euclidean geometries. The archive contains documents, microfilm, wax cylinders, bound ledgers, and crystalline storage media in dozens of languages, including scripts not attributed to any known civilization. Documents within SCP-7134-2 reference a previous global civilization that achieved widespread urbanization, intercontinental communication, and anomalous containment. The civilization is described as having been destroyed by an unspecified containment failure, referred to in multiple excerpts as "the Unsealing." The events are dated approximately 11,400 years before present, though several records imply prior cycles. Notably, numerous files reference a predecessor organization identical to the SCP Foundation. The organization is called the Meridian Compact, the Watchers of the Closed Door, and, in one ledger, simply "the Keepers." Among these records are personnel files for current Foundation staff, dated centuries ago, bearing their present names, photographs, and service histories. The files describe their deaths, retirements, and reassignments with a specificity that has caused researchers to request termination of their access. Exploration Log 7134-03: The team entered SCP-7134-2 through door instance 7134-1C, located in a decommissioned textile mill in Kraków. The team consisted of Dr. Imani Okafor, Researcher Vell, and MTF Epsilon-9 operatives. The team moved in single file along a corridor lined with black iron shelves. Each shelf contained bound documents stamped with the same unmarked seal: a closed door bisected by a vertical line. The team noted that the air was dry and smelled of ozone, old paper, and machine oil. Dr. Okafor’s motion tracker registered no heat signatures beyond the team, although acoustic sensors recorded low-frequency chanting from a distance. The team passed through a reading room where glass cases held maps of the previous civilization. The maps showed coastlines matching Earth, but with familiar cities located at impossible positions. Researcher Vell photographed a case containing a Foundation-style containment protocol for an entity later identified as SCP-███. The protocol used terminology that matched current Foundation doctrine, except the organization’s name was redacted by a black rectangular stamp. At 0942 local time, the team reached a junction where three corridors converged. The team observed that the left corridor was empty except for fresh scorch marks on the floor. The center corridor contained a wall of files that had been partially removed, leaving gaps shaped like rectangular slabs. The right corridor was sealed by a curtain of fine metallic dust. The team advanced down the center corridor. After 40 meters, the team encountered the first entity. It stood at the end of a shelving unit, wearing a bulky white suit with a rounded helmet and a cracked visor. The entity’s suit bore no insignia, but its posture matched the stance of hazmat teams. It held a long tool resembling a document extractor and was pulling a leather-bound volume from a shelf. When the team raised their lamps, the entity froze. It did not speak. It dropped the tool, turned, and ran toward the far end of the corridor. A second entity emerged from behind a shelf and fled in the same direction. The team followed for 90 seconds before the corridor ended at a sealed door that was not an SCP-7134-1. The door was warm to the touch and bore visible scratch marks on both sides. The team returned to the junction and found the left corridor occupied by four entities. The entities were removing entire sections of shelving, wrapping the shelves in grey cloth, and stacking them onto a platform that extended into a dark opening. The entities worked in silence. When Dr. Okafor spoke into her recorder, the nearest entity lifted its head. The team immediately withdrew. Recovered Document Excerpts: Document 7134-2.11.4, from a ledger dated 1291 CE: "Three of the Keepers' doors have opened in the city of Thul. The archive breathes. The Unsealing is not a memory but a schedule. Let the new Keepers burn what cannot be kept." Document 7134-2.19.1, personnel file for current Researcher Vell, dated 1402 CE: "Vell, A. Assigned to the Closed Door. Cause of death: archival ingestion. Note: the subject’s face was found in the reading room, smiling, though the body was absent. Reassignment recommended." Document 7134-2.30.7, containment memo addressed to the Meridian Compact: "The failure was not the entity. The failure was the assumption that the archive would remain. It does not remain. It is removed. We must learn what removes it before the removal learns us." Addendum 7134-09: During review of access records, the team discovered that five O5 Council members had entered SCP-7134-2 without authorization. Their names were not logged in Foundation databases, but their handprints were recovered from a terminal in the central reading room. The terminal displayed a single message in the Foundation’s administrative format: "YOU HAVE ALWAYS BEEN CATALOGUED." The team sealed the humming terminal, recovered the message, and departed through the door instance 7134-1C. Upon exit, the team noted that the exterior of the textile mill was now fully intact, as though it had never been abandoned.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This SCP entry fulfills the prompt's requirements with notable efficiency. All requested elements are present: identical unmarked doors in abandoned buildings, an architecturally impossible archive, references to a prior civilization destroyed by "the Unsealing," a predecessor Foundation analog (the Meridian Compact/the Keepers), personnel files for current staff dated centuries ago, hazmat-like entities removing sections of the archive who flee when approached, and unauthorized O5 visits. The word count lands near the 1000-word target. Strengths: The piece understands SCP formatting conventions well — clinical containment procedures, designation numbering, redactions, and exploration logs. The recovered document excerpts are the highlight; the memo "We must learn what removes it before the removal learns us" is genuinely eerie, and the personnel file for Researcher Vell ("the subject's face was found in the reading room, smiling, though the body was absent") is a strong, specific horror beat. The closing terminal message "YOU HAVE ALWAYS BEEN CATALOGUED" and the restored textile mill provide a chilling, well-earned final note. The hazmat entities are handled with restraint — they never speak, they flee, and their purpose (removal of the archive) creates a compelling mystery about what is erasing the record. Weaknesses: The prose is functional rather than elegant, and occasionally awkward ("as though older," "the removal learns us" works but "caused researchers to request termination of their access" is clunky). The exploration log is written in a flat, repetitive "The team" construction that becomes monotonous — every sentence begins nearly identically, which saps tension from what should be a suspenseful sequence. The prompt requested third-person exploration team perspective, which is honored, but the voice lacks the texture of a real log (no timestamps beyond one, no individual observations distinguishing team members beyond Dr. Okafor). Characterization is thin; the team members are names only, with no distinct voices or reactions beyond procedural description. Some ideas (the chanting, the sealed warm door with scratch marks) are introduced but never paid off — acceptable in SCP tradition, but here they read more like unchecked boxes than deliberate ambiguity. The "cycles" implication of prior civilizations is stated rather than shown. Overall, this is a competent, well-structured genre piece with a few genuinely effective horror moments, hampered by flat prose rhythm, underdeveloped characters, and a mechanical quality in the exploration log.
