+ Classic sci-fi: Offworlder (Le Guin) — Score: 57.8
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi: Offworlder (Author style: Le Guin) Write a chapter following a young diplomatic envoy sent to address tensions on a distant human colony where humanity has diverged into distinct subspecies through both natural adaptation and separation of lineages. Against protocol, the envoy slips away from official functions to walk the streets alone, encountering markets, ordinary citizens, and social structures that contradict the official briefings. Upon returning to their quarters, the envoy is reprimanded by Command, and is tasked with approaching the stationed Minister of Science (a political posting rather than scientific). A challenging conversation ensues, in which the envoy's wits and will are tested, by a seasoned political operator looking to test the mettle of the offworlder. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The city had no walls, which was the first lie in my briefing. It rose from black basalt shelves, its streets narrow, its people small, quick, their skin the blue-grey of deep water, their eyes bright as polished stone. They wore little: thin sashes, woven bands, sometimes only a knot at the shoulder. My official cloak, dark green and heavy, made me look like a traveling tree. Children stopped to touch the hem. A woman sold fruit and asked if I had eaten. I answered in the trade tongue, and she laughed, not at the words but at the formality. In the market I saw what the briefing had called residual tribalism. There were no tribes. There were clans, but they kept no land; they kept songs, debts, and a shared way of binding cloth. Two men argued over a price of salt. A child ran between them, and both stopped, not in fear but in courtesy. I was told these people were violent, hungry, and prone to ritual exile. They looked tired, clever, and very much alive. When I returned, the corridor of my quarters was bright and cold. No one offered me a place to sit. They watched. Command was waiting in the small reception room, its faces arranged in the polite mask of official concern. "You were seen alone," said Director Vale, without looking at me. "I was walking," I said. "You were exposed. You wore our uniform in public. You spoke to citizens. You failed to file a movement report." "I filed a note with the embassy." "Notes are not reports." Director Vale set a glass of water before me, though I had not asked for it. "The colony is unstable," he said. "The Governor wants a statement of concern. We need facts, not impressions now." "I have impressions," I said. "The briefings were wrong." "The briefings were based on intelligence." "Intelligence," I said, "can be a very polite word for fear." Vale's eyes did not move. "You are a young envoy. Your job is to observe, not to judge." "If I observe, I must judge what I see." "Within limits." He gave me the new task in a voice so level it seemed to have no edges. "Tomorrow you will meet Minister Orenne." "Science?" I asked. "Science is the title," he said. "The ministry handles adaptation, lineage, and public health. Orenne is not a scientist." "He is a politician who has learned to speak in the language of science." "Will he be hostile?" "He will be curious. That is worse." "Because I am young?" "Because you are offworlder. Because you have not yet decided what you are here to protect." I left with the taste of water in my mouth and the weight of his words in my throat. At the ministry, Orenne received me in a room with no desk. He was older than I had expected, lean, with close-cropped silver hair and hands that moved as if they were thinking. "Sit," he said. "You may take off your cloak. It is hot." "I did not. I was told to keep my uniform." "You were told many things." He smiled, but the smile did not reach his eyes. "The offworlder arrives with a map and calls the territory a mistake." "I was told your people were divided by blood," I said. "We are divided by choice," he said. "Blood is only the excuse." "By lineage?" "By adaptation. Some of us are taller, darker, more resistant to the dry winds. Some are shorter, with broader chests and slower hearts. The old families call this purity." "The new families call it survival. Both are wrong, and both are useful." "In the market," I said, "I saw no signs of conflict." "In the market, you saw what you were permitted to see." "That is a strong claim." "It is a careful one." He leaned forward. "You walked alone. You touched the city. You will tell me what you saw, or I will tell you what I believe you saw." "I saw people selling, buying, arguing, laughing." "Did you see who paid for the salt?" "Yes." "Did you see who owned the salt?" "The cooperative." "The Governor rules." I said nothing. "Your silence is a report," he said. "I am here to address tensions," I said. "Not to choose sides." "Everyone chooses sides. The question is whether you choose them openly." "If I choose openly, I become part of the conflict." "If you choose secretly, you become a tool." "And if I choose neither?" He laughed, a dry sound. "Then you are a diplomat. Congratulations." "You test me." "I test everyone." "Because I am young?" "Because you are new. Because you carry the old world in your uniform." I looked at his hands. "What do you want now?" "I want to know if you can be trusted." "By whom?" "By yourself." The question sat in the room like a stone. I thought of the market, the fruit seller, the child running between the men. I thought of the cloak, heavy and green, and the way the children had reached for it. "I cannot be trusted," I said, "if I do not tell you what I saw." "Then tell me." "I saw a city that was not what we were told. I saw people who had changed, and who had chosen to remain human. I saw a government, too." "I saw a minister who used truth to keep power." Orenne studied me. "That is not a report," he said. "It is a beginning." "Beginnings are dangerous." "So are endings." He walked to the window. Outside, the basalt shelves glittered in the thin sun. "If you stay," he said, "you must learn our language. Not the trade tongue. The other one." "What is it?" "The language of choice." I looked down at my cloak. "Teach me," I said. He said, "Take off your cloak." I did not. I loosened the clasp at my throat. I let the city in now.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece attempts a Le Guin-style anthropological sci-fi register, and partially succeeds. The opening market scene is the strongest section: concrete sensory details (blue-grey skin, basalt shelves, the heavy green cloak, the fruit seller's laughter) establish the colony's texture efficiently, and the envoy's observation that "there were no tribes... they kept songs, debts, and a shared way of binding cloth" is a genuinely Le Guin-like move—correcting an official category with a lived one. However, the piece degrades as it goes. The Command reprimand and the Orenne conversation devolve into rapid-fire, unattributed dialogue exchanges that read more like a screenplay transcript than prose. Le Guin's dialogue is embedded in thought, gesture, and interiority; here the exchanges are stripped to bare lines, losing rhythm and emotional grounding. The conversation with Orenne is meant to be a duel of wits, but it relies on aphorisms ("Blood is only the excuse," "Your silence is a report," "The language of choice") that gesture at depth without earning it. The salt/cooperative exchange gestures at political complexity but is underdeveloped. The ending is the weakest element: "I let the city in now" is a tidy, symbolic gesture that arrives too easily—the envoy's shift from protocol-bound to open happens in a single loosened clasp, an unearned transformation. The final line also misplaces the object ("I did not. I loosened the clasp") in a way that muddles the action. The prose is competent and mostly restrained, avoiding purple excess, and the voice is consistent. But the piece tells more than it shows in its second half, the emotional stakes remain abstract, and the "challenging conversation" never achieves real tension because Orenne's challenges are rhetorical rather than situational. It's a solid imitation of surface Le Guin without her patience or moral specificity. + Biopunk: Polymerase Chain Reaction — Score: 51.8
Prompt:
Biopunk -- Polymerase Chain Reaction Write a chapter set in a near-future post-apocalyptic world where corporate genetic engineering was designed with built-in obsolescence—engineered DNA lasting only one generation to maximize profits before societal collapse. Follow a biohacker working with salvaged equipment to splice viable food crops for their settlement using rapidly degrading genetic material. As world building / window dressing, include details about jury-rigged lab equipment, and the physical toll (and unexpected upsides) of using untested genetic modifications as medicine. The plot of this chapter is centred around a black market contract. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The PCR block sat on a drum welded to a car battery, its lid held by a bolt from a dead washing machine. Mara wiped the glass door with an iodine rag. Four empty Helixia canisters held reagents, their logos peeling like old skin in the cold gray dawn now. Helixia had sold engineered crops with expiry cassettes, sequences that collapsed after one generation. Farmers swore the plants remembered profit. Now, in the settlement's root cellar, seed stocks crumbled to ash, their genomes failing before they could feed another winter before the first frost could take them again this year. Mara opened a vial of corn DNA rescued from a moldy ear. The liquid was brown, thin, full of broken fragments. She had only minutes before the polymerase denatured. PCR would amplify the useful pieces, copying what remained into strands strong enough to splice before the last base called it. The contract lay on the table, signed in grease pencil. A trader wanted viable wheat seed by the next moon, payment in clean water, fuel, and a sealed medical ampoule. Refusal meant starvation. Acceptance meant Mara had to make dead genes behave in the field by spring or die now. Mara's arm ached where she had injected an untested growth serum the previous night. Helixia's old formulae were not meant for humans. Her veins looked dark under pale skin, and her breath tasted of iron. She flexed her fingers and felt a strange warmth spread through her chest all night. The serum had costs. Her sleep was shallow, her dreams full of green static. Yet her eyes now caught faint infrared from the heater, and small cuts sealed faster than before. Medicine, here, was a gamble with teeth and Mara kept a knife close because the knife had opinions now. She loaded the PCR tubes with primer, buffer, and the degraded template. The reagent canisters had once held proprietary enzymes, now empty and chipped. She capped them with caps from a broken centrifuge, a device built from a motor and a salad spinner that spun like a prayer sometimes too. The block clicked. Temperature rose, then fell, then rose again. Denature, anneal, extend. Mara watched the numbers on a cracked display, counting cycles like beads. Each pass copied the fragments, building a ladder of short strands from the wreckage of old Helixia corn and a little hope for the field. The wheat needed cold tolerance, but the wheat DNA was worse than the corn. Mara mixed the amplified fragments with a splicing enzyme salvaged from a veterinary kit. If the edit caught, the crop might survive frost and feed the settlement before the traders came back hungry and armed again. A tremor ran through Mara's hand. The untested mods were rewriting her, too. She could smell ozone before a storm, and her pulse slowed when she was afraid. Useful, maybe, but the price was a constant ache behind her ribs like a wire pulled tight inside her chest at night. The trader's name was Kade. He wore a coat stitched from biotech uniforms, the Helixia logo bleached white. He did not ask how Mara would make the seed. He only asked if she understood that late meant debt and debt had collectors who liked keeping fingers as trophies for years. She used the last clean canister for the spliced mixture. Its label read Helixia Crop Stabilizer, now a joke. The canister's inner seal had failed years ago, so Mara lined it with melted wax from a candle and a prayer from the old world that might still work today too. When the cycles ended, the gel tray glowed blue under a salvaged lamp. A faint band appeared where it should. Not enough. Mara ran the reaction again, adjusting the temperature by one degree, coaxing the broken code into obedience as if it were alive and willing to listen once more. Outside, children coughed in the wind. The settlement's fields were brown, the last Helixia soybean plants withering before they could set pods. Mara knew that without viable seed, the next season would be a slow death by hunger and the traders would smell it from the road and come soon. The mods gave her other gifts. She could taste salt in the air, predict rain, and feel the PCR block's heat through the table. Her body was becoming a patchwork of corporate experiments, a living instrument tuned by desperation and the memory of better days that never came back then. Kade's runner arrived at dusk, a thin girl with a scanner that could read old biotech tags. She wanted a sample of the spliced seed, a proof of life, or Mara's contract would be posted on the black market as broken and her name marked for bounty hunters tonight only. Mara transferred the amplicon into a tube wrapped in foil. The PCR product was still fragile, a chain of copies that could collapse if the temperature shifted. She kept it against her chest, where the modified serum made the skin warm and the pulse steady against the cold dusk now. The spliced wheat had not germinated yet, but the DNA band promised structure. Mara imagined roots pushing through frozen soil, leaves uncurling, grain filling. If the edit held, it would be the first stable crop since the expiry cassettes broke the world and the first true food in years again. The serum had also changed her fear. She no longer flinched at the trader's threats. Instead, her mind cataloged exits, distances, and the strength of doors. It was useful, but it made her feel less human, more optimized like a machine with a soul running low on oil now too. Mara handed the sample to the runner. The scanner beeped, then went quiet. The girl nodded, sliding a token into Mara's palm. The contract was alive, and the next moon was close. Mara turned back to the PCR block, ready to make the dead grow before the frost could fall.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece fulfills the prompt's core requirements: a biopunk post-apocalypse built on Helixia's one-generation engineered crops, a biohacker (Mara) running PCR on salvaged equipment, jury-rigged lab details (car battery, salad-spinner centrifuge, wax-lined canisters), physical tolls and unexpected upsides of self-administered genetic mods, and a black market contract with the trader Kade driving the chapter's plot. World-building details are economical and effective—the expiry cassettes, the bleached logos on Kade's coat, the runner's scanner. However, the prose has a persistent, distracting tic: sentence-final temporal tags that read as machine-generated filler ("in the cold gray dawn now," "before the first frost could take them again this year," "as bounty hunters tonight only," "that never came back then," "a prayer... that might still work today too," "running low on oil now too"). These appended "now/too/again" endings recur constantly and feel like a model straining for poetic cadence without understanding it. They damage otherwise serviceable sentences and are the piece's most amateurish feature. The narrative is coherent and appropriately paced for 1000 words, moving through setup, contract stakes, lab procedure, and a partial resolution (the sample handed over, contract alive, work ongoing). The ending is suitably grim-but-hopeful without incongruous positivity. Mara is a believable, competent protagonist; her fear-cataloging and dehumanization ("more optimized like a machine") is a nice touch, though characters beyond her are thin—Kade is a stock menacing trader, the runner a cipher. Dialogue is minimal and functional. Imagery is mixed: some strong moments (logos peeling like old skin, counting cycles like beads, debt collectors keeping fingers as trophies) sit alongside vague or strained ones ("green static" dreams, "a gamble with teeth," "the knife had opinions now"—the latter is confusing rather than evocative). The science is hand-wavy but internally consistent enough for the genre. Emotionally, the piece is competent but not deeply engaging; stakes are stated more than felt, and the settlement's desperation is told rather than shown. There are no major unearned transformations or tonal failures, but also little that surprises—the plot beats are familiar post-apocalyptic beats. + Classic sci-fi: The Azra Gambit — Score: 53.0
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi (Author style: Asimov) The Azra Gambit Colonial mars is being mined by corporations who take leases on indentured labourers. The thing they are mining is Azra, a recently discovered exotic metal which accelerates radioactive decay to such a rate that it is greatly sought after for interstellar drives and weapons alike. This has created both a gold rush and an arms race as various interests vie for control and endeavour to unlock Azra's secrets. The story follows Arthur Neegan, a first generation settler and mining engineer. Upon discovering that his unassuming plot sits atop an immense Azra vein, he is subjected to a flurry of interest and scrutiny. Write the next chapter in this story, in which an armed retinue descends on Arthur's home and politely but forcefully invites him to a meeting with some unknown party off-world. The insignia look like that of the Antares diplomatic corp -- diplomatic in name only. Arthur finds himself in the centre of a political tug of war. The chapter involves a meeting with this unknown party, who makes Arthur an offer. The scene should be primarily dialogue, interspersed with vivid description & scene setting. It should sow hints of the larger intrigue, stakes & dangers. Include Asimov's trademark big-and-small-picture world building and retrofuturistic classic scifi vibe. The chapter begins with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, wondering just what he's gotten involved in. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
Arthur Neegan sat in the transfer vessel's passenger compartment, his boots pressed flat against a deck plate that hummed with residual reactor vibration. A small display screen on the wall cycled through various system diagnostics in green text. "Pressure nominal. Hull integrity nominal. Social tension," he muttered, "not nominal." The screen ticked along: coolant, shielding, grav compensation, radiation count. Outside, the transfer ship held course through the dark, its hull marked with no company logo, no colonial flag, only a faint serial number that looked more like a legal citation than an identification. The air smelled of recycled oxygen and polished metal, the particular scent of places where important decisions were made before anyone admitted they were being made quietly. Behind him, two men in charcoal jumpsuits stood with the patient posture of guards who had been told to look bored. Their cuffs bore the Antares diplomatic seal: a silver circle bisected by a blue band, with a stylized star at its center. Diplomatic, Arthur thought. At the far end of the compartment, a woman sat with her hands folded in her lap. "Mr. Neegan," she said. "Ms. Vail?" "You have the right not to answer questions. You do not have the right to remain on that plot indefinitely." Arthur looked at the ceiling. "I'm not a corporation. I'm an engineer. I found a vein under my house." "Then you are in possession of an unregistered strategic deposit." "Under the Colonial Charter, surface discoveries belong to the settler for a period of—" "Which charter, Mr. Neegan?" He stopped. She smiled without warmth. "There are three. The old Terran Mining Statutes, the Martian Compact, and the Antares Interstellar Accord. Which one do you intend to cite?" Arthur had the unpleasant sensation of a trap closing around his feet. "The one that says I can keep my home." "That one has not been ratified by the Interstellar Council." "Then why am I being asked to leave my home?" "Because you are being asked to make a decision." "Who are you working for?" he asked. "Antares Diplomatic Corps." "Right." "Antares is a neutral station, Mr. Neegan. We manage negotiations between the mining syndicates, the Terran fleets, and the colonial governments. We do not take sides." "Then why are there armed men in my house?" "They are here for your protection." "From whom?" "From those who believe that Azra should not be divided." Arthur looked at her. "Azra is a metal." "An unstable one." "It accelerates decay. That's what the mining pamphlets say." "That is what the public version says." She leaned forward slightly. "Azra does not merely accelerate decay. It alters the probability field of radioactive transitions. In small quantities, it makes drives efficient. In large quantities, it makes weapons unpredictable. In the wrong quantities, it can make a starship's reactor fail in a matter of seconds." Arthur felt the cold of the compartment settle into his shoulders. "You're saying it's dangerous." "I'm saying it is valuable enough to start wars." Arthur said, "There are people on Mars who depend on those drives. Colonies, hospitals, freighters. If Azra can make travel safer—" "Then it must be controlled." "By whom?" "By those willing to bear the responsibility." Arthur laughed once, sharply. "That's what every corporation says before they sign a lease." "Corporations bear the cost. Governments bear the blame. Engineers bear the consequences." She said it flatly, without accusation. "Your plot sits on a vein that extends for several kilometers. The core samples you took were taken without authorization. The readings you transmitted were intercepted. Three mining companies have filed claims. Two military attachés have requested your detention. One senator has asked for your plot to be declared a protected cultural site." "Cultural site?" "A convenient fiction. It would freeze the land while the legal questions are settled." Arthur thought of his mother's garden, the thin red soil, the first house he had ever owned. "They can't just take it." "They can. But they will not, if you agree to a meeting." The question came out before he could stop it. "Who?" The woman reached into a side pouch and placed a small card on the table. It was plain, without a name, but embossed with the same silver circle and blue band. "The meeting is off-world. A private station. You will be escorted by the Antares Diplomatic Corps. You will be offered a choice." "What choice?" "Whether to become a symbol, a witness, or a partner." Arthur stared at the card. "A partner in what?" "In understanding what Azra is." The vessel's lights dimmed for a second, then returned. The screen changed again: destination trajectory confirmed. Arthur looked at the guards, at the woman, at the card. He thought of the drilling rigs outside his window, the corporate surveyors with their polite smiles, the indentured laborers waiting at the gates for leases that would bind their children to the dust. He thought of the way the ore had glowed faintly when he first broke through the cap rock, as if the metal remembered some older fire. "If I refuse?" he asked. "Then you remain on Mars. And Mars remains what it is." "A mine?" "A prize." Arthur picked up the card. "Where is this station?" "Beyond the asteroid belt. Neutral ground." "Neutral," he said, "is a word people use when they have already chosen." The woman stood. "The meeting will begin in six hours. You will be given a suit, a credential, and a list of questions you are not to ask. You will also be given a small device. If you press it, a signal will be sent to the station. They will know you have arrived. They will also know you are afraid." Arthur looked at the screen. The green text continued its endless cycle. "Is that a threat?" "It is a courtesy." "Then I suppose I'd better not be afraid." The woman smiled, and for the first time it looked almost human. "No, Mr. Neegan. I suppose you would not."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The chapter opens correctly per the prompt (Arthur aboard the transfer vessel) and delivers a dialogue-heavy scene with an Antares diplomatic representative, an offer, and hints of larger intrigue. The Asimovian flavor is present: legalistic sparring over charters, exposition of Azra's physics delivered through conversation, and a coolly rational power dynamic. The dialogue is crisp and functional, with some genuinely good exchanges ("Neutral is a word people use when they have already chosen"). The three-charters trap is a nice Asimov-style legal-worldbuilding touch. Weaknesses: the scene is somewhat generic — the mysterious woman offering vague choices ("symbol, witness, or partner") is stock thriller fare. The offer itself remains frustratingly abstract; the prompt asked for an offer, and what Arthur receives is mostly a card and an invitation to another meeting, which slightly dodges the requirement. Vail's exposition about Azra altering "probability fields" is a bit hand-wavy. The "fear device" beat is a nice touch but the ending exchange is a touch neat. Description is competent but sparse; the retrofuturistic texture could be richer. Prose is clean, unpretentious, appropriately plain in the classic mode. Characters are functional rather than deeply nuanced — Vail is a type, Arthur a decent everyman. Emotionally it engages moderately without deep complexity. + Contemporary romance: Darkroom Revelations — Score: 61.2
Prompt:
Darkroom Revelations Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of Dani, a 25-year-old assertive art student known for her bold style and take-charge attitude in relationships. For the past semester, she's been quietly fascinated by Elliot (he/him), a 19-year-old boy in her experimental photography class. Dani has been intrigued by his unconventional masculinity: killer thrift-shop-nu-goth style, soft demeanour and quiet intellect. When they're paired for a final project requiring late nights in the darkroom, Elliot tentatively shares that he's been questioning his gender identity and expression. Set during one of these intimate darkroom sessions where the red light creates a confessional atmosphere. Explore Dani's complex attraction—her usual assertiveness complicated by her desire to protect Elliot's vulnerability, her excitement at witnessing his self-discovery, and her confusion about what this means for her own identity as someone typically attracted to more defined gender presentations. The narrative should capture the tender awkwardness of their conversations, Dani's internal struggle between taking charge and wanting to give Elliot agency, and the unexpected chemistry that develops as both find themselves in uncharted territory. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The red darkroom lamp turned everything the color of wine, and I stood at the enlarger trying to remember how to be in control. I, Dani, am twenty-five, an art student who has built a bold style and a take-charge attitude in relationships, the kind of person who names desire before it can hide. For the past semester, I had been quietly fascinated by Elliot, a nineteen-year-old boy in my experimental photography class. He wore killer thrift-shop-nu-goth: velvet, lace, boots too large, a soft demeanour, and a quiet intellect that made the room lean closer without noise in the dark. Our final project required a series of portraits, and the professor paired us with a casualness that felt like fate. Late nights followed. The darkroom became a confessional: red light, trays, the smell of chemicals, and the slow reveal of images in the bath. Elliot stood beside me, careful and warm, while I fixed the paper, set the timer, and tried to keep my voice steady. There was a tender awkwardness between us, the kind that happens when two people are learning how to share a small space without stepping on each other's shadows while the small fan ticked low. Elliot hummed a soft tune while waiting for the images to reveal in the chemical bath. It was not a song with words, only a low line that moved under the silence. I watched his mouth, then his hands, then the paper lifting from the solution. The tune made my pulse do something stupid. I am used to taking charge, to steering conversations and bodies toward clarity, but this quiet melody pulled me into a different rhythm. For the first time, I wanted to be led, even if only for the length of one developing print in the red dark. I had always been drawn to more defined gender presentations: broad shoulders, hard jawlines, the confident architecture of a man who knew exactly what he was. Elliot unsettled me because he did not announce himself. His masculinity was unconventional, gentle, and thoughtful, a puzzle I wanted to solve without solving. I felt excited, almost giddy, at the thought that I was witnessing his self-discovery. At the same time, I felt confused. If my attraction relied on certainty, what did I do with a person who was becoming? I did not want to flatten him into something I already knew well. One night, after the third print had dried, Elliot set down the tongs and looked at the tray as if it might answer for him. 'I need to tell you something,' he said. His voice was small, but not weak. 'I have been questioning my gender identity and expression. The way I dress, the way I move, the parts of being a boy that feel inherited instead of chosen.' He paused, watching me. I wanted to take charge, to reassure him, to make the moment safe. Instead, I held still and let his words land where they needed to, now. My usual assertiveness felt dangerous. I wanted to protect Elliot's vulnerability, to wrap it in promises and control, but I also knew that protection could become possession. He was not a project to fix, even though our final assignment demanded images. I had to give him agency, even when my hands ached to steer. The red light made my face look less certain than I felt. I am someone who takes charge, but I was learning that taking charge sometimes means asking what the other person needs, and then trusting the answer without making it about me, all at once. Chemistry arrived without warning, in the space between our hands over the print. He would ask about exposure, and I would answer, but the questions were no longer only about light. 'Do you feel safe here?' he asked once, and the question hung in the red air. I laughed, then stopped, because laughter felt too bright. 'I do,' I said, 'but I am not sure I have done it before.' He nodded, as if that were enough, and the tenderness of the moment made my chest ache. We were both in uncharted territory, and it did not frighten us yet. I was not used to being unmoored. My identity had always been built on boldness: I knew what I wanted, I pursued it, and I made room for it. Elliot made me question whether that certainty was strength or armor. I was attracted to him, but not in the simple way I expected. I was attracted to his softness, his intelligence, his willingness to be uncertain. I was excited to witness his self-discovery, and I was terrified that my excitement might make me careless with him. I did not want to rush him or make him small in the dark. 'What do you want me to do?' I asked, because I could not stand the not-knowing. Elliot looked at the bath, where a new image was slowly appearing. 'Tell me what you want,' he said. 'But do not decide for me.' I swallowed. 'I want to be here. I want to be careful. I want to know if you are interested, and I want you to have the space to say yes, no, or maybe.' The words were not a command. They were an offering, and that frightened me more than silence. It felt true and new to me now. Elliot hummed the soft tune again as the image finished revealing, the shadows deepening into a face I almost recognized. He held the print under the water, then lifted it, and for a moment we both stopped breathing. 'Stay?' he asked. I wanted to answer with the old boldness, the take-charge certainty I had built my life around. Instead, I let my hand rest near his, not touching, but close enough to feel the heat. 'Stay,' I said. In the red dark, we were both becoming. The red light held us like a secret neither of us had named yet.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece fulfills the prompt's requirements: first-person Dani, darkroom setting, Elliot's disclosure, Dani's internal conflict between assertiveness and giving agency, and the tentative chemistry. However, it does so in a conspicuously literal way—early paragraphs essentially recite the prompt's character sheet ("I, Dani, am twenty-five, an art student who has built a bold style and a take-charge attitude"), which reads as exposition rather than organic characterization. This is the piece's central weakness: it tells us who Dani is rather than letting her voice and behavior demonstrate it. The darkroom imagery is serviceable (red light as confessional, prints revealing in the bath) but underdeveloped—the photography process is used mostly as backdrop and metaphor rather than as lived, sensory experience. The prose is clean and controlled but rarely surprising; phrases like "the confident architecture of a man" and "we were both becoming" gesture at depth without quite earning it. Some lines are genuinely good ("protection could become possession," "a puzzle I wanted to solve without solving"), while others are flat or awkward ("The tune made my pulse do something stupid," "the tenderness of the moment made my chest ache"). Dialogue is sparse and slightly stilted; Elliot's "Tell me what you want. But do not decide for me" is thematically neat but doesn't sound like a tentative nineteen-year-old. The emotional beats arrive on schedule rather than accumulating naturally—Dani's confusion about her attraction to "a person who was becoming" is stated plainly rather than dramatized. The ending ("The red light held us like a secret neither of us had named yet") is soft-focus and a touch sentimental, though not unearned. Overall: competent, coherent, emotionally sincere, but mechanical in its adherence and tell-heavy in execution. It reads like a checklist executed with above-average craft. + Contemporary romance / drama: Stolen Moments in Roma — Score: 57.8
Prompt:
Contemporary Romance / Drama: Stolen Moments in Roma. Write a series of interconnected short scenes and dialogues that span a single day in modern-day Rome, in narrative form. This will form the beginning of a larger story. Alessandra, a fiery, independent Roman woman who works as a motorcycle courier, nearly collides with Ben, a somewhat clumsy, overly polite British academic on sabbatical, who is engrossed in a guidebook near the Trevi Fountain. The initial encounter is a clash of cultures and personalities – Alessandra is all sharp wit and rapid-fire Italian, while Ben is flustered apologies and awkward attempts at speaking the language. However, as they sort out the near-miss, a spark of unexpected humor and connection emerges. Alessandra, it quickly becomes clear, is a whirlwind of energy and mischief. She's a self-admitted troublemaker with a secret penchant for kleptomania, a detail she doesn't explicitly reveal, but which manifests in subtle, daring acts throughout the day. She impulsively decides to take Ben on a wild, unsanctioned tour of Rome, dragging him in some specific instances far outside his comfort zone. Ben, despite his initial apprehension and inherent politeness, finds himself utterly captivated by Alessandra's unapologetic spirit and zest for life. He is drawn into her orbit, a willing participant in increasingly outlandish situations, a quiet rebellion brewing beneath his scholarly exterior. The narrative should primarily consist of short, vivid scenes and dialogue exchanges, revealing their contrasting personalities and backgrounds, and the growing, ambiguous tension between them. Ben is captivated by Alessandra's energy and the thrill of breaking free from his routine. There's a clear sense that Alessandra is toying with Ben, pushing his boundaries and enjoying his reactions, but her own feelings remain somewhat enigmatic. The day should be a rollercoaster of exhilarating, slightly dangerous, and humorous moments, leaving Ben completely disoriented but utterly smitten. Explore the underlying tension & chemistry between them, culminating in some payoff as they part ways (or not -- your choice). Include this detail: Write in narrative prose, using immersive storytelling. 1000 words.
Model Output:
Stolen Moments in Roma The Trevi Fountain was a riot of elbows, cameras, and bad advice. Ben held his guidebook open like a shield, reciting the dimensions of the sea horse, when a matte-black motorcycle hissed around the corner like a black cat with a grudge. Alessandra did not brake. She swerved, one boot scraping stone, and stopped three inches from his knee. “Scusa,” she said, in English with a knife in it. “You are standing in the path of a woman with a deadline.” “I’m so sorry,” Ben said. “I was only—” “Only what? Reading? Here? Among the pigeons?” She gestured at the crowd. “You look like a lost comma.” He blinked. “I beg your pardon?” “I said you look like a lost comma. Small, polite, and completely in the wrong sentence.” She looked down at her phone. “Damn it. If I miss this delivery, my cousin will call me again. You have a car?” “I don’t drive in Rome.” “Good. Then you’re useless but available.” She kicked the stand down. “Get on.” “I—what?” “Back. Now. Before I change my mind.” He should have said no. He was on sabbatical, in Rome for a week, with a notebook full of footnotes and a heart that had been orderly for years. Instead, he climbed onto the back of the motorcycle, arms uncertain, and felt the city lurch under them. “Where are we going?” he shouted over the engine. “Wherever the day decides.” She took him first to the Spanish Steps, not to sit, but to race a scooter up the staircase. Ben clutched her waist as they climbed, then descended, then stopped at a café where Alessandra ordered two espresso without asking. “You drink?” she asked. “I didn’t know if I could.” “Life is a thing you drink before you know if you can.” She sipped hers in one go, then palmed a marble from a child’s game near the table. Ben saw. He did not say anything. At Campo de’ Fiori, she made him taste a fried artichoke from a cone. He burned his tongue. She laughed, not cruelly, but with the bright surprise of a bird escaping a cage. “You have a very serious face for a man with pepper in his mouth,” she said. “I’m a historian.” “Of what?” “Of nothing important, apparently.” She winked. They moved through the city like a rumor. She stopped at a bookshop and lifted a pen from a display, rolling it between her fingers. At a flower stall, she took a red carnation from a bucket and tucked it behind Ben’s ear. “You look like a tourist now,” she said. “I feel like a criminal.” “Better.” They ran into Marco near the Tiber, an old acquaintance with a tattooed forearm and a scooter leaning against the wall. He saw Ben first, then Alessandra, and his expression became a warning. “Ben,” Marco said, in careful English. “You are with Alessandra?” “I am.” Marco looked at her. “Alessandra, you are doing the thing.” “What thing?” she asked. “The thing where you find a person who is too polite to run and you make him feel alive.” Ben turned to her. “Is that true?” Alessandra shrugged. “I make people feel Rome. It is not my fault Rome is dangerous.” Marco leaned closer to Ben. “She is brilliant. She is also a fire you do not hold. She will take your wallet, your heart, maybe your left shoe. Leave before sunset.” Alessandra smiled, all teeth. “Marco, you are jealous. You have not stolen anything interesting in years.” Marco laughed. “I stole a whole pizza once.” “That was embarrassing.” Ben, still holding the espresso cup, felt something shift under his ribs. He had come to Rome to study the city from a distance, through dates and citations. Alessandra had handed him a pen, a flower, a stolen marble, and an engine. “Where next?” he asked. She looked at him for a long moment. Her eyes were dark, quick, amused. “Somewhere you will not like.” “I like not liking.” She grinned. “Then climb on.” They went to Trastevere after dark. She parked near a courtyard where a band played accordion and a woman was selling lemon cakes. Alessandra led Ben inside, past tables of laughing strangers, to a stone bench under a pergola. The air smelled of basil, warm stone, and river water. “You are quiet,” she said. “I am trying to decide if I am in a dream.” “Good. Dreams are easier to leave.” “You are leaving.” She did not answer. She set the red carnation on the bench between them, then the marble, then the pen. Three small objects, arranged like a secret. Ben stared at them. “What are those for?” “For you. In case you forget.” “Forget what?” “That for one day, you were not a comma.” He wanted to say something clever, something scholarly, something safe. Instead he said, “I think I remember.” She touched his wrist, briefly, as if testing whether he was real. “You are very strange, Ben.” “So I am told.” “By Marco?” “By everyone.” She laughed, low and warm. “Good. I hate normal.” A busker began to play something old and sweet. The courtyard filled with light. Alessandra leaned closer, and for a moment the city outside ceased to exist; there was only her breath, the heat of her skin, the faint scent of motor oil and citrus. “Will you come back?” she asked. “Tomorrow?” “When.” He looked at the objects on the bench, then at her. “If you promise to steal something.” “I promise nothing.” “Then I will have to steal you first.” She stared at him, then smiled, slow and dangerous. “You are learning.” They did not kiss. Not yet. But as she stood and brushed the carnation from the bench, she took his hand and led him out into the Roman night, streetlamps turning the cobblestones into gold. Behind them, the marble, the pen, and the flower remained on the stone bench, waiting like small promises.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece delivers the requested structure: interconnected short scenes across a single Roman day, a near-collision at the Trevi Fountain, contrasting personalities, escalating boundary-pushing, subtle kleptomania (marble, pen, carnation), and a parting-that-isn't-a-parting with ambiguous romantic tension. The "lost comma" motif is genuinely charming and pays off at the end ("you were not a comma"), which is the story's strongest structural choice. Strengths: the prose is economical and often witty ("a black cat with a grudge," "English with a knife in it," "They moved through the city like a rumor"). Dialogue crackles in places, and Alessandra's aphoristic style ("Life is a thing you drink before you know if you can") suits her character. The three stolen objects arranged on the bench is a lovely, understated climax. Weaknesses: the Marco scene is a clumsy device — a character who exists purely to explain Alessandra to the reader ("She will take your wallet, your heart...") is textbook tell-don't-show. Ben's transformation from cautious academic to "I will have to steal you first" is pleasant but arrives a bit easily; the story coasts on charm rather than earning his boldness through a genuine turning point. Some imagery is stock (streetlamps turning cobblestones into gold, the scent of basil and warm stone). Alessandra's enigmatic quality occasionally tips into vagueness rather than mystery. The ending with the objects "waiting like small promises" is a touch sentimental for a character defined by restlessness. Still, this is a confident, well-paced piece with a consistent voice and real chemistry between the leads. + Cozy sci-fi: The Last Outpost — Score: 50.9
Prompt:
Cozy sci-fi The Last Outpost Nettle (or Nets to her friends) bartends at The Last Outpost -- a lazy hub for miners and merchants in an asteroid belt on the Andromeda outer rim. Escaping from her past life, Nets found a home here at the Outpost. They have, thus far, tolerated Net's flaws which she tries to keep in equilibrium with her assortment of talents. Her evenings involve chatting with patrons, negotiating the drama, intrigue, problems & love lives of the diverse crowd that filter through the Outpost. Tonight is no different, at least, until a frazzled looking stranger, tentacled dreads askew, quietly plops down at the bar: "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." Write a chapter in this story. Establish conflict for narrative interest. Don't resolve the conflict within this chapter. Aim for about 60% dialogue. First person, present tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The Last Outpost hums at a lazy 54 hertz. I keep the bar polished, the lights low, and the complaints filed where they belong. Tonight it smells of cinnamon coolant, stale coffee, and recycled air. I'm wiping the same spot when the stranger plops down. "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." Her tentacles are frayed dreads, askew, her skin blue-gray. She looks like she's been through a hull breach and a laundry cycle. "First or second double?" I ask. "First. The second one's for when I'm dead." I pour. Vega whisky burns like an engine start. I slide the glass across. "Name?" "Kestrel. Or don't ask." "I ask. It's bar policy." "Then you can write it down and use it to file your complaints." I don't write it down. I keep wiping the same spot, a small dark circle near the edge. "You look like you've got a problem," I say. "Problem's got a ship, a warrant, and a very bad temper. She's called Vex." "Vex is a name, not a diagnosis." "She's a collector. I borrowed something from her." "Then pay her back." "I can't. It's not money." "What is it?" "A data seed. Small, warm, and currently singing in my jacket like a trapped bird." I stop wiping. The rag stays flat under my hand. "Where?" "Here." She taps her chest. "If they scan me, they'll hear it." A miner clears his throat. "Nets, you got a problem?" "Quiet, Orin. Private conversation." "Everything here is private until it isn't." "Then make it private." Orin shrugs, but his eyes stay on Kestrel's twitching tentacles. Kestrel leans in. "I need a place to hide." "Not here." "Your back room. The one with the old med bay." "That's not a hiding place. It's a storage closet with a broken bed." "It's behind a wall that doesn't show on my scanners." "Because I keep the scanners broken." "See? You're already helping." "I'm keeping the peace. There's a difference." The comm chimes. I don't answer. It chimes again, polite. "Who is that?" Kestrel asks. "Nobody." "It says 'Last Outpost, this is Vex. You have a guest. Return her, or we'll start asking your patrons very personal questions.'" I look at the comm, at Kestrel, at the same spot, polished like a little moon. "You didn't hear that," I say. "I heard it loud enough." "Good. Then you know the rules." "The rules are: no fights, no weapons, no talking about the past." "And no bringing trouble to the door." "I brought trouble to the door. I'm sorry. I didn't know the door was this quiet." "It's quiet because I keep it that way." "Then keep it that way." "I can't keep a ship out of the sky." "No. But you can keep me out of sight." The room leans in. Mirel, merchant in gold thread, watches from the end of the bar. Her fingers tap an expensive rhythm. "Mirel," I say, "you're buying a round if this gets ugly." "I'm buying a round if you let me buy a round." "Deal." Mirel smiles. "I like you, Nets. You're always so certain you're not involved." "I am not involved." "Yet." Kestrel's glass is empty. I pour another without being asked. "Tell me what you stole," I say. "A manifest. A list of ships that were paid to disappear. Vex's people think it's in a vault. It's not. It's in me." "Why?" "Because someone has to carry it, and I'm the only one who can hide it where they can't scan it." "Where's that?" "Inside the seed. It's not just data. It's a living archive. It feeds on heat. If I get scared, it sings louder." Her tentacles tremble. The whisky shivers. "Is it singing now?" "Yes." "Can you stop it?" "No. Can you?" "What happens if it sings too loud?" "It becomes a beacon. Vex will find me by the sound." "Then we need to make it stop." "I can't make it stop. I can only make it quieter." "Whisky?" "Help." "Whisky first." "You're the barkeeper." "I'm the only barkeeper." "That's what I thought." I wipe the same spot. Circle, circle, circle. "No," I say. Outside, the belt turns in slow, cold rings. Somewhere beyond the dust, a ship is holding position, patient as a debt. The bar's old heater coughs, and the ceiling lights flicker in a pattern I recognize all too well. The door opens. Cold air smells of dust and ozone. A man steps in, face too many angles, black coat hem steaming. "Last Outpost," he says. His voice is flat, but his eyes are not. "We're looking for a woman with tentacles and a bad habit of stealing." Kestrel goes very still. I keep wiping. "Sit down," I say to him. "Buy a drink. Then ask your questions." "I'm not here to drink." "Everyone's here to drink. That's the only law." He looks at Kestrel. The seed in her jacket hums, a thin wire about to snap. "Last chance," the man says. "Hand her over, and this place stays exactly as it is." I set the rag down, pick it up, wipe the same spot. "Ask me a question," I say. "If I like the answer, I'll tell you something." The man blinks. "What kind of question?" "Any question." "Where is she?" I smile, the smile I use when gravity plates act up. "I don't know who you're talking about." His eyes move to Kestrel. Her tentacles curl inward, a flower closing. "That," I say, "was the answer." The comm chimes again. Not Vex. The station's warning tone: outer doors sealing. Mirel stands. "Nets, you started this." "No," I say. "I'm just finishing the round." The door is closed, the light red, and the man reaches under his coat. I keep wiping the same spot on the bar counter. "Kestrel," I say, "if you have a plan, now's the time." "I have a seed, a whisky, and a very bad idea." "Good enough." The man's hand moves. I don't stop wiping.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece adheres well to the brief: first person, present tense, cozy sci-fi bar setting, roughly 60% dialogue, conflict (Vex's collector arriving) established and left unresolved at a cliffhanger. The voice is consistent — dry, laconic, bartender-as-observer — and the "wiping the same spot" motif works as a nervous tic, though it is repeated to the point of self-parody by the end. The worldbuilding touches (cinnamon coolant, gravity plates, data seed that feeds on heat) are economical and evocative. Weaknesses: the dialogue, while plentiful, is often stilted and overly aphoristic. Characters trade cryptic one-liners that sound alike — Kestrel, Nets, even the collector all speak in the same clipped, quippy register, flattening distinct voices. Several exchanges are confusing rather than intriguing ("First or second double?" / "First. The second one's for when I'm dead" is fine, but "I don't know who you're talking about" followed by "That was the answer" is muddled logic). The "singing seed" mechanic is introduced and then mostly dropped in favor of a generic standoff. The ending cliffhanger ("The man's hand moves. I don't stop wiping.") is serviceable tension but borders on formula. Some plot logic strains believability: Vex broadcasting over the comm to the whole bar undermines the "quiet" tone the narrator insists on, and Nets's rapid shift from refusal to complicity is undermotivated. Emotionally, the piece is cool to the point of detachment — engaging but not moving. + Young adult drama: Gone South — Score: 59.8
Prompt:
Young adult drama Gone South Taylor is a 16 year old teen with a history of "concerning behavioural patterns" (or that's how the stupid smug school counsellor worded it on the phone call to Mom). It shouldn't be a surprise: When you live in a backwater town in Tennessee, your choices are: a. be mind-fuckingly bored, or b. invent some drama. Two days ago, Taylor came out to their family as trans. This disclosure was *not* in the category of invented drama -- it was, in fact, the real deal, and a long time coming. It didn't go well. The last 48 hours had been pure disaster. In a moment of desperate inspiration, Taylor had decided to get the hell out of dodge. And so an escape plan was hatched and executed within the space of 30 minutes. That was last night. Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets. Taylor navigates this new world, not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are. Write in Taylor's voice, and incorporate their internal monologue as they grapple with intense & conflicting emotions. Also incorporate dialogue with the interesting characters Taylor meets. First person, mixed tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The strap on my backpack keeps slipping off my shoulder. Every time I tug it back, I feel like I'm pulling myself together. New Orleans hits different: river water, old paper, something sweet burning. The sun is too friendly. I have been here since last night, but my brain is still in the parking lot where the van driver tossed my duffel like I was garbage. "You're not going anywhere, kid." I am going somewhere. I'm here. My name is Taylor, but I haven't said it out loud in two days. In Tennessee, Taylor was a problem. In New Orleans, maybe it's just a name. I walk. My pockets are light. I have fourteen dollars, a dead phone, a wrong map, and a backpack that keeps trying to leave me. The strap slips. I tug it. My neck aches from holding my head up like I belong. I need water. I need a bathroom. I need to know if people are kind or dangerous. New Orleans makes you feel seen and sold. My mom said, "We don't have room for that in this family." Not "I'm scared." Not "I love you." Room. As if I were furniture. The backpack strap slips again. I catch it with both hands and stand there, looking ridiculous. "You're doing it wrong," someone says. I turn. A girl, maybe my age, sits on the curb. Dark hair, jagged. Yellow tank top, hole in the shoulder. Sneakers that look like they've crossed state lines. Her eyes are sharp. Maybe mean. Hard to tell. "Doing what wrong?" I ask. "Standing there like you're waiting for permission." She points at my backpack. "That thing's stealing your posture." I look down. The strap is hanging off one shoulder. "Thanks. I was just—" "Trying not to cry?" My throat closes. "No." "Okay. I'm Marisol." She says it like a door opening. I don't say my name. That feels important. "Taylor," I finally say. She nods. "Taylor. That's a good name for someone who's about to do something stupid." I almost laugh. "That's the first nice thing anyone's said to me in two days." Marisol's face changes, just a little. "Yeah? What did they say?" I tell her about the van driver. I don't tell her about my mom. Not yet. Marisol listens with her chin in her hands, and when I finish, she says, "You came to New Orleans with no plan." "It was a plan," I say. "It was a panic." "It was a plan made by panic." She grins. "I like that. I like panic." We walk together. She knows the city like a secret code. She tells me which corners to avoid, which people to pretend not to see, which places will let you drink fountain water. "The fountain near the old church," she says. "Nobody cares. The woman with the blue scarf? She'll give you a pretzel if you smile." "Why are you telling me this?" I ask. Marisol shrugs. "Because you're new and you look like you're about to make a mistake." "What mistake?" "Trusting the wrong person." I stop walking. "You're the wrong person?" Her grin fades. "Maybe. Maybe not. That's the fun part." I hate that I want to believe her. I hate that I'm so tired of being careful that I'd rather be scared and alive. My backpack strap slips. I tug it. Marisol notices. "You need a break," she says. We sit on a bench under a tree. Marisol pulls a granola bar out of her bag. It's bent. She offers me half. I take it. It tastes like cardboard and sugar, and I'm grateful. "Where are you from?" she asks. "Tennessee." "Backwater?" "Very." "Family problem?" I chew slowly. "Identity problem." She nods. "Oh. That's a family problem." I look at her. "You say that like you know." Marisol's eyes go away for a second. "I know a lot of things. I just don't get to use them." "Like what?" "Like how to disappear." My stomach drops. "You're a runaway?" She laughs, but it's thin. "Runaway, homeless, lost, escaped, temporarily misplaced. People use a lot of words for the same thing." "How long?" "Long enough to be good at it." I want to ask if she's safe. I want to ask if she has a place to sleep. I want to ask if she's ever been hurt. Instead I say, "Do you have money?" She looks at me. "No." "Me neither." We sit in the quiet. A dog barks. A bus hisses. Marisol picks at the granola bar wrapper. "I sleep in a church basement sometimes," she says. "Not all the time. Not all the churches. There's a woman there who asks questions, but she asks them like she wants to help, not like she wants to catch you." "Is that safe?" "Safe is a lie we tell ourselves so we can keep walking." I hate how true that sounds. My phone buzzes. I almost panic. It's a text from my mom: WHERE ARE YOU. I stare at the letters. My hands shake. I turn it off. Marisol sees. "You don't have to answer." "I don't know who to trust." She points at me. "Start with the person who gives you half a granola bar." "That's not a lot of trust." "It's a start." The sun starts to go down. New Orleans turns gold and purple. The air gets heavy. I feel the city pressing against me, all its music and heat and danger. I need a place to sleep. I need a shower. I need someone to tell me my name is okay. I need to be brave, but bravery feels like a coat that doesn't fit. Marisol stands. "Come on. I know a spot." "Where?" "You don't need to know yet." My backpack strap slips off my shoulder. I let it hang there for a second. Then I pick it up, tuck it under my arm, and follow her. I don't know if I'm making a mistake. I don't know if Marisol is kind or dangerous. I don't know if New Orleans will save me or swallow me. But for the first time in two days, I'm not walking alone, and that feels like a door cracking open. The street lights come on. Marisol's shadow stretches long in front of me. I step into it, and for now, that is enough. I am not alone tonight.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece follows the prompt reasonably well: first person, mixed tense, Taylor's voice, a day in New Orleans, a fellow runaway with hints of secrets, internal monologue, dialogue. The prose style is deliberately clipped and fragmentary — short declarative sentences, repeated motifs (the backpack strap, the name). This creates a distinctive voice, though at times it reads as mannered and self-consciously "literary minimalism," with the repetition becoming a tic rather than a device. The strap-slipping motif is used four or five times; once or twice would be effective. Strengths: the dialogue between Taylor and Marisol is often sharp and characterful ("It was a plan made by panic," "Safe is a lie we tell ourselves so we can keep walking"). Marisol is sketched with economy and has genuine intrigue. The emotional beats — the mother's "we don't have room for that in this family," the dead phone buzzing to life — land well. The ambivalence about trust is sustained rather than resolved, which is appropriate. Weaknesses: the fragmentary style flattens some emotional complexity into aphorism. Taylor's trans identity is handled almost too lightly — mentioned once, then mostly displaced by the runaway plot, which feels like a dodge. The ending leans warm ("I am not alone tonight") but this is earned by the granola-bar gesture, so it's acceptable, if slightly tidy. Some lines are overwrought ("bravery feels like a coat that doesn't fit," "New Orleans makes you feel seen and sold"). The plot is thin — walking, talking, following — though the prompt asked for exactly that. Marisol's "issues and secrets" are gestured at rather than developed, but the prompt only requires meeting her, so this is fine. Overall: a competent, voice-driven piece with genuine moments, held back by stylistic self-indulgence and slight emotional evasion. + Dystopic-comedy: My Apocalypse Buddy — Score: 70.2
Prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear. [characters] - the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time - midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. 1000 words.
Model Output:
My Apocalypse Buddy The end of the world had not arrived with thunder. It had arrived with administrative disappointment, as if the sky had filed a complaint and gone home. This was useful, Midas thought, because it meant there was no one to blame except everyone. He sat on a crate labelled FRAGILE in a language no one still spoke, staring at the valley below. The sun was doing its best, which meant shining through ash, old smoke, and the general suspicion that it had been replaced by a slightly less competent model. Chewy sat beside him. Chewy was a stuffed koala of animo-tronic construction, from the Before Time, when machines spoke while appearing to be made of felt, buttons, and optimistic fluff. His left ear was bent at an angle that suggested he had once witnessed a miracle and was still deciding whether to believe in it. “We need water,” Midas said. Chewy blinked his button eyes. “We need water,” Midas repeated, “because if we don’t find water, the goats will look at us with hope that usually precedes litigation.” Chewy’s panel glowed a cheerful blue. Then, in a voice like a radio station trapped in a friendly throat, he said, “Hydrate your dreams! Now with thirty percent more feeling!” “Quality assurance is a lifestyle,” Chewy added. Chewy had been found in a ruined shopping arcade, half-buried in shoes that once promised to walk you into tomorrow. He had been dead, or convincingly unconscious, until Midas kicked him while looking for fungus. Chewy had opened one eye and said, “Warranty void if seal is broken,” which had started a friendship neither fully understood. Home Base, a stone wall, a leaky roof, a goat, and the shared belief that the outside was worse, had been low on water for two days. The cistern leak appeared to be caused less by engineering failure and more by the universe making a point. The point was that he was bad at planning. “The spring is over the ridge,” Midas said. “We leave before the sun gets mean, fill the barrels, and are back before the goats unionize.” Chewy’s ears twitched. “Do not let your day be merely adequate.” “Thank you,” Midas said. “I’ll try to let it be adequately disastrous.” They set out with two barrels, a rope, a knife, a banner for Brainy Munchies, and confidence that was mostly decorative. The road had been swallowed by weeds and old vehicle bones. Midas had a knack for trouble, and the world arranged its hazards accordingly. The first problem was a ravine. It had not been there the previous week. Now it yawned across the path with the casual confidence of a chasm waiting for someone stupid to pass by. “Bridge,” Midas said. There was no bridge. There was, however, a tree, a rope, and a branch that looked as if it had been holding on out of spite. Chewy examined the branch. “This product has been tested by people who were not entirely awake.” Midas tied the rope to the branch, tested it, and tested it again, because testing was the only thing standing between him and the ground. He swung. For one brief, glorious moment, he was airborne. Then the branch made a sound like a disappointed accordion and let go. Midas landed in brambles that had clearly been waiting for him personally. He emerged, bleeding slightly, with a leaf in his hair and a new appreciation for other people’s decisions. Chewy, who had not swung, stood at the edge of the ravine, looking at him with the patience of a customer service representative. They found the spring, smaller, muddier, and more guarded than expected. A badger had established a presence there with the authority of a landlord who had never intended to leave. Midas attempted to negotiate. The badger attempted to bite his hand. The negotiation ended quickly. Chewy, seeing an opportunity to be useful, said, “Premium hydration for premium customers only.” Midas, not missing the chance, said, “What’s your name?” The badger did not answer. It looked at him with the irritation of a creature interrupted during a very important bite. In the end, they filled the barrels by taking turns: Midas held the badger at bay with a stick, and Chewy recited slogans until the badger, baffled, moved to a more promising patch of dirt. It was not a victory, exactly. It was the sort of thing that happened when two parties agreed to stop pretending. On the way home, the barrels became a problem. The first barrel broke on a rock. The second, which had been leaking from the beginning, developed a strategic reduction in capacity. The water sloshed out in a manner that suggested it had opinions. Chewy said, “Every drop counts.” They continued with the second barrel, now half-full, and a growing sense that the world was editing itself, removing inconvenient things until only the essentials remained. The essentials were Midas, Chewy, a goat that had followed them home, and a badger that had followed them out of curiosity. They reached Home Base in multiple ways, which was a phrase Midas used when he wanted to avoid explaining exactly how. First, he walked. Then he crawled. Then he rolled, because the goat had decided the barrel was a toy and the barrel had decided to be a wheel. Chewy, being animo-tronic, simply kept pace while emitting a soft, steady glow. Petra, the settlement’s only other resident, looked at them from the doorway. She kept the goats and the grudges. “You’re late.” “We had a ravine.” “And a badger.” “And a branch.” Chewy added, “Your day could be better.” Petra took the barrel, inspected it, and said, “Half the water, and a goat that thinks it owns us.” Midas looked at the goat. The goat chewed with the slow satisfaction of a creature that had been right all along. “I feel worse for wear,” Midas said. Chewy’s panel dimmed to amber. “You’re worth a warranty.” It was, he decided, the closest comfort left behind.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece delivers a Pratchett-adjacent wry tone with reasonable success: the animatronic koala spouting marketing slogans ("Warranty void if seal is broken," "Hydrate your dreams!") is a genuinely funny conceit, and the bureaucratic-apocalypse framing ("administrative disappointment") lands well. The structure follows the prompt: deliberation, mission gone sideways (ravine, badger, barrels), and return "in multiple ways" — the latter handled with a literal joke that acknowledges the prompt's odd phrasing, which is clever but slightly winking. Strengths: consistent dry voice, good comic similes ("patience of a customer service representative," "irritation of a creature interrupted during a very important bite"), economical worldbuilding, and a coherent arc. Chewy's slogan-speak is a strong running gag with a touching payoff ("You're worth a warranty"). Weaknesses: the story is underdeveloped in places. Petra appears abruptly near the end with no prior setup, making the ending feel rushed and the settlement's stakes unclear. The badger negotiation resolves too easily. Some jokes over-explain themselves ("which was a phrase Midas used when he wanted to avoid explaining exactly how" undercuts the joke rather than enhancing it). The prose occasionally tells rather than shows ("a growing sense that the world was editing itself"). The ending's emotional beat is nice but thin; the "closest comfort left behind" line is slightly muddled grammatically. Character interiority for Midas is minimal — he's a vehicle for gags more than a person. The word count is roughly on target. Dialogue is mostly functional; Chewy's lines are the highlight, Midas's are serviceable. Nothing is purple or overwrought; the tone stays controlled. The plot beats (ravine, badger, broken barrel) are predictable in a genre-familiar way, though executed with charm. Overall: a competent, amusing piece that fulfills the brief without transcending it. Mid-to-high scores for voice, coherence, and engagement; moderate deductions for thin characterization, rushed ending, and some unearned convenience. + Romance: Love in the Limelight — Score: 49.3
Prompt:
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write one scene within a larger story set in Wales. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The scene takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The bell over the door of Cwm Bookshop clanged just as the rain found the window. Rhys Vale came in sideways, hood up, sunglasses on, looking less like a man seeking shelter than a fugitive from a bad dream. Behind him, the street was already swelling with camera flashes. Elin was shelving poetry when she looked up. “We’re not a café,” she said. “And we don’t serve celebrity.” “I’m not asking for a flat white,” he said, voice too smooth for the narrow shop. “Just thirty seconds. Maybe a minute if you’re feeling merciful.” “I’ll pay for the minute.” “Deal.” “Thirty seconds is a lot of money in a place this size.” “I’ll buy the shop. I’ll buy the poetry, the postcards, the little ceramic dragon by the till.” Elin glanced at the dragon. “He’s not for sale.” “Of course he isn’t. He has taste.” “He has a chipped horn. That’s not taste, that’s history.” Rhys lowered the sunglasses just enough for her to see his eyes. “I like chipped things,” he said. “They’ve been somewhere.” “Everything in this shop has been somewhere. That’s rather the point.” From outside, a shutter clicked. Then another. “Can you dim the lights?” “Please.” “We can’t keep the lights down. We’re a bookshop.” “I know what you are. I can see the shelves.” He turned back to her. “You’re the owner?” “I’m the owner, the stockist, the cleaner, and the person who will politely ask you to leave if you block the doorway.” “It does look like a film still.” “That’s because you’re blocking the display of Welsh nature writing.” “Nature writing. My favourite.” “Don’t say that. You’re going to say you love it because it sounds calm and green and nothing like your life.” He smiled, but it didn’t land. “You’re perceptive.” “Mostly.” “I’m a bookseller. We read people for a living. Most of them need a novel before they need a drink.” A flash went off outside. Rhys’s jaw tightened. “Right. So. If I don’t leave, what do I do?” Elin looked at him, then at the window, then at the narrow gap behind the poetry shelves. “You can hide in the back. There’s a stockroom. It smells of damp cardboard and regret, but the paparazzi won’t go in there.” “Regret? You keep regret in stock too?” “It’s seasonal.” He followed her, brushing his shoulder against a shelf of travel guides. “Quietly.” She led him through a gap in the books and into a low room where boxes were stacked to the ceiling. A model railway ran along the top of a workbench, curving around a miniature slate quarry and a tiny chapel with a white door. Rhys stopped. For once, the charm went out of his voice. “Is that a gauge one?” Elin looked at him. “You know gauge one?” “I know it’s not gauge zero. I can tell by the ballast.” She stared. “Ballast?” “Little stones. You fake it with grit, but proper ballast is sorted by size and colour.” He was already crouching by the bench, careful, as if the whole world had narrowed to the track. “That quarry is good. Did you do the weathering yourself?” “Mostly.” “Mostly? That’s a bit like saying the sea is mostly wet.” Elin felt something warm and inconvenient move behind her ribs. She crossed her arms. “I painted the chapel at two in the morning after a delivery van broke down. So don’t make it sound like art.” “It sounds like art.” “It sounds like a woman losing an argument with a ladder.” He looked up, and his smile was smaller now. “Do you do a lot of things at two in the morning?” “Enough to know how they taste.” Outside, the rain drummed on the skylight. In the shop front, a camera flash strobed again, but the sound was muffled, distant. Rhys ran a finger along the edge of the track without touching the train. “I built one once. Terrible. I was on location in Cornwall, bored, and I thought, what’s the worst thing a famous man can do in a quiet village?” “Buy a model railway and make a mess of it.” “And?” “I made a mess of it.” “Naturally.” “Of course you did.” “Then I fixed it. Badly. But I fixed it.” He looked at her. “Do you fix things badly?” “Only when I’m being modest.” “Ah. There it is.” “Don’t ‘there it is’ me.” He grinned, but it was a real grin, the kind that made his face look younger and less like a cover. “You like the trains.” “I like making small things that don’t need me to perform for them.” The words came out sharper than she intended. Rhys didn’t flinch. “That’s a very honest thing to say in a room full of books.” “Too true.” “Books don’t ask you to be charming.” “No, but they do ask you to be still.” She looked at the miniature chapel again. The white door was no bigger than her thumbnail. “Stillness is overrated.” “Is it? Or do you just pretend it is because you’re afraid of what you might hear if you stopped moving?” The silence between them changed. Elin felt it land in her chest before she could argue with it. “You read too much,” she said. “I read what I need to.” “And what do you need?” He was quiet for a moment. “To be liked. It’s embarrassing, isn’t it? For someone who looks like this.” He gestured vaguely at his own face. “Everyone thinks I’m full of myself. And I am, a little. But mostly I’m just hungry for the next yes.” “The next smile that isn’t for the cameras. The next person who’ll look at me and not see the name first.” Elin studied him. The famous face was there, yes, but so was the man crouched by the model railway, careful with his hands. “You’re not very good at this,” she said. “At what?” “Being honest. You do it like a bad accent.”
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The scene delivers its premise competently: a famous actor, Rhys Vale, ducks into a Welsh bookshop fleeing paparazzi, and the owner, Elin, deflects his charm while quietly succumbing to it. There are genuine pleasures here — the ceramic dragon with the chipped horn ("that's not taste, that's history"), and the model railway detour, which is the scene's best invention. The railway gives Rhys something to be sincere about, and his confession about needing to be liked is the emotional pivot the prompt requested. However, the piece has significant craft problems. Most damaging is the dialogue formatting: long stretches of unattributed lines run together in single paragraphs, and the reader repeatedly loses track of who is speaking. In several exchanges the speakers appear to swap mid-paragraph, and some lines ("I'll pay for the minute" / "Deal") read as if both belong to one speaker. For a prompt that explicitly asks for "primarily dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character," this is a serious failure — the two voices are not clearly distinct, both trading in the same dry, clipped wit, and the muddled attribution makes an already-similar dialogue harder to follow. The railway subplot, while charming, is also a bit of a cheat: it's a convenient shared-interest device that accelerates intimacy faster than the scene has earned, and Rhys's knowledge of gauge one and ballast arrives from nowhere. Elin's internal fluster is mostly told ("Elin felt something warm and inconvenient move behind her ribs") rather than shown through behavior. The scene also simply stops rather than resolves — no ending beat, no exit from the stockroom, no return to the paparazzi threat — leaving the piece feeling truncated, like an excerpt of an excerpt. The prose itself is serviceable and occasionally sharp, with Welsh texture (slate quarry, chapel) used well, though the setting is thin beyond the stockroom. Rhys's confession is the strongest moment but is delivered a touch too neatly, and Elin's "You do it like a bad accent" is a good closing jab undermined by the abruptness of the cut.
